**Vân-pui Sai-hrua** — Mizo (Lushai) (the Lushai Hills, Assam (now Mizoram)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Lorrain names the stars: Castor and Pollux in Gemini, Procyon in Canis Minor, Sirius, and a few others. The first element vân-pui is the great vault overhead.

> Vân-pui Sai-hrua, n . the name of a constellation—a bow-like configuration formed by Castor and Pollox in Gemini, Procyon in Canis Minor, Sirius, and a few other stars.
> <br>— J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Vân-pui Sai-hrua, p. 544 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/lorrain_query.py?page=544))

<sub>Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A figure drawn ACROSS three modern constellations, which is what makes Lorrain's list worth having: he maps the Lushai sky onto the Western one star by star instead of assuming they divide it the same way.</sub>

**Letung (A); Wachi ala puzya (B); Aochi (C)** — Rengma Naga (the Rengma country, Naga Hills (now Nagaland), and the Mikir Hills) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

A girl and her lover who ran away together. The Western Rengmas say he is cutting a stick for her.

> Castor and Pollux are Letung (A), Wachi ala puzya (B), Aochi (C). They are a girl and her lover who ran away together. The Western Rengmas say he is cutting a stick for her.
> <br>— J.P. Mills, The Rengma Nagas (London: Macmillan, 1937), p. 245 ([source](https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.3979))

<sub>The eloping pair joins the Lushei Chongmawi and Hrangchhuana, who are also lovers and also two bright stars, and the Garo sisters and Angami Star-Girls, who are not. Mills letters his three Rengma languages: (A) the southern section of the Western Rengmas, (B) the northern section of the Western Rengmas, (C) the Eastern Rengmas. The letters are reproduced from his own key at p. xv.</sub>

**स्वस्तिक · svastika** — Hindi (Pan-Hindi (national print)) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

The book's भारतीय नाम for the constellation in its complete 88-constellation concordance. Muley himself notes (p. ~16) that uniform Indian names across languages were still to be settled — the set is part report of circulating usage, part proposal. Prose: 'त्रिशंकु या स्वस्तिक के नाम से भी जाना जाता है', plus the suggestion that ancient India may have known the figure as शूल.

*No quotation: Gunakar Muley, Akash Darshan (New Delhi: Rajkamal Prakashan, 1993), Appendix 4, 'Tara-mandal suchi', pp. 344-347, and p. ~132 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*

## Antares

**Modern:** Antares · α Scorpii · Scorpius  
**Sanskrit database:** `jyeshtha` — Jyeṣṭhā (Antares) ([entry](../star-names/star-names.json))  
**Named in 6 languages:** Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Santali, Sinhala, Telugu

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Telugu | తాటిరిక్క | *tāṭi-rikka* | the palmyra star | vernacular |
| Marathi | अडवण्या | *aḍavaṇyā* | the obstructors / hinderers | folk |
| Santali | — | *Argom* | a clod-crusher, a harrow without teeth | tribal |
| Kannada | ಜೇಟೆ | *jēṭe* | — | borrowed |
| Malayalam | കേട്ട / തൃക്കേട്ട | *kēṭṭa / tṛkkēṭṭa* | തൃ- (< തിരു) is the honorific 'sacred' | borrowed |
| Sinhala | දෙට, දෙටු | *deṭa, deṭu* | — | borrowed |

**తాటిరిక్క · tāṭi-rikka** — Telugu (Telugu country (Madras Presidency: Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema, Telangana)) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

The month Jyeṣṭha is named from it: tāṭi-rikka-nela.

> తాటి or తాడి [Tel. Infl. of తాడు.] adj. Belonging to the palmyra tree. … తాటిరిక్క the constellation called జ్యేష్ఠా. తాటిరిక్కనెల the month called జ్యేష్ఠి మాసము.
> <br>— Brown, C. P., A Telugu-English Dictionary, new ed., thoroughly revised and brought up to date (Madras: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, 1903), s.v. తాటి tāṭi, p. 521 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/brown_query.py?page=521))

<sub>This is one of a complete set of Telugu descriptive names for the lunar mansions that Brown records piecemeal under their first elements. They are formed X-cukka / X-rikka ('X-star') or X-rūpu-rikka ('X-shaped star'), and are entirely independent of the Sanskrit names, which Telugu also has. Motivation not stated by Brown; the palmyra fruits in Jyeṣṭha in the Telugu country, which is the likeliest link, but this is inference and is not asserted here.</sub>

**अडवण्या · aḍavaṇyā** — Marathi (Maharashtra) · *folk* · confidence: certain

names both the asterism and the rain that falls under it

> अडवण्या aḍavaṇyā f pl (अडविणें) A term for ज्येष्ठानक्षत्र and for the rain which falls under it.
> <br>— J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. अडवण्या, p. 17 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%85%E0%A4%A1%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%A3%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>One of a set of Marathi cultivators' names in which a nakṣatra is renamed for what its rains DO to the crop. From अडविणें 'to obstruct'. Molesworth carries a second, homophonous headword अडवण्या 'that obstructs or hinders' immediately after, confirming the derivation.</sub>

**Argom** — Santali (Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha) · *tribal* · confidence: likely

A farming implement seen in the sky: three stars in a line with a fourth at the apex.

> Argom. A constellation so named. It is part of the constellation Scorpio, and is composed of 4 stars, three of which are in line, and the other at the apex of the triangle. The star at the apex is Antares, or cor scorpii, a star of 1st. magnitude.
> <br>— Campbell, A Santali-English Dictionary (1899), s.v. Argom, p. 20 ([source](https://archive.org/download/cu31924096339464/cu31924096339464_djvu.txt))

<sub>Deliberately not equated with Jyeṣṭhā: the nakshatra is Antares with σ and τ Sco, whereas Argom is a four-star harrow whose apex happens to be Antares. Campbell's separate homonym entry Argom 'a clod crusher, a harrow without teeth' fixes the literal sense.</sub>

**ಜೇಟೆ · jēṭe** — Kannada (Karnataka (Mysore, Canara, Deccan)) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

> ಜೇಟೆ jēṭe. = ಜೆಷ್ಟೆ. Tbh. of ಜ್ಯೇಷ್ಠೆ (Śmd. 370).
> <br>— Kittel, F., A Kannaḍa-English Dictionary (orig. Mangalore: Basel Mission, 1894); cited from the revised and enlarged edition, [Madras] University of Madras, 1968-71, as keyed for DSAL, s.v. ಜೇಟೆ jēṭe, p. 696 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/kittel_query.py?page=696))

<sub>REPRESENTATIVE FORM. Compare Telugu జెష్ట jeṣṭa (Brown p. 469), which Brown says has drifted from 'elder sister' to 'a plague, a pest, gibberish' — the same tadbhava, but in Telugu it has left the sky and become an insult. Kittel's tatsama ಜ್ಯೇಷ್ಠೆ (p. 701) is the astronomical one: 'the eighteenth lunar mansion, being a part of scorpio'.</sub>

**കേട്ട / തൃക്കേട്ട · kēṭṭa / tṛkkēṭṭa** — Malayalam (Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore)) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

Tṛkkēṭṭa is one of the inauspicious birth-stars in Kerala reckoning; Gundert lists it under ഗണ്ഡാന്തം (p. 329), the perilous junctions of the asterism cycle.

> കേട്ട kēṭṭa kēṭṭa തൃക്കേട്ട T. M. (Tdbh., ജ്യേഷ്ഠ; ചേ ട്ട Pandora) The 18th lunar asterism in Scorpion.
> <br>— Gundert, A Malayalam and English Dictionary (1872), s.v. കേട്ട kēṭṭa, p. 293 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/gundert_query.py?qs=%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%87%E0%B4%9F%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9F&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>Gundert's parenthesis '(ചേട്ട Pandora)' refers to Cēṭṭā/Jyeṣṭhā the goddess of misfortune, whom he likens to Pandora — the asterism and the ill-luck goddess share the name. Gundert gives no separate name for Antares as a star apart from the asterism.</sub>

**දෙට, දෙටු · deṭa, deṭu** — Sinhala (Sri Lanka) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

> දෙට, දෙටු deṭa, deṭu , a . E. of ජ්‍යේෂ්ඨ .
> <br>— Carter, A Sinhalese-English Dictionary (Colombo, 1924), s.v. දෙට, දෙටු deṭa, deṭu, p. 297 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/carter_query.py?qs=%E0%B6%AF%E0%B7%99%E0%B6%A7&matchtype=default&searchhws=yes))

<sub>Carter's 'E. of' = 'Eḷu form of' (verified against Carter's own abbreviation key), i.e. Sanskrit jyeṣṭha in Sinhala phonology. Clough anchors the asterism to the sky: 'Jyeshthá ... the eighteenth, comprising three stars of which one is [α] Scorpionis figured by a ring or earring' (p. 196). Antares itself has no independent Sinhala name — Jayatilaka's only entry is the twentieth-century English loanword අන්ටරේස් anṭarēs, '[lw. Eng. Antares]' (p. 317).</sub>

**Daatiya / Daatlo** — Bhili (Bhil villages, north-western Maharashtra) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

If the Moon passes beside Leo it is a good omen; if it merely grazes the head of Leo, a bad one.

*No quotation: Shreya Shetye, Ganesh Halkare and Aniket Sule, 'Bhil, Pawra and Kokna astronomy', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 26(2), 441-468 (2023), p. 464 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— Shreya Shetye, Ganesh Halkare and Aniket Sule, 'Bhil, Pawra and Kokna astronomy', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 26(2), 441-468 (2023), p. 464 ([source](https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/2023JAHH...26..441S))

<sub>In copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, the convention this database already uses for the Gondi entries in tribal.json. The survey covered 210 people in 17 meetings across the Bhil, Mavchi Bhil, Vasave Bhil, Pawra and Kokna communities of north-western Maharashtra. tribal.json recorded 'Bhili: nothing' and named this paper as a lead it could not obtain; this entry closes that gap. The Sickle of Leo is also the Western asterism name, arrived at independently: the curve of Regulus, Eta, Algieba, Zeta, Mu and Epsilon Leonis really does look like a reaping hook. The digital text of this paper is unreadable — the embedded font subsets carry no ToUnicode map, so extraction yields a substitution cipher, and several different ciphers at that. Every Bhil, Pawra and Kokna reading in this file was therefore taken from a rendered page image, not from extracted text.</sub>

**Murda; Duf; Shika; Ladavya** — Gondi (Nagpur region: Chandrapur, Yavatmal, Gondia (Maharashtra), Adilabad (Telangana), Balaghat, Seoni, Mandla (Madhya Pradesh)) · *tribal* · confidence: likely

The body of Leo is a dead man, head at Eta Leonis, one hand at Algieba and the other at Regulus, legs at Delta and Theta Leonis. Delta Leonis is the pall-bearer, the stars of Virgo are the procession, and the whole thing moves west to east across the sky.

*No quotation: Vahia & Halkare, 'Aspects of Gond Astronomy', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 16(1), 29-44 (2013); preprint arXiv:1306.2416 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— Vahia & Halkare, 'Aspects of Gond Astronomy', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 16(1), 29-44 (2013); preprint arXiv:1306.2416 ([source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.2416))

<sub>In copyright: paraphrased throughout and never quoted, per this compilation's rules, so the quote field is null. The survey covered 15 Gond villages in March 2011, with identifications checked by projecting a sky chart for the informants and later in a planetarium, which is why the modern identifications are given as reported. The most elaborate narrative constellation in the Gond material and one with no counterpart in the nakshatra system, which cuts this stretch of sky into Maghā, Pūrva- and Uttara-Phalgunī with quite different figures.</sub>

The Arabic name that gives English 'Vega'. Its pair, nasru'ṭ-ṭāʼir 'the flying eagle', is Altair; Platts calls the dual nasrain 'the constellations of the Eagle and the Lyre'.

> A نسر nasr , s.m. A vulture; — an eagle: — nasruʼt̤-t̤āʼir, or nasr-ě-t̤āʼir, s.m. 'The flying eagle,' the constellation of the Eagle: — nasruʼl-wāqěʻ, s.m. 'The falling vulture,' the constellation of the Lyre.

<sub>confidence likely rather than certain because Platts glosses the terms as constellations (Lyra, Aquila) whereas in Arabic usage they name the bright stars Vega and Altair. name_native gives the headword نسر only; the compounds are printed in roman.</sub>

**Bele kombro** — Santali (Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha) · *tribal* · confidence: likely

<sub>Campbell himself hedges ('probably Vega'), so the identification is his and is graded likely. The compound is transparent from his own entries: 'Bele. An egg', and kombro 'thief'. The final syllable of kombro is illegible in both Internet Archive scans (printed 'kombroio' and 'kombroiii').</sub>

**Potam bele** — Santali (Santal Parganas, Jharkhand / adjoining Bengal and Odisha) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

<sub>potam is the imperial pigeon, Carpophaga sylvatica (Campbell s.v.), bele an egg. The bird-and-eggs motif recurs across the whole set with different stars attached: Mundari puts the dove at Aldebaran with two egg stars beside it, Gondi puts Purad and Mes east of Sirius. Santali is the only one that also supplies the thief.</sub>

One of the Sanskrit names for the Western constellations that Dikshit credits to Bal Shastri Jambhekar (d. 1846) and reports as current: 'पाश्चात्यांनीं कल्पिलेल्या बाकीच्या राशींस संस्कृत संज्ञा शास्त्री जांभेकर यांनीं दिल्या आहेत. त्याच हल्लीं मराठींत येतात.' (p. 35-36). The eighth-magnitude star of 1885 is S Andromedae; the great nebula in the same पुंज is described at p. 186.

> सन १८६६ मध्यें उत्तरमुकुटांत दुसऱ्या प्रतीची, सन १८७६ मध्यें हंसराशींत तिसऱ्या प्रतीची, व सन १८८५ मध्यें देवयानी पुंजांत आठव्या प्रतीची, अशा तारा दिसत होत्या.

**Manganchi** — Garo (the Garo Hills, Assam (now Meghalaya)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

The four upright posts between which the wood for the cremation was heaped; the brightest of the four is the post to which the sacrificial buffalo was tethered.

> (11) Manganchi (Square of Pegasus) represents the four upright posts between which the wood for the cremation was heaped up. The brightest of the four stars is said to represent the post to which the buffalo for sacrifice was tethered.
> <br>— Major A. Playfair, The Garos (London: David Nutt, 1909), p. 86–87 ([source](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.500276))

<sub>The Mundas see the same four stars as Singbonga's bedstead and the Lakhers as a sheet of bamboo matting. All three read the square as a made rectangular thing; only Garo reads it as four separate uprights and singles out the brightest.</sub>

**Samdur** — Kolami (Kolam villages of Yavatmal and Chandrapur districts, Vidarbha, Maharashtra, and adjoining Adilabad, Telangana) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Eight of ten villages. Animal asterisms are seen around the Square — a peacock, a buffalo, a frog, a deer, a horse and sometimes a pig — and their relative brightness is taken to forecast the strength of the coming rain.

*No quotation: M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 2, p. 71 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 2, p. 71 ([source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3044))

<sub>In copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, the convention this database already uses for the Gondi entries in tribal.json. One of the items in the paper's Table 2, which records for each belief how many of the ten Kolam villages surveyed reported it. The Kolams were foragers until about fifty years before the survey. A rain-gauge built out of a constellation. CORRECTED: this entry previously said that no name is printed for the individual animals. Table 2 prints none, but the appendix names all of them — Namli the peacock, Barre the buffalo, Pande the frog, Mekam the deer, Gurram the horse and Ture the pig — and they are now six entries of their own, with the recorders' suggested constellations carried as disputed.</sub>

**maraṅ parkom ipilko; Siṅgboṅga gitikente parkom ipilko** — Mundari (Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

On so great and splendid a bed none but Siṅgboṅga can be supposed to sleep.

> A great bed is seen there, viz., the Great Square delineated by Alpharatz in Andromeda, and Scheat, Markab, Algenib in Pegasus. These four stars are the maraṅ parkom ipilko, also called Siṅgboṅga gitikenteą parkom ipilko
> <br>— Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925 ([source](https://archive.org/download/dli.bengal.10689.20088/10689.20088_djvu.txt))

<sub>parkom is the same string cot that Santali makes into the old woman's bed in Ursa Major. The Mundas run the cot image through four parts of the sky: the god's bed here, the co-wives' bed in Lupus, the bier in Ursa Major, and the watchman's pallet implied by the ember stars.</sub>

*No quotation: Gunakar Muley, Akash Darshan (New Delhi: Rajkamal Prakashan, 1993), Appendix 4, 'Tara-mandal suchi', pp. 344-347, and p. ~289 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— Gunakar Muley, Akash Darshan (New Delhi: Rajkamal Prakashan, 1993), Appendix 4, 'Tara-mandal suchi', pp. 344-347, and p. ~289 ([source](https://archive.org/details/akash-gunakar))

<sub>Paraphrased, no quote: the book is in copyright (© Shanti Gunakar Muley, first ed. February 1993). Name read from the printed भारतीय नाम column of the Appendix 4 table on the scan's page images (leaves 172-173). The book grew from serials in Navbharat Times (1988-89) and Saptahik Hindustan (1991-92), so the names reached a national Hindi readership.</sub>

**शर्मिष्ठा · śarmiṣṭhā** — Marathi (Maharashtra) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

One of the Sanskrit names for the Western constellations that Dikshit credits to Bal Shastri Jambhekar (d. 1846) and reports as current: 'पाश्चात्यांनीं कल्पिलेल्या बाकीच्या राशींस संस्कृत संज्ञा शास्त्री जांभेकर यांनीं दिल्या आहेत. त्याच हल्लीं मराठींत येतात.' (p. 35-36).

> इ० स० १५७२ च्या नोव्हेंबरपासून सुमारें १६ महिने वृषपर्वा व शर्मिष्ठा ह्यांच्या मध्यें एक प्रदीप्त तारा दिसत होती.
> <br>— S. B. Dikshit, Jyotirvilas, 2nd ed. (Bombay, 1893; 1st ed. 1892), p. 182 ([source](https://archive.org/details/india.history.resource.92658))

<sub>Quote transcribed verbatim from the scan's page images (leaf = printed page + 25 up to p. 40, + 30 in the taraka chapter), not from the OCR layer, which garbles conjuncts here. Tycho's 1572 supernova placed between Cassiopeia and Cepheus.</sub>

**Mangripe** — Garo (the Garo Hills, Assam (now Meghalaya)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

The bearing of the corpse to the funeral pyre — the opening scene of the funeral of the moon's mother, which is the single story the Garo sky tells.

> (1) Mangripe (Cassiopeia, lit. the carrying of the bedy) represents the bearing of the body to the funeral pyre.
> <br>— Major A. Playfair, The Garos (London: David Nutt, 1909), p. 86 ([source](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.500276))

<sub>'bedy' is the scan's damage for 'body', which the same sentence prints correctly two words later. THE GARO SKY IS ONE NARRATIVE. Fourteen names, and all but the two Venus names belong to a single funeral: the cremation of Norekbak-Norekding, also called Asima-Dingsima, mother of Susime the moon. No other tradition in this database organises its whole star-list as episodes of one event.</sub>

**Namli / Namali** — Kolami (Kolam villages of Yavatmal and Chandrapur districts, Vidarbha, Maharashtra, and adjoining Adilabad, Telangana) · *tribal* · confidence: disputed

One of the five or six animals that stand around Samdur and forecast the monsoon by their brightness. Landgi Pod reads the peacock as a bad sign, Chinchpod as less rain, Kakban as less rain. Six of the ten villages knew the animals.

*No quotation: M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 2 row 12, p. 71, and Appendix 1.2.2 (Janguguda), p. 80 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 2 row 12, p. 71, and Appendix 1.2.2 (Janguguda), p. 80 ([source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3044))

The identification is the recorders' own suggestion, offered in one sentence at Janguguda and not attributed to the informants, so the confidence is set to disputed and the suggestion is carried in modern_star rather than asserted. From the village-by-village appendix rather than the summary tables, which is where most of the Kolam and Banjara vocabulary actually is; the appendix was re-read after Vahia, Yadav and Menon's NCSM book (see the caveats) showed that this compilation had worked from the tables alone.</sub>

**Sohlu vang araipa** — Mara (Lakher) (the Lakher country, southern Lushai Hills (now southern Mizoram) and the Chin Hills) · *tribal* · confidence: disputed

Five stars formed out of four men and a flying fox's skin which they were stretching out to dry when the great darkness descended.

> Sohlu vang araipa is a constellation of five stars formed out of four men and a flying fox's skin which they were stretching out to dry when the great darkness descended on the world. This is possibly Cassiopeia.
> <br>— N.E. Parry, The Lakhers (London: Macmillan, 1932), p. 496 ([source](https://archive.org/details/lakhers032949mbp))

<sub>Five stars in a W, read as four men holding a skin stretched between them. The Garos read the same five as a corpse being carried. Khazanghra, also called Thimzing, is the Lakher 'great darkness', the mythical eclipse at which everything then alive was turned to stone or to stars. Nearly every Lakher star-name below is an episode interrupted by it.</sub>

**Gongpatad; Beduk** — Kolami (Kolam villages of Yavatmal and Chandrapur districts, Vidarbha, Maharashtra, and adjoining Adilabad, Telangana) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

The colour of a lunar eclipse tells you which creature is eating the Moon: pale if it is the caterpillar Gongpatad, dark if it is the frog Beduk. Bhimnala reverses the pair, giving red for the scorpion and black for the frog.

*No quotation: M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Appendix 1.2.6 (Landgi Pod), p. 82 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Appendix 1.2.6 (Landgi Pod), p. 82 ([source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3044))

<sub>In copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, the convention this database already uses for the Gondi entries in tribal.json. The Kolam solar eclipse is a debt being collected and is already in this file; the lunar eclipse is an animal at its meal, and the shade of red is the evidence for which animal. A forecast run backwards — the sky is read to identify the creature rather than the creature to predict the sky. From the village-by-village appendix rather than the summary tables, which is where most of the Kolam and Banjara vocabulary actually is; the appendix was re-read after Vahia, Yadav and Menon's NCSM book (see the caveats) showed that this compilation had worked from the tables alone.</sub>

**Āwk** — Mizo (Lushai) (the Lushai Hills, Assam (now Mizoram)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

The verb is impersonal and takes the creature as subject: 'the Āwk eclipses the sun'.

> Āwk, n . the name of a fabulous creature which is supposed to swallow the sun or moon at the time of an eclipse. Some say that the awk is the spirit of a Pawi chieftain. Āwkin a lem, Āwkin ni a lem, Āwkin thla a lem. [and] âwk lem, n . an eclipse; ni âwk lem, a solar eclipse; thla âwk lem, a lunar eclipse.
> <br>— J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Āwk, p. 20 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/lorrain_query.py?page=20))

<sub>Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. The Indian eclipse-swallower is Rāhu everywhere in the Sanskritic material; the Mizo one is a named local ghost, the spirit of a Pawi chief. Creates the object 'Eclipses' in this database, which had none.</sub>

**Giran** — Pardhi (fourteen Pardhi villages of the Amravati and Yeotmal districts, Vidarbha, Maharashtra, surveyed 2016-2018) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Glossed with Marathi grahaṇ. Solar and lunar eclipses were reported in ten villages each, a story about them in six, and an omen — bad in eight villages, good in three — in eleven.

*No quotation: Ganesh Halkare, Purushottam Dahedar, Wayne Orchiston and M.N. Vahia, 'Astronomy of the Pardhi tribe of central India', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 22(1), 179-194 (2019), Table 4, p. 184 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— Ganesh Halkare, Purushottam Dahedar, Wayne Orchiston and M.N. Vahia, 'Astronomy of the Pardhi tribe of central India', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 22(1), 179-194 (2019), Table 4, p. 184 ([source](https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/2019JAHH...22..179H))

<sub>Giran is Sanskrit grahaṇa worn down, and is the one plainly borrowed word in the Pardhi sky. That eleven villages read an omen from it and three of them read a good one is the sort of split the single-village sources in this database cannot show. In copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, on the convention this file uses throughout. The paper prints each name in Devanagari as well as roman; name_native is null because the Devanagari in the available scan cannot be read with the confidence this database requires of a native-script field, exactly as for the Korku and Bhil entries.</sub>

**(figure recorded, name not)** — Rengma Naga (the Rengma country, Naga Hills (now Nagaland), and the Mikir Hills) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

When the sun is eclipsed it is believed that some very great man has died somewhere; the moon is eclipsed when a tiger eats it.

> When there is an eclipse of the sun it is believed that some very great man has died somewhere. The moon is eclipsed when a tiger eats it.
> <br>— J.P. Mills, The Rengma Nagas (London: Macmillan, 1937), p. 245 ([source](https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.3979))

<sub>ENTERED WITHOUT A NAME, on the same footing as the two nameless entries already in this file: Mills gives the belief and no Rengma word, and the belief is worth the record because it splits the two eclipses between two entirely different causes. The eater is a tiger here, a dog among the Lakhers, an awk among the Mizo, and Rāhu everywhere on the mainland.</sub>

**ކޭތަ · keytha** — Divehi (Mahl) (the Maldives, and Minicoy (Maliku) in Lakshadweep, which speaks the same language and keeps the same calendar) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

Maniku glosses it 'eclipse, occultation' and derives it from Sinhala ketu, the dragon's tail or descending node.

*No quotation: Hassan Ahmed Maniku, A Concise Etymological Vocabulary of Dhivehi Language, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka, Special Volume XLIV (Colombo, 2000), s.v. keytha, p. 144 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*

<sub>In copyright, so the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null. The comet-word doing duty for the eclipse. Kashmiri kēth in northwest.json is the same Sanskrit ketu used for a comet and for the descending node; Divehi has narrowed it to the event itself.</sub>

RAKSHAS DISHA IS THE PARDHI WORD TOO. The Pardhi southern quarter in tribal_fieldwork.json is rakshasbaku, the demons' quarter, and the Gonds of Lodha call the same quarter Rakshas Disha. Gondi is Dravidian and Pardhi Indo-Aryan; both take the south from the same Sanskrit rākṣasa, and both put the demons there while the Gonds put the bad people in the north. The two traditions disagree about which end of the axis is dangerous. Entered on a re-read of the paper prompted by Vahia, Yadav and Menon's NCSM book (see the caveats), whose Table 4.2 condenses this row and made its absence here visible.</sub>

Dubaguda gives north Telganam and south Kalam; Kakban gives north Kaland and south Telagnaam. **Aphilu** — Mara (Lakher) (the Lakher country, southern Lushai Hills (now southern Mizoram) and the Chin Hills) · *tribal* · confidence: disputed

Four stars representing the corners of a piece of bamboo matting, which was being made when the great darkness fell.

> Aphilu is a constellation of four stars, representing the corners of a piece of bamboo matting, which was being made when Khazanghra fell, and the matting was turned into stars. This is possibly the Square of Pegasus.
> <br>— N.E. Parry, The Lakhers (London: Macmillan, 1932), p. 496 ([source](https://archive.org/details/lakhers032949mbp))

<sub>'Possibly' is Parry's and the grade follows it. Three unrelated traditions read this square as something woven or built flat: Lakher matting, Garo four cremation posts, Mundari a bedstead with a fire under it. Khazanghra, also called Thimzing, is the Lakher 'great darkness', the mythical eclipse at which everything then alive was turned to stone or to stars. Nearly every Lakher star-name below is an episode interrupted by it.</sub>

**bursi ipilko** — Mundari (Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand) · *tribal* · confidence: likely

The dying embers of the fire the threshing-floor watchman keeps under his cot on cold nights. Hoffmann adds that Mundas who do not know the maraṅ parkom group transfer the name to the Pleiades.

> Near the middle of the Great Square there are a few small stars, amongst which Upsilon and Tau, just numerous enough to suggest a fire of dying embers. So these are the bursi ipilko.
> <br>— Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925 ([source](https://archive.org/download/dli.bengal.10689.20088/10689.20088_djvu.txt))

<sub>Also entered separately at vol. II s.v. Bursi-ipilko, 'a group of stars described under ipil'. The transferred use for the Pleiades is recorded by Hoffmann as a mistake of his informants, which is itself worth keeping.</sub>

**bursi kumbuṛu ipilko (bursi repą ipilkiŋ)** — Mundari (Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand) · *tribal* · confidence: likely

Three men creep up on a sleeping watchman to steal embers from the fire under his cot; two of them are these stars, lying west of the bed on a line pointing at the fire.

> The fire thieves, bursi repą ipilkiŋ, are Lambda and Iota to the West of the bed, on a line pointing to the fire.
> <br>— Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925 ([source](https://archive.org/download/dli.bengal.10689.20088/10689.20088_djvu.txt))

<sub>Two names for the same pair: Encyclopaedia Mundarica vol. II gives the headword Bursi-kumbuṛu-ipilko (kumbuṛu 'thief'), the ipil article gives bursi repą ipilkiŋ (repą 'to steal from one another').</sub>

## Seasonal and agricultural star-markers

**Modern:** unidentified — see ഞേങ്ങോല്‍  
**Sanskrit database:** `ashvayuj` — Aśvayuj (Sheratan) ([entry](../star-names/star-names.json))  
**Named in 4 languages:** Malayalam, Sema (Sumi) Naga, Tamil, Tulu

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Malayalam | ഞാററുവേലി | *ñāṟṟuvēli* | 'the ñāṟṟu times' (variant ഞാററുവാല) | vernacular |
| Tulu | — | *Paggu, Besha, Kártél, Áte, Sóna, Nirnala, Bóntel, Járde, Perárde, Puyintél, Máyi, Suggi* | — | vernacular |
| Malayalam | മുഴക്കോല്‍ | *muḻakkōl* | 'cubit-rod, measuring rod' (മുഴം a cubit + കോല്‍ rod) — the carpenter's 24-finger measure | folk |
| Tamil | ஐப்பசிக்குழப்பம் | *aippaci-k-kuḻappam* | the Aippaci turmoil | folk |
| Sema (Sumi) Naga | — | *Phoghwosülesipfemi (the Belt, used as a calendar)* | — | tribal |

**ഞാററുവേലി · ñāṟṟuvēli** — Malayalam (Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore)) · *vernacular* · confidence: likely

The days within an asterism-period that are fixed on for transplanting rice.

> ഞാററുവാല , — വേലി V1. days fixed upon for transplanting.
> <br>— Gundert, A Malayalam and English Dictionary (1872), s.v. ഞാറു ñāṟu, p. 412 (sub-entries ഞാററുവാല, ഞാററുവേലി) ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/gundert_query.py?qs=%E0%B4%9E%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%B1%E0%B5%81&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>This is Gundert's printing of the word that modern Malayalam writes ഞാറ്റുവേല ñāṟṟuvēla, the name of the twenty-seven asterism rain-periods. Marked 'likely' because Gundert prints വേലി (with retroflex l and final i) rather than വേല, and glosses it only as 'days fixed upon for transplanting'; whether the two are the same word or a near-homophone is not settled by this entry alone.</sub>

**Paggu, Besha, Kártél, Áte, Sóna, Nirnala, Bóntel, Járde, Perárde, Puyintél, Máyi, Suggi** — Tulu (South Canara (Tulu Nadu)) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

These, and not any star, are what Tulu cultivation runs on: Sturrock states that all the operations of cultivation are regulated by the solar months, which alone are well known to the cultivating classes in Tuluva proper, while written leases follow the lunar reckoning because they are drawn up in Kannada by Brahmins.

> …there are Tulu names for the solar, but not for the luni-solar months, thus— Sanskrit. Tulu. Mésha. Paggu. Vrishabha. Besha. Mithuna. Kártél. Karkataca. Áte. Sinha. Sóna. Kanya. Nirnala. Tulá. Bóntel. Vrischika. Járde. Dhanus. Perárde. Makara. Puyintél. Kumbha. Máyi. Mína. Suggi.
> <br>— Sturrock, Madras District Manuals: South Canara, vol. I (Madras, 1894), p. 216 ([source](https://archive.org/download/dli.ministry.08447/GR386_djvu.txt))

<sub>Included because it is the negative answer to the agricultural-star question for Tulu, stated positively. Where Malayalam divides the year by twenty-seven asterism-periods (ñāṟṟuveḷa) and names each after a star, Tulu divides it by twelve solar months with wholly native names that are not star-names at all. Sturrock romanizes only; no Kannada script is printed, so name_native is null. The quote is from the archive.org OCR and its accents are as OCR'd.</sub>

**മുഴക്കോല്‍ · muḻakkōl** — Malayalam (Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore)) · *folk* · confidence: disputed

Second name of the same asterism as ഞേങ്ങോല്‍; the agricultural use is given at that entry.

> മുഴക്കോല്‍ CS. 1. ആശാരിക്കോല്‍ carpenter's rod of 24 വിരല്‍ . 2. the constellation ഞെ ങ്ങോല്‍ .
> <br>— Gundert, A Malayalam and English Dictionary (1872), s.v. മുഴം muḻam, p. 846 (sub-entry മുഴക്കോല്‍, sense 2) ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/gundert_query.py?qs=%E0%B4%AE%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%B4%E0%B4%82&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>Both Malayalam names for this asterism are craftsmen's straight-edges — a plough-beam and a carpenter's rule. That two independent entries in Gundert cross-reference each other rules out a printing slip.</sub>

**ஐப்பசிக்குழப்பம் · aippaci-k-kuḻappam** — Tamil (Tamil Nadu (coast)) · *folk* · confidence: certain

A WEATHER TERM keyed to an asterism-named month — the practical end of the Tamil star-calendar, matching āṟāmīṉ-aṟavōṭṭu among the seamen.

> ஐப்பசிக்குழப்பம் aippaci-k-kuḻappam , n. < ஐப்பசி +. Rough weather at the setting in of the north-east monsoon in October; ஐப்பசிமாதத்தில் தோன்றுகிற புயல். (J.)
> <br>— Tamil Lexicon (University of Madras, 1924-36), s.v. ஐப்பசிக்குழப்பம், vol. I p. 578, marked (J.) ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/tamil-lex_query.py?qs=%E0%AE%90%E0%AE%AA%E0%AF%8D%E0%AE%AA%E0%AE%9A%E0%AE%BF%E0%AE%95%E0%AF%8D%E0%AE%95%E0%AF%81%E0%AE%B4%E0%AE%AA%E0%AF%8D%E0%AE%AA%E0%AE%AE%E0%AF%8D&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>Aippaci and the Pleiades passage of āṟāmīṉ-aṟavōṭṭu mark the same weather from two directions — the month named for the first asterism and the sun's transit of the third. Together they are the whole of the agricultural and maritime star-calendar recoverable from these lexica; nothing more specific (sowing-stars, harvest-stars, named navigation stars) was found in the Tamil Lexicon, Winslow, or in Thurston's Castes and Tribes of Southern India.</sub>

**Phoghwosülesipfemi (the Belt, used as a calendar)** — Sema (Sumi) Naga (the Sema country, Naga Hills (now Nagaland)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Sowing of paddy is reckoned to begin when Orion stands in the zenith, or when it has reached the position the sun holds at about 2 p.m. — a time of day the Semas name, lubagholo. The other sign is the call of the kasupapo, a cuckoo. Hutton adds that the whole Sema calendar depends on the time of sowing, and that in some eastern villages there is no real calendar at all, only names for the times of year.

> The sowing of paddy is generally reckoned to begin when the constellation of Orion (Phogwosülesipfemi) is in the zenith or when the voice of the Kasupapo is heard in the land.
> <br>— J.H. Hutton, The Sema Nagas (London: Macmillan, 1921), p. 62, 220, 251 ([source](https://archive.org/details/semanagas00hutt))

<sub>ORION AS THE CLOCK OF THE AGRICULTURAL YEAR, stated three times in the book. This is the same use the Mundas make of it in ordinary speech — araṛ ipilko hāṛeṇnate, 'about two hours after Orion had crossed the meridian' — and it is the strongest evidence in the database for why Orion is the most densely named object in it. Hutton's spelling of the name varies between pages and both forms are given.</sub>

I have deliberately NOT read it as the Pleiades, even though 'hen and chickens' is a standard European name for that cluster and Praharaj gives 'Hen and chickens' among the western names of Kṛttikā (p. 4095); the Assamese entry does not say so. The literal meaning is my reading of the compound and is marked as such.</sub>

## Mars

**Modern:** Mars

**Awsichakeipa** — Mara (Lakher) (the Lakher country, southern Lushai Hills (now southern Mizoram) and the Chin Hills) · *tribal* · confidence: likely

The tiger that came to eat the mother and daughter at their weaving. It is redder in colour than other stars.

> The tiger is known as Awsichakeipa, and is redder in colour than other stars. Awsichakeipa is identified by Savidge as the planet Mars.
> <br>— N.E. Parry, The Lakhers (London: Macmillan, 1932), p. 494 ([source](https://archive.org/details/lakhers032949mbp))

<sub>The identification is the missionary F.W. Savidge's, not Parry's own, and is carried as his — hence `likely`. A RED STAR CALLED THE TIGER turns up twice in the north-east: Hutton records an Angami 'big red star' that is a tiger behind the Star-Girls, and Lorrain gives Mizo Si-kei-sen, 'the red tiger star', already in this file as Mars. Parry adds that the Lusheis call a reddish star in the middle of the sky Sikeisen, 'the golden cat', and thinks it probably Mars too. Khazanghra, also called Thimzing, is the Lakher 'great darkness', the mythical eclipse at which everything then alive was turned to stone or to stars. Nearly every Lakher star-name below is an episode interrupted by it.</sub>

**Si-kei-sen, Si-sakei** — Mizo (Lushai) (the Lushai Hills, Assam (now Mizoram)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Lorrain gives two senses at one headword: the planet Mars, and Betelgeuse. One name for the two conspicuous red objects in the sky, planet and star alike.

> Si-kei-sen, n . 1. the planet Mars. 2. Betelgeux. (Same as Sisakei. ) [and, p. 419] Si-sakei, n . 1. the planet Mars. 2. Betelgeux. (Same as Sikeisen. )
> <br>— J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Si-kei-sen, p. 417 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/lorrain_query.py?page=417))

<sub>Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A RED-STAR CATEGORY RATHER THAN A NAME FOR ONE BODY. Tamil cem-mīṉ 'the red star' does the same job in this database, covering Mars and Arundhatī, and Malayalam has ceṅṅāyi. Mizo, Tamil and Malayalam are unrelated; the category is the sky's, not the language's.</sub>

**Sukari, Sukkari** — Pardhi (fourteen Pardhi villages of the Amravati and Yeotmal districts, Vidarbha, Maharashtra, surveyed 2016-2018) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Recorded in nine villages, as was the conjunction of Venus and Mars.

*No quotation: Ganesh Halkare, Purushottam Dahedar, Wayne Orchiston and M.N. Vahia, 'Astronomy of the Pardhi tribe of central India', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 22(1), 179-194 (2019), Table 5, pp. 184-185 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— Ganesh Halkare, Purushottam Dahedar, Wayne Orchiston and M.N. Vahia, 'Astronomy of the Pardhi tribe of central India', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 22(1), 179-194 (2019), Table 5, pp. 184-185 ([source](https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/2019JAHH...22..179H))

<sub>MARS AS THE FEMININE OF VENUS. Sukari is Sukar with a feminine ending, so the two brightest wandering objects the Pardhi name are a matched pair. No other source in this database pairs the planets by gender in this way, and the paper does not comment on it. In copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, on the convention this file uses throughout. The paper prints each name in Devanagari as well as roman; name_native is null because the Devanagari in the available scan cannot be read with the confidence this database requires of a native-script field, exactly as for the Korku and Bhil entries.</sub>

**jan(d)rʔum-tuj** — Sora (the Sora country of the Ganjam and Koraput hills, Odisha and northern Andhra) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

> jan(d)rʔum-'tuj, the planet Mars, [tuj-, contr. of tui-tuj-ən, a star,]
> <br>— G.V. Ramamurti, Sora-English Dictionary (Delhi: Manager of Publications, 1938), s.v. jan(d)r'ʔum-'tuj, p. 120 ([source](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.98075))

<sub>Sora names three planets — Venus twice over, Jupiter twice over and Mars — and no constellations except the two lunar mansions. That is an unusual shape for a tribal sky in this database, where the planets are usually the last thing named, and it is consistent with Ramamurti's own note that the Oriya astrologers have been at work.</sub>

## The rainbow

**Modern:** the rainbow  
**Named in 4 languages:** Gondi, Kolami, Lambadi (Banjara), Mara (Lakher)

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gondi | — | *Kamarpatta; Gulel* | — | tribal |
| Kolami | — | *Ayak / Aikawa / Ayyakawa* | 'the grandparents' — Ayyak the grandfather at the violet end and awa the grandmother at the red | tribal |
| Mara (Lakher) | — | *Meisakupa* | — | tribal |
| Lambadi (Banjara) | — | *Indra-dhanush* | 'Indra's bow' | borrowed |

**Kamarpatta; Gulel** — Gondi (Nagpur region: Chandrapur, Yavatmal, Gondia (Maharashtra), Adilabad (Telangana), Balaghat, Seoni, Mandla (Madhya Pradesh)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

At Matharjun a rainbow appeared while the survey was in the village and the informants named it Kamarpatta on the spot (p. 35). At Chalisbodi it is Gulel, and the paper adds that it is also called the bow of a bow and arrow (p. 37).

*No quotation: Vahia & Halkare, 'Aspects of Gond Astronomy', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 16(1), 29-44 (2013); preprint arXiv:1306.2416, Table 5 row 8, p. 39 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— Vahia & Halkare, 'Aspects of Gond Astronomy', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 16(1), 29-44 (2013); preprint arXiv:1306.2416, Table 5 row 8, p. 39 ([source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.2416))

<sub>In copyright: paraphrased throughout and never quoted, per this compilation's rules, so the quote field is null. The survey covered 15 Gond villages in March 2011, with identifications checked by projecting a sky chart for the informants and later in a planetarium, which is why the modern identifications are given as reported. COUNT DISCREPANCY IN THE SOURCE, LEFT AS IT STANDS: Table 6 (p. 40) marks the rainbow in one village only, but the village accounts record it at two, Matharjun and Chalisbodi. Both words are current in Marathi and Hindi — kamarpaṭṭā a waist-belt, gulel a catapult — which is the compiler's observation and not the paper's, but it agrees with the paper's own remark that the figure is a bow. Compare the Kolam rainbow, which is the bow of the god Bhimayak, and the Banjara one, which is Indra's bow outright. Entered on a re-read of the paper prompted by Vahia, Yadav and Menon's NCSM book (see the caveats), whose Table 4.2 condenses this row and made its absence here visible.</sub>

**Ayak / Aikawa / Ayyakawa** — Kolami (Kolam villages of Yavatmal and Chandrapur districts, Vidarbha, Maharashtra, and adjoining Adilabad, Telangana) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Four of the ten villages. Read as the sign that the current rains have ended. At Landgi Pod it is instead the bow of Bhimayak, one of the five Kolam gods.

*No quotation: M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 2 row 24, p. 71, and Appendix 1.2.10 (Kakban), p. 84 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 2 row 24, p. 71, and Appendix 1.2.10 (Kakban), p. 84 ([source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3044))

<sub>In copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, the convention this database already uses for the Gondi entries in tribal.json. THE ONLY NAME IN THIS DATABASE THAT DIVIDES A SKY OBJECT BY COLOUR AND PUTS A PERSON AT EACH END. The two ends of the arc are the two grandparents, and which end is which is stated: the grandfather at the violet, the grandmother at the red. Ayak is also the Kolam word for their gods — the paper lists five primary gods, the Ayak, headed by Bhimayak — so the rainbow is named for the old people and for the gods at once, and the Landgi Pod reading of it as Bhimayak's bow falls out of the same word. From the village-by-village appendix rather than the summary tables, which is where most of the Kolam and Banjara vocabulary actually is; the appendix was re-read after Vahia, Yadav and Menon's NCSM book (see the caveats) showed that this compilation had worked from the tables alone.</sub>

**Meisakupa** — Mara (Lakher) (the Lakher country, southern Lushai Hills (now southern Mizoram) and the Chin Hills) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

The tail of a celestial creature; the account continues past the page quoted here.

> A rainbow is called Meisakupa, and is the tail of a celestial
> <br>— N.E. Parry, The Lakhers (London: Macmillan, 1932), p. 499 ([source](https://archive.org/details/lakhers032949mbp))

<sub>The quote breaks where the page does. The rainbow is not a star but is entered on the same footing as the Rengma solar halo and the Pardhi lunar halo — sky phenomena that these sources record in the same breath as the stars, and that the database would otherwise silently drop.</sub>

**Indra-dhanush** — Lambadi (Banjara) (Banjara tandas of Vidarbha, Maharashtra (villages in the Nagpur–Amravati–Yavatmal region)) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

One of six villages. Read as the sign that the current spell of rain has ended.

*No quotation: M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 1 row 26, p. 69, and Appendix 1.1.4 (Kasola), p. 79 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 17(1), 65-84 (2014), Table 1 row 26, p. 69, and Appendix 1.1.4 (Kasola), p. 79 ([source](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.3044))

The recorders mark it as taken from the modern languages, and it is entered as borrowed on their judgement. THE RAINBOW IS A BOW IN ALL THREE COMMUNITIES SURVEYED and the only question is whose: Indra's here, the god Bhimayak's among the Kolams, and among the Gonds a gulel, a catapult, with no owner named. From the village-by-village appendix rather than the summary tables, which is where most of the Kolam and Banjara vocabulary actually is; the appendix was re-read after Vahia, Yadav and Menon's NCSM book (see the caveats) showed that this compilation had worked from the tables alone.</sub>

**Modern:** Corvus · Corvus  
**Sanskrit database:** `hasta` — Hasta (Gienah) ([entry](../star-names/star-names.json))  
**Named in 3 languages:** Hindi, Kashmiri, Marathi

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hindi | काक | *kāka* | the crow | vernacular |
| Marathi | — | *Hasti Nakshatra* | the Elephant asterism | folk |
| Marathi | हत्ती | *hattī* | elephant | folk |
| Marathi | हत्तीबार | *hattībāra* | the elephant-crop | folk |
| Kashmiri | ह॑स्तु॒ | *hostu* | — | borrowed |

**काक · kāka** — Hindi (Pan-Hindi (national print)) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

The book's भारतीय नाम for the constellation in its complete 88-constellation concordance. Muley himself notes (p. ~16) that uniform Indian names across languages were still to be settled — the set is part report of circulating usage, part proposal.

*No quotation: Gunakar Muley, Akash Darshan (New Delhi: Rajkamal Prakashan, 1993), Appendix 4, 'Tara-mandal suchi', pp. 344-347, and p. ~130 is in copyright and is paraphrased only.*
> <br>— Gunakar Muley, Akash Darshan (New Delhi: Rajkamal Prakashan, 1993), Appendix 4, 'Tara-mandal suchi', pp. 344-347, and p. ~130 ([source](https://archive.org/details/akash-gunakar))

<sub>Paraphrased, no quote: the book is in copyright (© Shanti Gunakar Muley, first ed. February 1993). Name read from the printed भारतीय नाम column of the Appendix 4 table on the scan's page images (leaves 172-173). The book grew from serials in Navbharat Times (1988-89) and Saptahik Hindustan (1991-92), so the names reached a national Hindi readership.</sub>

**Hasti Nakshatra** — Marathi (Satara district, Deccan) · *folk* · confidence: certain

names the heavy westerly downpour of September, distinguished by cultivators from the regular south-west monsoon

> it is known as the fall of the Hasti Nakshatra or the Elephant Guest-house.
> <br>— Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. XIX: Satara (Bombay: Government Central Press, 1885), p. 19 ([source](https://archive.org/details/wbsl.15257))

<sub>Independent confirmation, from revenue-survey fieldwork rather than a dictionary, of the elephant reading of Hasta that Molesworth records s.v. हत्ती. The sentence quoted is preceded by: 'A heavy burst, often six inches, of westerly rain nearly always happens in September. The people do not regard this as part of the regular south-west monsoon' — that lead-in is quoted here in the printed reading rather than the scan's, which garbles it as 'A heavy bursty often six inches^ of westerly rain nearly alw^ays happens'. The Nasik volume (Vol. XVI, 1883, p. 15) has the same: the rains end 'until the Hasta Nakshatra or sign of the Elephant in the first half of October' (the scan prints 'Rasta'), and it calls the September-October rains 'the elephant showers'. Roman only; no Devanagari is printed in the Gazetteer.</sub>

**हत्ती · hattī** — Marathi (Maharashtra) · *folk* · confidence: certain

हत्तीचें उथाण, the sultriness of the Hasta period; Pr. पडेल हत्ती तर पाडील भिंती, 'if the elephant falls it will bring down walls' — of torrential rain

> हत्ती hattī m (हस्ती S) An elephant. Pr. हत्तीबरोबर बैलाचें वारगोळें. 2 The thirteenth nakshatra or lunar mansion. Note. This asterism is properly named हस्त, being designated by a hand, not by an elephant. It is by popular understanding, howsoever extensive or established, or howsoever inclusive of the erudite or educated, that it is named हत्ती, and that it acquires references and associations as outpouring heavy rain. Pr. पडेल हत्ती तर पाडील भिंती.
> <br>— J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. हत्ती, p. 885 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%B9%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%80&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>A pure case of folk reanalysis, and Molesworth says so in as many words: हस्त means 'hand', but Marathi speakers — learned ones included — hear हत्ती 'elephant', and the whole weather-imagery of the asterism (an elephant's downpour, walls knocked flat) follows from the mishearing. This is the answer to 'what does Marathi call Corvus': not a crow, an elephant. The reanalysis has entered ritual: Molesworth s.v. हस्तागौर (p. 892) describes 'the image or figure of गौरी seated upon an elephant, and worshiped whilst the sun is in हस्तनक्षत्र', and s.v. गजगौरीव्रत (p. 219) the same rite as performed when 'the sun enters the constellation of elephant'.</sub>

**हत्तीबार · hattībāra** — Marathi (Maharashtra) · *folk* · confidence: certain

the second fruit crop of the year, ripening under Hasta

> हत्तीबार hattībāra m (Elephant-crop.) A term for the fruit-crop which ripens under हस्तनक्षत्र, i. e. the second crop. The two other crops are मृगबार & आंबेबार.
> <br>— J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. हत्तीबार, p. 885 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%B9%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A4%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%AC%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B0&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>Shows the star-name in load-bearing agricultural use: the farming year's three fruit crops are named मृगबार, हत्तीबार and आंबेबार, two of the three after asterisms.</sub>

**ह॑स्तु॒ · hostu** — Kashmiri (Kashmir valley) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

The thirteenth of the twenty-seven lunar mansions.

> hostu 1 ह॑स्तु॒ । हस्तः, नक्षत्रविशेषः m. the thirteenth of the twenty-seven lunar mansions or lunar asterisms, in Sanskrit hasta, said to be shaped like a hand and to be part of the constellation Corvus.
> <br>— Sir George Abraham Grierson, A Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language, compiled partly from materials left by the late Pandit Isvara Kaula (Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1916-1932), s.v. hostu, p. 354 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/grierson_query.py?page=354))

<sub>Grierson prints the roman, the Śāradā-derived Devanagari and a Sanskrit gloss for every headword, so the romanization here is the source's own and nothing is transliterated by the compiler. The hand-shape and the identification with Corvus are Grierson's.</sub>

> <br>— Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925 ([source](https://archive.org/download/dli.bengal.10689.20088/10689.20088_djvu.txt))

<sub>Compare Kurukh, where the blacksmith's bellows (lohrā-capuā bīnkō) is the name of the Pleiades and not of a figure in Auriga. Same implement, same word, different stars — good evidence that the naming is independent rather than borrowed one way.</sub>

**ಬ್ರಹ್ಮಹೃದಯ · Brahmahṛdaya** — Kannada (Karnataka (Mysore)) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

The Sūrya-siddhānta tradition's name, in Kannada.

> ವರ್ಗಕ್ಕೆ ಸೇರಿದ ದೇದೀಪ್ಛಮಾನವಾದ ಈ ತಾರೆಯು  ಉತ್ತರಾರ್ಧ ಗೋಳದ ಸ್ವಾತಿಯೊಡನೆಯೂ, ಬ್ರಹ್ಮಹೃದಯದೊಡ  ನೆಯೂ ಕಾಂತಿ ವಿಷಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಅಗುಸ್ಥಾನಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ಹೋರಾಡುವಂತೆ  ಕಾಣುತ್ತದೆ.
> <br>— N. Venkatesha Ayyangar (transl.), Jyotirvinodini (Bengaluru: Karnataka Sahitya Parishattu, 1931; Karnataka Vaijnanika Grantha Mala 1), Appendix III (alphabetical sky-index), pp. 301-306 ([source](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.363462))

## 'Sky' as a word

**Modern:**   
**Sanskrit database:** `tarapatha` — Tārāpatha (the firmament ('star-road')) ([entry](../star-names/star-names.json))  
**Named in 3 languages:** Kannada, Kashmiri, Telugu

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kannada | ಮೀನ್ವಟ್ಟೆ | *mīnvaṭṭe* | the star-road / fish-road | vernacular |
| Telugu | చుక్కలతెరువు | *cukkala-teruvu* | the street of the stars | vernacular |
| Kashmiri | नब् | *nab* | — | borrowed |

**ಮೀನ್ವಟ್ಟೆ · mīnvaṭṭe** — Kannada (Karnataka (Mysore, Canara, Deccan)) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

One of three synonymous Kannada 'star-road' compounds: mīn-vaṭṭe, aṟil-vaṭṭe (p. 105), tārage-vaṭṭe (p. 752).

> — ಮೀನ್ವಟ್ಟೆ. -ಬಟ್ಟೆ. the sky (ಆಕಾಶ Kk. 12).
> <br>— Kittel, F., A Kannaḍa-English Dictionary (orig. Mangalore: Basel Mission, 1894); cited from the revised and enlarged edition, [Madras] University of Madras, 1968-71, as keyed for DSAL, s.v. ಮೀನ್ mīn 2, p. 1328 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/kittel_query.py?page=1328))

<sub>COGNATE PAIR with Telugu చుక్కలతెరువు cukkala-teruvu 'the street of the stars = the sky'. Both are formed star-word + road-word, in each case with the language's own material; Sanskrit tārāpatha (db id 'tarapatha') has the same figure but is not the source of either.</sub>

**చుక్కలతెరువు · cukkala-teruvu** — Telugu (Telugu country (Madras Presidency: Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema, Telangana)) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

A wholly Dravidian compound for the firmament; teruvu is 'street, road'.

> చుక్కలతెరువు the sky ఆకాశము. చుక్కలరేడు the moon.
> <br>— Brown, C. P., A Telugu-English Dictionary, new ed., thoroughly revised and brought up to date (Madras: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, 1903), s.v. చుక్క ṭsukka, p. 449 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/brown_query.py?page=449))

<sub>COGNATE PAIR. This is the exact structural twin of Kannada ಮೀನ್ವಟ್ಟೆ mīnvaṭṭe / ಅಱಿಲ್ವಟ್ಟೆ aṟilvaṭṭe / ತಾರಗೆವಟ್ಟೆ tāragevaṭṭe, all 'star-road = sky' (Kittel pp. 1328, 105, 752). Both languages inherit the figure independently of Sanskrit tārāpatha, which uses the same image.</sub>

**नब् · nab** — Kashmiri (Kashmir valley) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

> nab नब् । नभः m. the sky, the atmosphere, heaven, firmament.
> <br>— Sir George Abraham Grierson, A Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language, compiled partly from materials left by the late Pandit Isvara Kaula (Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1916-1932), s.v. nab, p. 619 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/grierson_query.py?page=619))

<sub>Grierson prints the roman, the Śāradā-derived Devanagari and a Sanskrit gloss for every headword, so the romanization here is the source's own and nothing is transliterated by the compiler. Sanskrit nabhas. Entered because the Kashmiri sky words are almost the whole of what this dictionary has that is not a nakshatra name.</sub>

## Altair

**Modern:** Altair · α Aquilae · Aquila

**തിരുവോണം / ഓണം · tiruvōṇam / ōṇam** — Malayalam (Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore)) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

Names the national festival of Kerala: Gundert, 'the national feast on new moon of Sept. lasting 10 days, when Paraśurāma is still said to visit Kēraḷa'.

> തിരുവോണം (S. ശ്രവണം ) 1. the 22nd asterism including Aquila (in Cancer V1.). 2. the feast ഓണം in August.
> <br>— Gundert, A Malayalam and English Dictionary (1872), s.v. തിരുന്പുക tirumpuka, p. 459 (sub-entry തിരുവോണം); and s.v. ഓണം ōṇam, p. 184 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/gundert_query.py?page=459))

<sub>The clearest case in Malayalam of an asterism name outgrowing astronomy: Ōṇam is now first a harvest festival and only second a star. Gundert's ഓണം entry (p. 184) leads with 'The 22nd constellation, Aquila'.</sub>

The book's भारतीय नाम for the constellation in its complete 88-constellation concordance. Muley himself notes (p. ~16) that uniform Indian names across languages were still to be settled — the set is part report of circulating usage, part proposal.

> <br>— N. Venkatesha Ayyangar (transl.), Jyotirvinodini (Bengaluru: Karnataka Sahitya Parishattu, 1931; Karnataka Vaijnanika Grantha Mala 1), Appendix III (alphabetical sky-index), pp. 301-306 ([source](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.363462))

<sub> Form verified against the archive.org OCR of the book (2026-08-18); the appendix indexes every name alphabetically. Quote is a verbatim byte-slice of the archive.org OCR (imperfect OCR quoted as scanned; the page images are the authority).</sub>

**hirumea parkom ipilko** — Mundari (Chota Nagpur plateau, Ranchi district, Jharkhand) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

The bed two co-wives are fighting over — that is, the mastership of the house.

> The bed, hirumea parkom ipilko, is situated in Lupus, to the N. E. of the Southern Cross, and is represented by four stars, Alpha, Beta, Mu and Ro, which delineate a nearly equilateral parallelogram.
> <br>— Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VI, s.v. hirumea parkom ipilko, cols. 1751-1757 ([source](https://archive.org/download/in.ernet.dli.2015.14926/2015.14926.Encyclopedia-Mundarica-Vol-vi-1932_djvu.txt))

<sub>hirumea is the Mundari term for the relationship between two co-wives (vol. VI s.v.).</sub>

## Regulus

**Modern:** Regulus and the stars of Maghā · α, γ, ζ, η, ν Leonis · Leo  
**Sanskrit database:** `magha` — Maghā (Regulus) ([entry](../star-names/star-names.json))

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kashmiri | मग् | *mag* | — | borrowed |
| Malayalam | മകം | *makam* | — | borrowed |
| Tamil | மாசி | *māci* | from Skt. māgha, the month of the Magha asterism | borrowed |

**मग् · mag** — Kashmiri (Kashmir valley) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

The tenth of the twenty-seven lunar mansions.

> mag 1 मग् । नक्षत्रविशेषः f. N. of the tenth lunar asterism or lunar mansion, called Maghā in Sanskrit. It contains five stars — α (Regulus), γ, ζ, η and ν Leōnis (Śiv. 1861).
> <br>— Sir George Abraham Grierson, A Dictionary of the Kashmiri Language, compiled partly from materials left by the late Pandit Isvara Kaula (Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1916-1932), s.v. mag, p. 551 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/grierson_query.py?page=551))

<sub>Grierson prints the roman, the Śāradā-derived Devanagari and a Sanskrit gloss for every headword, so the romanization here is the source's own and nothing is transliterated by the compiler. Grierson gives the Bayer letters himself, which is unusual for a dictionary of this date and makes the identification his rather than the compiler's.</sub>

**മകം · makam** — Malayalam (Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore)) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

Proverbial: മകം പിറന്ന മങ്ക, 'a girl born under Makam' — an auspicious birth.

> മകം makam maγam 1. Tdbh. of മഘ . The 10th constellation (Regulus). മകമാം നാളന്നു KR. മകം പിറന്ന മങ്ക prov.
> <br>— Gundert, A Malayalam and English Dictionary (1872), s.v. മകം makam, p. 769 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/gundert_query.py?qs=%E0%B4%AE%E0%B4%95%E0%B4%82&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>Gundert's 'Tdbh.' (tadbhava) marking is his standard signal that the word has been through Dravidian phonology rather than borrowed whole.</sub>

**மாசி · māci** — Tamil (Tamil Nadu) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

The one Tamil month-name attested by name in the Caṅkam corpus itself, described there by its astronomical property: the month in which the day does not lengthen and the night grows.

> பகல்நீ(டு) ஆகா(து) இரவுப்பொழுது பெருகி மாசி நின்ற மாகூர் திங்கள்
> <br>— Patiṟṟuppattu 59, ll. 1-2 (Sixth Ten); Project Madurai e-text PM 0038 ([source](https://www.projectmadurai.org/pm_etexts/utf8/pmuni0038.html))

<sub>TEXTUAL NOTE: the Project Madurai e-text prints line 2 as 'மாசி நின்ற *மாகூர் திங்கள்*', the asterisks and bold flanking மாகூர் திங்கள் because that phrase is this poem's பெயர் (title-phrase), given as such in its colophon — they are editorial emphasis, not a lacuna, and the line is continuous. Line 1's '(டு)' and '(து)' are the editor's parenthesised restorations and are kept here as printed; nothing has been supplied by the compiler. The Tamil Lexicon (s.v. மாசி², vol. V p. 3147) cites this exact line as பதிற்றுப். 59, 2 and defines the word 'The 11th solar month = February-March', adding sense 2, 'The 10th nakṣatra. See மகம்²', from the commentary on Cilappatikāram 3, 123. HOMONYM: மாசி¹ on the previous page is 'mist, cloud' and 'a sea-fish', probably from மாசு.</sub>

**తేలురాశి · tēlu-rāsi** — Telugu (Telugu country (Madras Presidency: Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema, Telangana)) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

**ഭഗണം · bhagaṇam** — Malayalam (Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore)) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

A technical term of Kerala astronomy: ഭഗണം also means a complete revolution, and ഭഗണഭൂദിനങ്ങള്‍ 'revolutions and civil days in a caturyuga' is quoted from a Malayalam gaṇita text.

<sub>Gundert's citation 'Gan.' is a Malayalam mathematical/astronomical work — direct lexical evidence that the technical vocabulary of the Kerala school passed into the general language. Note also ഭഗണന്‍ 'an astrologer' in the same entry.</sub>

<sub>Not a name for the star but for its season — the counterpart, on the hot-weather side, of the rain-names अंधळ्या and कडप्या for the same asterism. Molesworth's dry 'Wonderful properties are ascribed to it' is his usual signal for popular belief he does not endorse.</sub>

**कडप्या · kaḍapyā** — Marathi (Maharashtra) · *folk* · confidence: certain

the rain falls when the bājrī sheaves are laid out to dry

> कडप्या kaḍapyā f pl (कडप An untied sheaf, a reap.) A term for the चित्रानक्षत्र and for the rain which falls under it. Because that rain falls when the कडपें of बाजरी are exposed to dry.
> <br>— J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. कडप्या, p. 128 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth_query.py?qs=%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%A1%E0%A4%AA%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%AF%E0%A4%BE&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>A COMPETING folk name for the same asterism as अंधळ्या — Citrā/Spica has at least two cultivators' names in Molesworth's Marathi, keyed to different consequences of the same rain.</sub>

**ചിത്ര / ചിത്തിര · citra / cittira** — Malayalam (Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore)) · *borrowed* · confidence: disputed

> ചിത്ര citra čitra S. (foll.) & ചിത്തിര 1. The 14th lunar asterism (Spica virginis; mod, bright star in Bootes); the month ചൈത്രം or മേടം .
> <br>— Gundert, A Malayalam and English Dictionary (1872), s.v. ചിത്ര citra, p. 361 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/gundert_query.py?qs=%E0%B4%9A%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%A4%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>Gundert gives two incompatible identifications in one breath — Spica, and 'mod. bright star in Bootes' (i.e. Arcturus). The second is an error, probably contamination from ചോതി/Svātī on the facing sense; Spica is the standard identification and is what the Sanskrit database carries.</sub>

**risaːl-tuj-ən** — Sora (the Sora country of the Ganjam and Koraput hills, Odisha and northern Andhra) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

<sub>Ramamurti gives a second Jupiter name, baːmbədaː- tuj-ən, at its own headword and adds that it is 'due to the influence of the Oriya astrologers' — a lexicographer marking the borrowed layer in the field, which is precisely what the register column of this database exists to do.</sub>

> नौकापुंजांत तिसरी एक तारा आहे. १८९३ च्या आरंभीं तिचे विषुवांश १०।४०।५५ आणि द० क्रांति ५९।७।१५ आहे. मेच्या १७ व्या तारखेस ही ७ वाजतां मध्यान्हीं येते. हिच्या तेजांत फार विलक्षण फेरफार होतो. परंतु त्याचा काळ सुमारें ४६ वर्षें आहे.

## Measuring the sky

**Modern:**   
**Named in 2 languages:** Mizo (Lushai), Tamil

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mizo (Lushai) | — | *suk-chen* | 'a pestle's length' | tribal |
| Tamil | சங்கு | *caṅku* | 'a stake, a peg, a spike' | borrowed |

**suk-chen** — Mizo (Lushai) (the Lushai Hills, Assam (now Mizoram)) · *tribal* · confidence: certain

Lorrain's example sentence is a traveller judging whether the village is reachable before dark.

> suk-chen, n . the height or length of a pestle. (Used to indicate the height of the sun, moon, or stars above the horizon, either before setting or after rising.) Ni sukchen a la awm, kan la ban ang = The sun is still the height of a pestle above the horizon, we shall reach (the village tonight).
> <br>— J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. suk-chen, p. 421 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/lorrain_query.py?page=421))

<sub>Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A NATIVE ANGULAR MEASURE, and the first in this database. The maritime traditions of the west coast measure star altitudes in fists and fingers — kai kanakku in Lakshadweep and Malabar, viral kanakku in Tamil Nadu, dhru in Gujarat — and this is the inland counterpart, reckoned from the household pestle. It creates the object 'Measuring the sky' in this database, which the maritime wave will fill.</sub>

**சங்கு · caṅku** — Tamil (Tamil Nadu) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

The Tamil Lexicon's second sense at this headword, after 'stake, peg, spike'.

> சங்கு⁵ caṅku , n . šaṅku . 1. Stake, peg, spike; முளை. 2. Gnomon or perpendicular column for measuring the altitude of the sun by the length of its shadow; நிழலினாற் பொழுதறிதற்காக நேரா…
> <br>— Tamil Lexicon, published under the authority of the University of Madras (Madras, 1924-1939), s.v. சங்கு⁵, vol. III p. 1229 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/tamil-lex_query.py?page=1229))

<sub>The second entry in the database's 'Measuring the sky' object, which Mizo suk-chen opened in northeast.json. The two are opposite methods: the Mizo hold up a pestle against the sky and count its lengths, the Tamil plant a post and read its shadow. The word is Sanskrit śaṅku and the instrument is the classical one, so this is the learned tradition rather than a fisherman's rule of thumb — see the summary on what could not be found of the latter.</sub>

## Aśvayuj (Sheratan)

**Modern:** Sheratan · β Arietis · Aries  
**Sanskrit database:** `ashvayuj` — Aśvayuj (Sheratan) ([entry](../star-names/star-names.json))  
**Named in 1 languages:** Tamil

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tamil | ஐப்பசி | *aippaci* | from Skt. āśvayuj, 'joined to the Aśvins' | borrowed |

**ஐப்பசி · aippaci** — Tamil (Tamil Nadu) · *borrowed* · confidence: certain

One of the twelve Tamil month-names still in daily use, all of them asterism-derived. The Lexicon records that the word also names the asterism itself.

> ஐப்பசி aippaci , n. < āšvayuj. 1. The seventh Tamil month, October-November; ஏழாவது மாதம். (உபதேசரத். 6.) 2. The first nakṣstra. See அசுவதி. (சீவக. 1770.)
> <br>— Tamil Lexicon (University of Madras, 1924-36), s.v. ஐப்பசி, vol. I p. 578; quoting Cīvakacintāmaṇi 1770 ([source](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/tamil-lex_query.py?qs=%E0%AE%90%E0%AE%AA%E0%AF%8D%E0%AE%AA%E0%AE%9A%E0%AE%BF&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact))

<sub>The Lexicon's derivations for the rest of the twelve, all verified at the same endpoint: சித்திரை Cittirai < citrā (p. 1391), வைகாசி Vaikāci < vaiśākha (p. 3849), ஆடி Āṭi < āṣāḍha (p. 219), ஆவணி Āvaṇi < śrāvaṇa (p. 249), புரட்டாசி Puraṭṭāci cf. proṣṭhapadā (p. 2769), கார்த்திகை Kārttikai < kṛttikā (p. 880), மார்கழி Mārkaḻi < mārgaśīrṣa (p. 3170), தை Tai < taiṣī (p. 2074), மாசி Māci < māgha (p. 3147), பங்குனி Paṅkuṉi < Pkt. phagguṇi < phalgunī (p. 2390). ஆனி Āṉi (p. 221) is the exception: the Lexicon gives it NO etymology at all, while recording that it also names the 19th nakṣatra (Mūlam) and the 21st (Uttirāṭam) — a gap worth flagging.</sub>

## Hercules

**Modern:** Hercules · Hercules  
**Named in 1 languages:** Marathi

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marathi | शौरि | *śauri* | Shauri (Krishna, the hero) | vernacular |

**शौरि · śauri** — Marathi (Maharashtra) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

One of the Sanskrit names for the Western constellations that Dikshit credits to Bal Shastri Jambhekar (d. 1846) and reports as current: 'पाश्चात्यांनीं कल्पिलेल्या बाकीच्या राशींस संस्कृत संज्ञा शास्त्री जांभेकर यांनीं दिल्या आहेत. त्याच हल्लीं मराठींत येतात.' (p. 35-36). शौरि renders the hero Hercules; the passage describes the solar apex, toward which 'our sun with its family' travels.

> सुमारें विषुवांश १७।२२।४० क्रांति उ० ३९।५६ या बिंदूकडे म्हणजे शौरिनामक पुंजांतील एका बिंदूकडे आपला सूर्य सपरिवार चालला आहे.
> <br>— S. B. Dikshit, Jyotirvilas, 2nd ed. (Bombay, 1893; 1st ed. 1892), p. 187 ([source](https://archive.org/details/india.history.resource.92658))

<sub>Quote transcribed verbatim from the scan's page images (leaf = printed page + 25 up to p. 40, + 30 in the taraka chapter), not from the OCR layer, which garbles conjuncts here. The only Indian name for Hercules in this record — Muley (1993) leaves the constellation as हर्क्यूलीज in Hindi.</sub>

## Saturn

**Modern:** Saturn  
**Named in 1 languages:** Tamil

| Language | Name | Romanized | Literally | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tamil | மைம்மீன் | *mai-m-mīṉ* | black star (mai 'blackness, collyrium') | vernacular |

**மைம்மீன் · mai-m-mīṉ** — Tamil (Tamil Nadu) · *vernacular* · confidence: certain

Named by colour, like veṇmīṉ 'white star' for Venus and cemmīṉ 'red star'. The Puṟanāṉūṟu line stacks three portents — the black star smoking, a comet appearing, Venus running to the south — and says the good king's land is watered even so.

> மைம் மீன் புகையினும், தூமம் தோன்றினும், தென் திசை மருங்கின் வெள்ளி ஓடினும்,
> <br>— Puṟanāṉūṟu 117, ll. 1-2 (by Kapilar); Project Madurai e-text PM 0057 ([source](https://www.projectmadurai.org/pm_etexts/utf8/pmuni0057.html))

<sub>The Tamil Lexicon (s.v. மைம்மீன், vol. V p. 3369, https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/tamil-lex_query.py?qs=%E0%AE%AE%E0%AF%88%E0%AE%AE%E0%AF%8D%E0%AE%AE%E0%AF%80%E0%AE%A9%E0%AF%8D&searchhws=yes&matchtype=exact) defines it 'The planet Saturn, as black in colour; சனி' and cites this line as புறநா. 117. This one couplet is the single richest Tamil astronomical line: it gives maimmīṉ (Saturn), tūmam (comet) and veḷḷi (Venus) in two lines, all three as omens of drought. No Sanskrit-database counterpart; the planets are not individually in that database.</sub>

## Findings, per research file

### Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi & Rajasthani

The Hindi-Urdu-Punjabi sky is stratified in three visible layers, and the lexicographic record of 1834-1896 lets each be dated. (1) A SANSKRITIC layer: Platts (1884) and Fallon (1879) simply carry the twenty-seven nakṣatras over as Hindi headwords (kṛttikā, rohiṇī, mṛg, mūl, svāti...), and Maya Singh's Panjabi Dictionary (1895, s.v. nachhattar, p. 786) prints the whole list of twenty-seven for Punjabi as well - so it is recorded here once and not itemised. What matters is that in living rural speech these appear in Middle-Indic reflexes, not tatsama forms: Grierson's Bihar Peasant Life (1885, §1082, p. 271) gives the generic word as nakhat / nachhattr / nichhattr and the individual asterisms as Rohni, Mirgsira, Aradra, Punarbas, Pukh, Maggha, Hast or Hathiya, Bināti/Siwāti - and they function not as stars but as sixteen-to-thirteen-day agricultural seasons, personified (Hathi rāni, 'Queen Hathiya'). (2) A PERSO-ARABIC layer entering through Urdu and fully naturalised: s̤uraiyā and parvīn for the Pleiades, suhail for Canopus, jabbār and jauzā for Orion, ʻaiyūq for Capella, jadī and quṭbī tārā for the pole star, farqadān for the Guards of Ursa Minor, suhā for Alcor, gardānak for the Pointers, banātu'n-naʻsh for the Bear as bier-and-daughters, kahkashāṅ for the Milky Way, nasru'l-wāqiʻ and nasru'ṭ-ṭāʼir for Lyra/Aquila. (3) A FOLK layer, which is where the real vernacular invention is. The Pleiades are 'the crowded-together ones' (kacpaciyā, gicpiciyā, kachbachiyā), a 'cluster' or ear-drop (guchchā tārā, jhumkā), or a hen with chickens (baccē-wālī murġī, gagan ke baccē-wālī murġī - Shakespear 1834 marks this last Deccani). Ursa Major is a piece of furniture with thieves at it: palang tīn cor, 'the bedstead and three thieves' (Shakespear 1834 p. 1949, also Deccani per Harris; Platts and Fallon unmarked); in Punjabi it splits, the four-star bowl being palang-pāwe 'the legs of the bedstead' and the three-star handle traṅgaṛ 'the net' (Dames, Panjab N&Q II.522), while O'Brien's Multani Glossary (1881, p. 62) makes traṅgar the whole Bear and notes the same word for the upper part of Orion. Fallon's sāt sahelyoṅ kā jhūmkā, 'the ear-drop cluster of the seven girl-friends', is the Bear again. The Milky Way is an elephant's road (hāthī kī rāh) or Hasta's road (hathiyā kī rāh), God's court-house (Bhagwān kī Kachahrī), the gate of heaven (Surg Dwārī), a white garland (Sufed Bādhī), and in Multani/Derawali the wake of Noah's ark (Berā dā Ghās). Venus at dawn is 'the star of the light' (ujāle-kā tārā), bhurkā/bhalkā, and in the Panjab 'the galloping star' (Tapt Tārā). Comets are brooms (jhāṛū) and tailed stars (ket, dum kā tārā, puchhalwālā tārā, dumdār sitārā). NEGATIVE FINDINGS: no vernacular name for SIRIUS could be verified - Platts, Fallon and Shakespear have no entry for it, the Sanskrit Lubdhaka/Mṛgavyādha do not surface, and Fallon (p. 801) misglosses Arabic suhail as 'the dog star', a conflation of Canopus with Sirius that Platts and Shakespear do not share; no ANTARES (no qalb al-ʻaqrab in Platts), no ARCTURUS beyond Sanskrit svāti, no CASSIOPEIA, no separate name for the HYADES. RAJASTHANI, recorded here in an earlier pass as a flat gap, is no longer one, and what it turned out to hold is the most unusual thing in this file. Two dictionaries that DSAL does host were reached on a later pass: Macalister's Dictionary of the Dialects Spoken in the State of Jeypore (1898), which is public domain, and Lalas's Rājasthānī Sabada Kośa (2nd ed. 2013), which is in copyright and is therefore paraphrased throughout. Macalister is nearly bare of sky vocabulary — no word for 'star' at all in the whole book — but yields सातरसा sātarasā for the Pleiades, which is not a reflex of Kṛttikā. Lalas yields the nakshatras as tadbhavas carrying weather-lore rather than astronomy (किरति kirati with its six stars and its lightning proverb, आदरा ādarā with five rain-couplets, three of them invoking Bhaḍḍaḷī by name — the female counterpart of the Ghāgh already quoted here for Bihar). But the find is a cluster no other language in this database has: RAJASTHANI ORIENTS ITSELF BY WHERE URSA MAJOR SETS. रिसिअस्त risiasta, 'the setting of the ṛṣis', is a point of the compass — the quarter between north and north-west — and three winds are named off it: ओकड़ ōkaṛa and दावौ dāvau, which damage the standing crop, and सूरयौ sūrayau, which in Śrāvaṇa is read as a sign of rain. The Great Bear here is not a figure to be named but a bearing to steer weather by. A SECOND PASS finished the object list and its result is a negative worth stating plainly: outside the wind cluster, RAJASTHANI NAMES THE SKY IN SANSKRIT.
