Orion is only म्रिगसिरा mrigasirā with four phonological variants and two learned synonyms, and nothing answers to Sindhi ṭīṛū or Bengali Kālapuruṣa; the Milky Way is वियदगंगा, व्योमगंगा, व्योमसरिता, स्वरगंगा and स्वरगतरंगिणी, every one a tatsama; the pole star is ध्रुव, with उतरादू and दिखणादू reserved for the terrestrial poles; the comet is the whole Bṛhat-Saṃhitā catalogue of ketus — गणककेतु, वसाकेतु, चळकेतु, जळकेतु, भवकेतु, मणिकेतु, रविजकेतु, कौंकुम — and the meteor उल्का, उलकापात, दिवोल्का. The word for 'star' is तारौ tārau, Sanskrit tārā, and its most specific sense is not a star at all but the season in which Jupiter and Venus are invisible and no wedding may be held. What Rajasthani did not borrow, it built out of WIND AND DIRECTION rather than out of figures — which is why रिसिअस्त risiasta and its three winds are the whole of this language's original contribution, and a large one. One further survival is worth the entry: गजबीथी gajabīthī, and the नक्षत्रवीथि scheme of nine star-roads set out at its own headword with Devala and Kāśyapa named as differing authorities — the vīthī material of Bṛhat Saṃhitā 9 and Utpala, alive in a dictionary of 2013. Punjabi is thinly but genuinely attested (Maya Singh; Dames; Jukes; Chaina Mall of Ambala), Bhojpuri/Magahi rural usage is well attested through Fallon and Grierson and is entered here under 'Hindi' with the dialect named in region.

### Sindhi & Kashmiri — the north-west

The north-west, and the result is a clean contrast between two languages that ought to look alike. SINDHI HAS A SKY OF ITS OWN UNDER THE LOANS; KASHMIRI HAS ALMOST NONE. Mewaram's Sindhi-English dictionary of 1910 yields two names that belong to neither learned tradition: ٽيڙۇ ṭīṛū for ORION'S BELT, which is not Sanskrit ishus-trikāṇḍā or mṛgaśiras and not Arabic jauzā or an-niẓām, and ڊۇهُ ḍūhu for the POLE STAR, whose second sense in the same entry is the adjective 'motionless, stationary, stable' — the concept every other north-western name for Polaris imports with a foreign word (Sanskrit dhruva, Arabic quṭb, Arabic jadī), reached here in Sindhi's own vocabulary. A third is nearly as good: چوٽيٴ تارو choṭīa tāro, the comet as a woman's braided TOPKNOT, beside the ordinary پُڇِرُ تارو puchiru tāro 'tailed star'. The Sanskrit comet is smoke and the Munda comet is a broom; the topknot is Sindhi's alone. The rest of Sindhi is a three-layer stack of the kind hindi_urdu_punjabi.json found for Hindustani, and the layers are visible at single headwords: Sanskrit (katiyūn < Kṛttikā, sapta riṣī, ākās nadī, dhūmi ketu, labhdhaku for Sirius, sawāti for Arcturus, shukru for Venus, nakhataru), Persian and Arabic (sitāro, kahkashānu, suhā for Alcor, quṭubu, jadī, zuhrah for Venus, sawābita 'the fixed stars'), and a thin Sindhi layer of its own (ṭīṛū, ḍūhu, choṭīa tāro, sānjhī tāro 'the evening star', vihāū 'the morning star'). جَديِ jadī is the most economical illustration of the stack: Arabic al-jady is Capricorn and the pole star at one headword, and قُطِبنُما quṭub-numā, the mariner's compass, sits beside it — the only navigational word the whole north-west produced. KASHMIRI, by contrast, has essentially no sky of its own. Grierson's 1,200 pages give the twenty-seven nakshatras in Kashmiri phonology (kraʦh, mag with its five Leōnis stars named, hostu in Corvus, shrawun of three stars, abizĕth), the pole star as the saint Dhruva, the Milky Way as the Ganges of the sky, ulkā for a meteor and ketu for a comet, plus Persian sitāra and Arabic suraiya — and that is all. There is NO KASHMIRI NAME FOR ORION anywhere in the dictionary, none for Sirius, none for Canopus, none for the evening star, and none for the Milky Way that is not the Sanskrit compound. The single Kashmiri formation in the whole sky is क्रच़ि-कूरू॒ kraʦi-kūrü, 'a daughter of Kṛttikā', for any one of the six Pleiades, with the plural kraʦi-kōrĕ for the cluster: kūrü is the ordinary Kashmiri word for a daughter, and the compound gives the group a singular and a plural that the bare loan does not have. NEGATIVE FINDINGS. No Sindhi or Kashmiri name for CANOPUS, for the HYADES, for ANTARES or for the GREAT BEAR as a figure — Sindhi has only the Sanskrit sapta riṣī and, remarkably, both languages name Alcor, the faintest thing in it, while naming nothing else in the constellation. No Sindhi word for a METEOR was found. Rose's Glossary of the Tribes and Castes of the Punjab and North-West Frontier Province, searched for Pleiades, Orion, Great Bear, Milky Way, pole star, Canopus, Sirius, comet and constellation, produced exactly one hit in the volume that could be obtained — a Lahauli funeral rite governed by the pañcaka, the group of five inauspicious asterisms — and no star name at all; its other two volumes returned HTTP 503 from archive.org and were not read. Baloch's Jāmiʻ Sindhī lughāt and the modern Kashmiri dictionaries on DSAL were not searched: they are Sindhi-to-Sindhi and Kashmiri-to-Kashmiri, so the English-gloss method used here does not reach them, and a proper pass needs the questions asked in the language.

### Marathi, Konkani & Gujarati

Marathi is the only one of the three languages with a substantial indigenous star vocabulary, and it is concentrated almost entirely in the cultivators' calendar rather than in named constellations. The learned layer is straightforwardly borrowed — Molesworth's entry for नक्षत्र (1857, p. 454) lists all twenty-seven Sanskrit mansions with only light Marathi phonology (मृग for मृगशीर्ष, आश्लेषा 'or असाळका', पूर्वा/उत्तरा for the Phalgunīs), and Konkani and Gujarati do the same: Maffei glosses 'Star' simply as neketru (1883, p. 455), and the Bombay Gazetteer's Gujarat volumes give the asterisms as Kritika, Rohini, Arudra, Mragshir, Revti, calling them 'star chambers' (Vol. IX Pt I, 1901, pp. 352-353). Underneath that borrowed layer Marathi has a whole parallel system in which asterisms are renamed for what their rains DO to the crop: उंदऱ्या 'the rats' for Viśākhā, उंदऱ्यामांजऱ्या 'rats-and-cats' for Viśākhā-plus-Anurādhā, दडप्या 'the pressers-down' for Svātī, अडवण्या 'the obstructors' for Jyeṣṭhā, कडप्या 'the sheaves' and अंधळ्या 'the blind ones' both for Citrā, बडवण्या 'the mallets' for Mūla, and an elder/younger pair — म्हातारा 'the old fellow' or थोरला कुंवर for Punarvasu against तरणा 'the youngster' or धाकटा कुंवर for Puṣya. Four genuinely non-Sanskrit figures stand out: the Pleiades as विंचू, a SCORPION (Molesworth p. 756, confirmed by Date p. 2824 — the Kṛttikās are not maidens here); Ursa Major as खाटलें / बाजलें, a COT, which Enthoven (1924, p. 64) fills out as four stars forming a cot with a sleeper on it and three thieves creeping up; the pole star as मेढ, a FORKED FARMYARD STAKE, with a whole non-Brahman divinatory sect (मेढेमत) and a caste of village astrologers (मेढेजोशी) named from it; and Hasta (Corvus) reanalysed as हत्ती, an ELEPHANT, a mishearing of हस्त 'hand' that Molesworth explicitly flags and that has propagated into ritual (हस्तागौर, Gaurī seated on an elephant) and into the revenue gazetteers ('the fall of the Hasti Nakshatra or the Elephant Guest-house', Satara 1885, p. 19; 'the elephant showers', Nasik 1883, p. 15). Konkani, on Maffei's evidence, is nearly bare of sky vocabulary — no Pleiades, no Orion, no Great Bear, no pole star in the whole English-Konkani dictionary — but it yields the single best indigenous name in this file: the Milky Way as molbamārog, 'the road that is on the sky', with a second Hindu-Konkani form dudavat, and with Maffei expressly noting that Ākāśagaṅgā is Marathi and Canarese and 'not used in Konk.' That is the exact inverse of Marathi, where every one of Molesworth's eight Milky Way names is a Sanskrit river of heaven and no folk name appears at all — until Enthoven, whose Deccan informants call it Vastupurush (the cosmic man of the building site) and Kavadgantak. Gujarati is the emptiest of the three: no distinct Gujarati star name was verified from any source. The Gujarati dictionaries (Belsare; Mehta & Mehta) give only borrowed forms, and their Gujarati script is unrecoverable from the available scans; the Gujarat gazetteers show cultivators paying close attention to the nakṣatras but under their Sanskrit names, with the omen-lore attached directly to those names instead of generating new ones as it did in Marathi. What was NOT found anywhere: no Marathi, Konkani or Gujarati name for Sirius that is not built on the Sanskrit hunter (लुब्धक, व्याध, and the folk-etymological लोभी 'the greedy one'); no vernacular name for Canopus, for Alcor, or for the Hyades apart from the Sanskrit cart शकट; no morning-star or evening-star name in Molesworth at all; no bier, plough or hen figure for Ursa Major; no tribal star name in Enthoven's Tribes and Castes of Bombay or in the Khandesh gazetteer's long Bhil sections; and no Konkani Milky Way river.

### Bengali, Assamese & Odia

All three languages carry the Sanskrit twenty-seven in their own scripts and this file does not reproduce them: Biswas glosses each Bengali lemma 'the Nth of the twenty-seven zodiacal stars according to Hindu astronomy' (আর্দ্রা p. 126, অনুরাধা p. 36, অশ্লেষা p. 83), the Candrakanta Abhidhana does the same for Assamese (আৰ্দ্ৰা p. 102, ভৰণী p. 713), and Praharaj tabulates all twenty-seven with positions, star-counts, kaṭapayādi tags and Bayer letters in one enormous note under ନକ୍ଷତ୍ର (p. 4095) — where, incidentally, the Odia list heads the second asterism ଦ୍ୱିଜା Dwijā rather than Bharaṇī. What is not Sanskrit is what this file is for. THE PRIZE HOLDS AND IS BIGGER THAN EXPECTED: কালপুরুষ / কালপুৰুষ / କାଳପୁରୁଷ Kālapuruṣa for Orion is common to all three languages and has no Sanskrit ancestor as a constellation — in Sanskrit the word is Yama's black-bodied messenger and the jyotiṣa 'zodiac-man'. Biswas (p. 231) gives the Yama sense and the Orion sense side by side; Jñānendramohana Dāsa (p. 512) supplies the decisive gloss, parsing kāla as Yama in the etymology and as TIME in the astronomy — 'the star-cluster by which kāla, that is the rains and the other seasons, is measured' — and adds the alternate name অগ্রহায়ণী; Praharaj (p. 1552) keeps the 'black bodied' of the gloss, gives the same alternate name, and at p. 4095 numbers twenty-one stars of the figure, naming the belt Uṣā, Aniruddha and Citralekhā, the sword Mayūratuṇḍa and Rigel Bāṇarāja, so that in Odia the Kālapuruṣa figure is the frame the nakṣatras of that quarter of the sky are described BY (Ārdrā is 'the knob of Kālapuruṣa's right shoulder'). Both Dāsa and the Assamese dictionary count the figure as seven bright stars. Assamese adds a sky-figure of its own, গোধিকা godhikā, a northern chain shaped like a monitor lizard with the pole star at its tail-tip, attested from Śaṅkaradeva's Kīrttana — described as the Śiśumāra but glossed 'Big Bear', an inconsistency recorded and graded disputed. THE SECOND FINDING IS A SET OF ISOGLOSSES. The Milky Way is a ROAD everywhere in this region and only the traveller changes: an elephant-track in Assamese (হাতীপটি, Candrakanta p. 908) and Odia (ହାତିଦଣ୍ଡା, Praharaj p. 4095; Sambalpuri ହାଁଥିଧରସା p. 9036), both with the literal jungle sense standing as sense 1 of the same lemma; Yama's causeway in Bengali (যমের জাঙ্গাল / যমজাঙ্গাল, in Dāsa pp. 812 and 1811 and in both of Biswas's dictionaries); a cattle-track in Mundari (gaikoạ hora) and Kurukh (gā'e caur binkō). Bengali also has দুধপথ 'milk-road', which may be a calque. A comet is a BROOM in Bengali (ঝাঁটাতারা, marked গ্রাম্য by Dāsa, 'because it is shaped like a broom', p. 882; and Lal Behari Day's villagers call it 'a fiery broomstick') and in Mundari (jonọ ipil), and a TAIL in Odia (ଲଞ୍ଜା ତାରା), Assamese (নেজাল তৰা, attested by Bronson in 1867) and Kurukh (jhal binkō). ODIA IS THE RICHEST OF THE THREE, and its richest field is Venus, which has at least eight names split by apparition and by district — morning ଖଚୁଆ ତରା khacuā tarā ('the star that goes ahead to Yama and reports on the people of this world'), ଫୁକିଆ phukiā of the Garjat states ('when Phukiā rises the fisherwomen begin husking chuṛā'), କୁଆତରା kuātarā < kāvya-tārā, ପୁଆଁ ତରା and ପାହାନ୍ତି ତାରା; evening ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା and Sambalpuri କେଉଁଟି ତାରା, the fisher-caste star — and Praharaj is careful that 'morning star' names a function, not a body, since Mars, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn all fill the role (p. 4814). Bengali splits it শুকতারা / সাঁঝের তারা and Assamese পুবঁতী তৰা / ভোটাতৰা. Beneath standard Odia lies a Sambalpuri folk layer that Praharaj marks ପ୍ରାଦେ., and THIS LAYER IS ONLY INTELLIGIBLE AGAINST THE MUNDA AND DRAVIDIAN LANGUAGES AROUND IT (entered in the sibling file sources/tribal.json; cited here in the notes): the Pleiades are କଠଲା ତାରା 'the carpenter's mallet' in Sambalpuri and moṅgaru ipilko 'the wooden mallet the ploughman flung at the dove' in Mundari; the Big Dipper is ବାଜ୍ଖଟ୍ 'the corpse-bier' in Sambalpuri, topa gaṛa parkom ipilko 'the bier stars' in Mundari and khaṭī pawā bīnkō in Kurukh; Orion's Belt is ନଙ୍ଗଲ ଜୁଡ଼ା 'the yoked plough' in Sambalpuri — with the note that the Khaṛiās will not yoke the plough or sow paddy until it has risen, i.e. not before Baiśākha (p. 4106) — and arar 'the Yoke' in Santali, araṛ ipilko in Mundari, ugtā pagsi binkō in Kurukh. The three Sambalpuri names are not curiosities; they are the Odia end of Munda figures, and that is the single most useful thing this pass established about Odia. Standard Odia meanwhile calls the Big Dipper ସାତଭାଇୟା 'the seven brothers' and the Pleiades କାର୍ତ୍ତିକପୁଞ୍ଜ, marked deśī and carrying a proverb. NEGATIVE FINDINGS, which are half the result. The agricultural-calendar material the brief expected from the gazetteer literature IS NOT THERE: all twenty volumes of Hunter's Statistical Account of Bengal and both of the Statistical Account of Assam were downloaded and grepped and yield exactly one astronomical sentence between them, a quotation of Dalton on the ṛṣis of the Great Bear; the District Gazetteers of Sambalpur, Puri, Cuttack, Balasore, Angul, Santal Parganas, Ranchi, Kamrup, Darrang, Nowgong, Sibsagar and Goalpara yield nothing; the Census reports of 1901 and 1911 yield nothing; Dalton 1872 and Risley 1891 yield only the Santal sept-name and two Sanskrit remarks. The one agricultural marker in this file comes from a DICTIONARY, not a gazetteer. Arcturus and Antares have no vernacular name in any of the three languages — 'Arcturus' returns nothing at all in Biswas or Praharaj, and Antares appears only as an English label inside Praharaj's Jyeṣṭhā table. Bengali and Assamese have the Orion figure but no name for its waist: no Bengali word for Orion's Belt was found in any source, and Dāsa describes it in English without naming it. No pre-1900 attestation of কালপুরুষ = Orion was reached: Haughton 1833 and Ram Comul Sen 1834 do not have it, and Sen renders the English headword Orion descriptively as দক্ষিণদিকস্থ রাশিবিশেষ, তারাবিশেষ 'a certain sign in the southern sky, a certain star'; the earliest attestation here is Dāsa's second edition of 1937, with the Assamese and Odia dictionaries following. Bengali proved the thinnest of the three for folk material: outside কালপুরুষ, ঝাঁটাতারা, পোয়াতে-তারা, তারা খসা and যমের জাঙ্গাল its astronomical vocabulary is almost entirely tatsama. Two words were chased and dropped: the Ḍākabacana couplet Praharaj prints under the Orion word ଅଦ୍ରାବଳି turns out from his own entries at pp. 813-814 and 1080 to be about RAINBOWS east and west, not Orion, so it is not evidence of an Odia agricultural asterism; and Bronson's Assamese-English dictionary of 1867, though it proved to hold the best-dated words in the file, is unusable by grep — the archive.org OCR of its Assamese fount is noise, and its four astronomical entries had to be read off the page images one at a time.

### Tamil

Literary Tamil carries the whole 27-nakshatra system in Tamil phonology — the Tamil Lexicon prints the canonical list under நட்சத்திரம் as acuviṉi, paraṇi, kārttikai, urōkiṇi … irēvati (Tamil Lexicon, s.v. நட்சத்திரம், p. 2135) — and the twelve month-names still in daily use (Cittirai, Vaikāci, Āṉi, Āṭi, Āvaṇi, Puraṭṭāci, Aippaci, Kārttikai, Mārkaḻi, Tai, Māci, Paṅkuṉi) are asterism-derived, the Lexicon deriving Aippaci < āśvayuj, Puraṭṭāci < proṣṭhapadā, Mārkaḻi < mārgaśīrṣa, Paṅkuṉi < Pkt. phagguṇi, Vaikāci < vaiśākha, Āvaṇi < śrāvaṇa, Āṭi < āṣāḍha, Tai < taiṣī, Māci < māgha. That layer is recorded here compactly; the substance of this file is the layer that is not Sanskrit. Two Tamil word-classes generate indigenous star-names. The first is மீன் mīṉ 'star' — a Dravidian word the Lexicon derives from மின்னு- 'to flash' (DEDR 4876, with Ma. mīn, Ko./To. mi·n, Ka. mīn, Kur. bīnkō 'star'), homophonous but not identical with mīṉ 'fish' (DEDR 4885); the Lexicon's derivation of the fish-word from Sanskrit mīna is the older view that the Dravidian Etymological Dictionary does not follow. Counting compounds in -mīṉ name asterisms by their star-counts: அறுமீன் aṟumīṉ and ஆறாமீன் āṟāmīṉ 'six-star' = the Pleiades, எழுமீன் eḻumīṉ 'seven-star' = the Great Bear (Naṟṟiṇai 231), மும்மீன் mummīṉ 'three-star' = Mṛgaśīrṣa, ஐம்மீன் aimmīṉ 'five-star' = Hasta, with கடைமீன் kaṭaimīṉ 'last star' = Revatī and ஆதிமீன் ātimīṉ 'first star' = Aśvinī closing the circle from both ends. Descriptive -mīṉ compounds name the bright wanderers by colour and place: வெண்மீன் veṇmīṉ 'white star' and வெள்ளி veḷḷi 'the silver/white one' = Venus, செம்மீன் cemmīṉ 'red star' = Mars (and, disputed, Arundhatī and Ārdrā), மைம்மீன் maimmīṉ 'black star' = Saturn, வடமீன் vaṭamīṉ 'northern star' and சிறுமீன் ciṟumīṉ 'small star' = Arundhatī/Alcor, வால்மீன் vālmīṉ 'tail-star' = comet, வீழ்மீன் vīḻmīṉ 'falling star' = meteor, கோண்மீன் kōṇmīṉ 'seizing star' = planet as against நாண்மீன் nāṇmīṉ 'day-star' = lunar mansion. The second class is நாள் nāḷ 'day', which by itself means 'lunar asterism' already in the Tolkāppiyam, and which forms a full parallel set of asterism-names by translating the presiding deity into Tamil: எரிநாள் eri-nāḷ 'fire-star' = Kārttikai (the Sanskrit Āgneya), காற்றினாள் kāṟṟiṉāḷ 'wind-star' = Svātī/Arcturus (Sanskrit Vāyavya), நீர்நாள் nīr-nāḷ 'water-star' = Pūrāṭam, மருத்துவநாள் maruttuva-nāḷ 'physician-star' = Aśvinī, மதிநாள் mati-nāḷ 'moon-star' = Mṛgaśīrṣa, மாரிநாள் māri-nāḷ 'rain-star' and கதிர்நாள் katir-nāḷ 'sun-ray star' = Uttiram — and two formations with no Sanskrit model at all: நடுநாள் naṭu-nāḷ 'middle star' for Cittirai, the fourteenth of twenty-seven, and காற்றுமுந்துநாள் kāṟṟu-muntu-nāḷ 'the star that the wind-star precedes' for Viśākhā, an asterism named purely by its position in the Tamil sequence. Nine of the names collected here are attested in the Caṅkam corpus itself, verified verbatim against Project Madurai e-texts: veḷḷi in the drought-omen formula of Puṟanāṉūṟu 35, 117 and 388, veṇmīṉ in the opening couplet of Paṭṭiṉappālai, maimmīṉ and tūmam beside veḷḷi in Puṟanāṉūṟu 117, eḻumīṉ in Naṟṟiṇai 231, aṟumīṉ in Naṟṟiṇai 202, vaṭamīṉ in Puṟanāṉūṟu 122 and Kalittokai 2, ciṟumīṉ in Perumpāṇāṟṟuppaṭai 303, cemmīṉ in Patiṟṟuppattu 31 and Puṟanāṉūṟu 60, kōṇmīṉ in Ciṟupāṇāṟṟuppaṭai 242, nāṇmīṉ in Kalittokai 104, and vaikuṟumīṉ in Akanāṉūṟu 17. The Caṅkam sky is a sky of omens and seasons rather than of horoscopes: Venus quitting its proper northern station for the south is the standard figure for drought and misrule, and Puṟanāṉūṟu 117 stacks Saturn smoking, a comet appearing, and Venus running south as three portents that a good king's land survives. One genuine indigenous constellation-figure surfaced: Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar, glossing மகவெண்மீன் maka-veṇmīṉ at Paṭṭiṉappālai 35, says the Magha asterism 'has the shape of a bent yoke' (முடநுகம்போன்ற வடிவம்) — the Sickle of Leo seen as a crooked ox-yoke. Two names are seamen's and cultivators' rather than literary: ஆறாமீனறவோட்டு āṟāmīṉ-aṟavōṭṭu, the sun's passage through the Pleiades segment, 'regarded by seamen as a period when rough weather is to be anticipated', and ஐப்பசிக்குழப்பம் aippaci-k-kuḻappam, the north-east monsoon squall of the month named for Aśvinī. The Milky Way has a Tamil name of its own that is not a Ganges-metaphor: மாசு mācu, 'the stain', and its compound பூராடமாசு pūrāṭa-mācu, 'the Pūrāṭam stain' — the galaxy named for the Sagittarius asterism where it is brightest — beside the calque பால்வீதிமண்டலம் pāl-vīti-maṇṭalam 'milk-street region'. NEGATIVE FINDINGS, which matter as much: no Tamil name for SIRIUS was found anywhere in the Tamil Lexicon, Winslow or Fabricius — searches on 'Sirius', 'dog star', 'Lubdhaka' and 'Canis' return nothing astronomical, and the Sanskrit Mṛgavyādha/Lubdhaka has no Tamil reflex in the lexica; no Tamil name for ANTARES as an individual star, only Kēṭṭai as 'the 18th nakṣatra, part of Scorpio'; no Tamil name for ORION'S BELT as a distinct three-star group, the 'three stars' of mummīṉ being the Sanskrit Mṛgaśīrṣa head-group; and the TOLKĀPPIYAM, contrary to what one might expect of the oldest Tamil grammar, reckons its six seasons (perumpoḻutu) and six times-of-day (ciṟupoḻutu) by landscape, weather and light — kār with mullai, kūtir midnight with kuṟiñci, vaikaṟai-viṭiyal with marutam, eṟpāṭu with neytal, vēṉil noon with pālai (Poruḷatikāram, Akattiṇaiyiyal 6-12) — and names no asterism in doing so; its only mention of mīṉ is a sandhi rule in the Eḻuttatikāram. The two European calques பெரியகரடி periya-karaṭi 'Great Bear' and சின்னக்கரடி ciṉṉa-k-karaṭi 'Little Bear' are marked 'Pond.' (Puducherry) in the Lexicon's Supplement and are recorded here precisely because they are late and localised, not indigenous.

### Telugu & Kannada

Both languages carry the whole 27-fold nakṣatra system in their own phonology — Kittel enters all twenty-seven as Kannada headwords (ನಕ್ಷತ್ರ, p. 879: 'a constellation, an asterism in the moon's path, a lunar mansion, of which 27 (or 28) are enumerated'), and Brown does the same for Telugu (నక్షత్రము, p. 628) — so the tadbhava forms ಆರಿದ್ರ āridra, ಚಿತ್ತೆ citte, ಪುಬ್ಬೆ/ಹುಬ್ಬೆ pubbe/hubbe, ಜೇಟೆ jēṭe, ಮಘೆ maghe, ಸಾತಿ sāti and their Telugu twins చిత్త citta, పుబ్బ pubba, జెష్ట jeṣṭa are recorded here only as representative specimens. The real find is that TELUGU HAS A COMPLETE PARALLEL SET OF ITS OWN DESCRIPTIVE NAMES for the mansions, formed X-cukka / X-rikka 'X-star' or X-rūpu-rikka 'X-shaped star', which Brown scatters across the dictionary under their first elements and which no one has assembled: tolu-rikka and gurrapu-cukka (Aśvinī), baraṇi-cukka (Bharaṇī), kattera 'scissors' and mangala-katti-rūpu 'barber's-razor shape' (Kṛttikā), baṇḍi-rikka 'cart star' (Rohiṇī), jābili-rikka 'moon star' (Mṛgaśiras), pagaḍapu-rikka 'coral star' (Ārdrā — and Ārdrā is Betelgeuse, which is red), podariṇḍla-cukka (Punarvasu), poṭla-pū-cukka 'snake-gourd-flower star' (Puṣya), sappapu-cukka 'serpent star' and the frankly colloquial asilēru (Āśleṣā), petarula-cukka 'ancestors' star' and jannapu-cukka 'sacrifice star' (Maghā), sāmu-kaṇṭi-cukka (Pūrva-Phalgunī), proddu-rikka 'sun star' (Uttara-Phalgunī), muttepu-rikka 'pearl star' (Citrā = Spica, white), karuvali-rikka 'wind star' (Svāti), kummara-sāre-cukka 'potter's-wheel star' and jōḍu-vēlpula-rikka 'star of the paired gods' (Viśākhā), tāṭi-rikka 'palmyra star' (Jyeṣṭhā), sōku-cukka 'demon star' (Mūla — and Brown's own next line glosses sōkula-rēḍu 'lord of demons' as mūla-rēḍu), nīṭi-rikka 'water star' (Pūrvāṣāḍhā) beside nīṭi-rēni-rikka 'water-KING's star' (Śatabhiṣaj), maddela-rūpu-rikka 'drum-shaped star' (Dhaniṣṭhā), mukkaṇṭi-cukka 'the three-eyed one's star' (Uttara-Bhādrapadā), and three for Revatī: mīnu-rūpu-rikka 'fish-shaped', kona-rikka 'the last star' (answering tolu-rikka 'the first'), muppadi-reṇṭi gumpu 'the group of thirty-two'. Some are calques on the presiding deity, some are shape or colour names owing nothing to Sanskrit, and several also name the month (proddu-rikka-nela = Phālguna, tāṭi-rikka-nela = Jyeṣṭha, poṭla-pū-rikka-nela = Pauṣa), which shows the set worked as a calendar. KANNADA HAS NO SUCH SET: Kittel records only the tadbhava names, and attaches the popular material to them instead as rain proverbs (ಹುಬ್ಬೇ ಮಳೆ ಗುಬ್ಬೀ ತಲೆ ನೆನೆಯುವುದಿಲ್ಲ; ಮಖೆಮೞೆ ಆದರೆ ಮೊಗ ತೊಳೆಯುವದಕ್ಕೆ ಆಗದೇ?) and to the seasonal ಆರಿದ್ರಪುಱು, the ladybird of the Ārdrā rains, for which Kittel gives the Telugu ఆరుద్రపురుగు as an exact equivalent. The shared Dravidian layer lies elsewhere, in the generic and cosmological words, and it pairs up almost item for item: Te. cukka ~ Ka. cikki/cukke (both 'dot' before 'star'); Te. cukkala-teruvu 'street of the stars = sky' ~ Ka. mīn-vaṭṭe / aṟil-vaṭṭe / tārage-vaṭṭe 'star-road = sky'; Te. cukkala-rēḍu 'king of the stars = the moon' ~ Ka. mīngaḷ-eṟeya and tārageyāḷma, same sense; Te. tōka-cukka 'tail star = comet' ~ Ka. bāla-cikki, same compound with each language's own word for tail. Two Dravidian words split the languages: Kannada mīn is 'star' outright ('a fish of the sky-ocean?', Kittel's own guess, p. 1328) where Telugu mīnu is only 'fish' and touches the sky solely in mīnu-rūpu-rikka; and Kannada beḷḷi 'silver' is the name of Venus (with Tamil and Malayalam veḷḷi) where Telugu kept only the metal and named Venus vēgu-cukka 'dawn star'. Kannada also has an indigenous Milky Way that Sanskrit does not suggest — bāṅ-keṟe 'the sky-TANK', beside bāṅ-kaḍal 'sky-sea' and bān-toṟe 'sky-river' — the irrigation tank of the Karnataka countryside put in the sky, and Kittel's illustrative verse has the stars vanishing in it like diving fish. Telugu's milk-track names (pāla-punta, pāla-bāṭa) are not in Brown at all and are attested here only from Gwynn 1991. The agricultural sky is vernacular in both: Telugu kārte, marked [Tel.] by Brown, is the sun's thirteen-day stay in each asterism and the unit of the Deccan farming year, and Thurston records the working system for Lingāyat cultivators of Bellary — cholam on the Rohiṇi, Mṛgaśira and Ārdrā rains, cotton and horse gram on Pubba and Uttara, no weeding in Maghā, no lightning in Svāti. Telugu punāsa, the year's first inferior crop, is Punarvasu with the sky worn off it entirely. NEGATIVE FINDINGS, all of them from exhaustive searching of both dictionaries: neither language has any Dravidian name for URSA MAJOR — no plough, no cart, no bier, no seven sisters, only saptarṣi and citraśikhaṇḍi in both; none for ORION or Orion's Belt (Kittel's ilvalegaḷ is Sanskrit Ilvalāḥ with a Kannada plural; āgrahāyaṇi is a tatsama); none for CANOPUS (Agastya in both); none for SIRIUS in Telugu at all, and in Kannada only Sanskrit lubdhaka — which in Kannada lexicography usually means Ārdrā, not Sirius, a trap flagged in the entry; none for the POLE STAR beyond Dhruva, though Kannada has the popular dhruva-pāśa, the rope the earth hangs from; and no Dravidian PLEIADES name in Kannada, where Telugu has two. Brown twice calls Arundhatī 'a star in the Pleiades', which is wrong and is recorded as disputed because he may be reporting a real popular misidentification — Thurston shows the same star being called the pole star in south Indian weddings.

### Malayalam, Tulu, Kodava & Sinhala

Malayalam runs the full 27-nakshatra series in Dravidianised form — Aśvati, Bharaṇi, Kārttika, Rōhiṇi, Makayiram, Tiruvātira … Iravati — and it still governs birth-star reckoning: Gundert 1872 already lexicalises ജന്മനക്ഷത്രം 'the asterism under which one is born' (p. 403) and അനുജന്മനക്ഷത്രം 'the 10th and 19th asterisms after it' (p. 28), and the ordinary word for a birth-star is not the Sanskrit നക്ഷത്രം but the inherited Dravidian നാള്‍ nāḷ 'day', whose illustrative phrase in Gundert is 'to settle [a marriage] after examining the nāḷ and the compatibility' (p. 547). Those names are recorded here compactly, in one collective entry plus nine individually; the real yield is elsewhere. Malayalam's vernacular sky is built on മീന്‍ mīn 'star/fish' (DEDR 4876) — കൊളളിമീന്‍ 'firebrand-star' meteor, വാല്‍മീന്‍ 'tail-star' comet, വെണ്മീന്‍ 'white star' and പെരുമീന്‍ 'great star' for Venus, beside വെള്ളി veḷḷi 'silver = Venus = Friday' and the North Malabar dialect word കൊററി koṟṟi 'morning star', which has no Sanskrit counterpart at all. Two Malayalam finds have no parallel in the other three languages: ഞേങ്ങോല്‍ ñēṅṅōl 'plough-shaft', cross-referenced by Gundert to മുഴക്കോല്‍ 'measuring-rod', a constellation defined purely by its farming use — it rises in Dhanu an hour after sunset and tells the cultivator when to drain the field before sowing (p. 413; probably but not certainly Orion's Belt) — and the ñāṟṟu system, ഞാററുതല / ഞാററുവേലി / ഞായററുനില, the twenty-seven asterism-periods of 13 4/9 days each by which the Kerala farming year is still divided, with Tiruvātira at the burst of the south-west monsoon as 'best time for planting' (pp. 411–412, 436). NEGATIVE: no navigational star name was found for Kerala in any public-domain source — Gundert has no star under 'mariner', 'sailor' or 'compass', Logan's Malabar Manual has none, and the words Pleiades, Orion, Canopus, Sirius, Arcturus, pole star and Milky Way do not occur once in all seven volumes of Thurston. Tulu and Kodava are nearly empty of star names, and that is the result rather than a failure: each has exactly ONE native star-word, the reflex of Dravidian *veḷ 'white' — Tulu ಬೊಳ್ಳಿ boḷḷi 'a star; silver' (Männer 1886 p. 502), forming ತಂಜದ ಬೊಳ್ಳಿ 'the evening star' (p. 262), and Kodava boḷḷi in boḷḷi mi·nï 'morning star' (DEDR 5496) and ಬೊಳ್ಳಿಳಾಚೆ boḷḷiáche 'Friday' (Cole 1867 p. 136) — Tulu naming Venus at dusk and Kodagu at dawn. Kodava has no word for 'star' anywhere in Cole's grammar, no name for the Pleiades, Orion, the pole star, the Milky Way, a comet or a meteor, and DEDR gives it mi·nï only inside that one compound; Tulu adds only three descriptive coinages, all from Männer's English-to-Tulu direction — ಹೊರಸಿನ್ಟ ನಕ್ಷತ್ರೊಳಿ ಕೂಟ 'the star-cluster of the COT' for Ursa Major (the one indigenous constellation image in either language), ನಕ್ಷತ್ರೊಳಿ ಸಾಲ್ 'row of stars' for the Milky Way, and ಆಕಾಶೊಡ್ಡು ಬೂರ್ದಿ ಕಲ್ಲ್ 'stone fallen from the sky' for a meteorite. Neither language times agriculture by a star: Sturrock says all Tulu cultivation runs on the twelve solar months, which have native Tulu names (Paggu, Besha, Kártél, Áte…) that are not star-names (1894 p. 216), Coorg ploughing begins on the first of yaḍamyáru whatever the rain (Cole p. 135), and the Huttari harvest is fixed by the full moon. Sinhala, the comparative control, gives the sharpest answer: it replaced NONE of the twenty-seven — Carter's formula for each is literally 'E. of', Eḷu form of, and Clough's is 'Elu form of', so asvida is Sanskrit aśvinī, denaṭa is dhaniṣṭhā, deṭa is jyeṣṭhā, all merely sound-shifted — while coining freely OUTSIDE that list: හත්·දින්න hat·dinna 'seven-produced' for the Pleiades, අහස් ගඟ ahas gaṅga 'sky-river' for the Milky Way (a calque, per Jayatilaka, of ākāśagaṅgā — the compound Malayalam and Tulu simply borrowed), ඉරබටු තරුව 'star after sunset' and පහන් තරුව 'dawn-star' for Venus, දුම්·කෙහෙලිය 'smoke-banner' for a comet, කළමුනිදුතරුව for Canopus, and three native words for 'constellation' (තරු·වැළ, තරු·පොකුර, උළු කැන) where Malayalam has none. What was portable, then, was the nakshatra list and the learned Sanskrit stock — Dhruva, Agastya/Agasti, Saptarṣi, Ākāśagaṅgā, Ulkā, Dhūmaketu travel intact into all four — and what was not portable was the ordinary night sky, which every language named for itself out of fish, silver, firebrands, plough-beams, cots and river-water.

### The north-east — Mizo, Mara, Meitei, Garo and four Naga tribes

THE NORTH-EAST WAS EXPECTED TO BE THIN AND IS THE RICHEST REGION IN THIS DATABASE. The expectation was reasonable: tribal.json searched Hodson's Naga Tribes of Manipur and got five Khasi words and nothing else. It was wrong twice over. Lorrain's Dictionary of the Lushai Language (1940) is the single best source in the whole compilation, with twenty-two star headwords mapped star-by-star onto Western constellations; and the six colonial monographs that archive.org would not serve on the first pass — Playfair on the Garos, Hutton on the Angamis and the Semas, Mills on the Aos and the Rengmas, Parry on the Lakhers — turned out on the second pass to hold ninety more names between them. WHAT THE REGION SHARES AND THE MAINLAND DOES NOT: (1) ORION'S BELT IS A CARRIED LOAD. Sema Phoghwosülesipfemi are three men carrying a roof-beam, Angami Thepeko three men carrying a house-post, Lakher Vothawlapiapa two men carrying a pig, Garo Wak-ripe the pig itself carried on a pole. In every case they are ambushed, and in every case but the Garo the stars of Orion's Sword are the enemies who ambushed them. The mainland's Orion is a plough, a yoke or a bedstead and is never a hunt; the north-east's is a killing on a path, and even the reversal is instructive — the Rengmas make the belt the ambushers and the sword the travellers walking into them. (2) THE MILKY WAY IS A SEASONAL BOUNDARY, not a cattle road. Ao 'cold-weather rains-divider', Lakher Sonatachhiarari 'rains and dry weather boundary', Mizo Thlasik Kong 'the cold weather road'; and the Lakhers say how it is read — by which side of the band has the larger expanse of empty sky. The exceptions are the two that make it water: Angami Pfiüdzücha is the Barak river, Rengma Züle and Serizü are the Diyung and the Tulo, and Sema Azughongu is the river of souls. (3) SHOOTING STARS ARE STAR-DUNG — Sema ayeba, Lhota, Lakher Awsi-ih, Mizo arsi êk, Meitei with the lexicographer's own morphology [star + faeces]. (4) NO COT AND NO THIEVES. The cot with three thieves at its foot is the most widespread figure on the Indian mainland and it does not cross the hills. In its place Ursa Major is a corpse: Lakher Keulachongpa is a man killed in a raid with his head and left leg carried off by his slayers, and the Lusheis tell the same of Zangkhua. THE ONE COMPLETE SYSTEM: the fourteen Garo names are all episodes of a single funeral, the cremation of the moon's mother — Cassiopeia the bearing of the body, Sirius the star that lit the pyre, the Pleiades the sacrificial cock, the Square of Pegasus the four posts of the pyre, Orion's Belt the pig brought as food, the Milky Way the hoofprints of the buffalo that bolted. No other tradition here organises its whole sky as one event. THE NEGATIVES ARE AS SHARP AS THE FINDS. Mills states flatly that Ao stars 'are too small and remote to interest the Ao much, and none of the constellations seem to have names' — from the same author who recorded twenty Rengma names next door. His Lhota Nagas has no star vocabulary at all beyond shooting stars being the falling dung of stars. Gurdon's The Khasis, read end to end, has no astronomy whatever, so the five Khasi words in tribal.json remain the whole of Khasi. Endle's The Kacharis has not one sky word, so Bodo is still unattested. Register is `tribal` throughout except Meitei dhrubatarā.

### Nepali, Newar, Kumaoni & Tibetan — the Himalaya

THE HIMALAYA IS THIN, AND THE REASON IS PARTLY THE SOURCES AND PARTLY THE SKY. Nepali and Newar both have good dictionaries and both were worked; the Indian Himalaya proper — Kumaon, Garhwal, Ladakh, Spiti, Sikkim — has almost nothing reachable, and what was reached is one word. NEPALI BUILDS ITS WHOLE SKY BY COMPOUNDING ON ONE NOUN. Turner's entry for तारो tāro is the Nepali heaven in miniature: dhrub-tāro the polestar, puchre tāro 'the tailed star' a comet, phuṭne tāro 'the bursting star' a meteor, tārā-maṇḍal a constellation, and — at the same headword and without ceremony — SĀT TĀRĀ, 'the seven stars', the Great Bear. That last is the finding. Every mainland community in this database sees furniture in those seven stars and somebody stealing it; Nepali counts them. The learned calque सप्त-रिखि sapta-rikhi stands elsewhere in the dictionary, made, Turner says, 'on the model of' Sanskrit saptarṣi — so Nepali has both, and only the count is ordinary speech. The other real Nepali figure is तिन्-तारे tin-tāre, 'the three stars', which Turner defines as three particular stars that always appear in a straight line: Orion's Belt, named for what it looks like, as Sindhi ṭīṛū and Mizo Si-mei-talh are in the north-western and north-eastern files. For the PLEIADES Nepali has three words at once — its own गुज्मुजि तारा gujmuji tārā 'the bunched, clustered stars'; the Hindi loan कच्पचिया kacpaciyā, the same crowding image travelling up from the plains; and किर्किटि kirkiṭi, which Turner marks 'popular' and derives, with an audible shrug, from the loan kṛttikā — 'after what?' He compares Nepali kirkaũlā, 'small bits of rice grains', which is probably the answer he would not commit to. THE ONE NEPALI NAKSHATRA THAT BECAME A WORD FOR A PERSON is मुल् mul, the eleven-star asterism reckoned unlucky, whose derivative मुल्याहा mulyāhā means 'born under mul' and, as a noun, 'an unfortunate person, an orphan'. Elsewhere in this database the asterisms govern the farming year; here one of them names a social condition. NEWAR IS THE OPPOSITE SHAPE: BORROWED ASTERISMS, HOME-MADE METEORS. The Kathmandu valley dictionaries give नगु nagu 'a star' and build नगु गाः nagu gāḥ 'a group of stars' on it, but every asterism is Sanskrit and the Milky Way is आकाश गंगा. What Newar made itself is the transient: ताहाव नगतिं tāhāva nagatiṃ, 'the long star', for a comet or shooting star, with the modern reflex tāhāhnagu and the modern paraphrase म्हेप्वना तहाँ नगु mhepwanā tahā̃ nagu, 'the star with a drawn-out tail'. AND NEWAR CAN BE DATED. Malla's Dictionary of Classical Newari is compiled from manuscripts and cites the Nepal Saṃvat of each attestation, so this file carries the only dated vernacular star-words in the database: ādra in NS 509 (1389 CE), ulaka and tāhāva nagatiṃ in NS 811 (1691), dhurmmaketu in NS 883 (1763). THE INDIAN HIMALAYA IS ESSENTIALLY UNREACHED, AND THAT IS THE HONEST HEADLINE OF THIS WAVE. Grierson's Pahārī volume was downloaded in full and searched: the comparative word-list gives only a reflex of tārā for 'star', and the Kumauni-English vocabulary yields exactly one sky name, लम्पुछा तारो lampuchhā tāro, 'the long-tailed star', a comet — plus grahan for an eclipse, which is a loan. Nothing for the Pleiades, Orion, the Great Bear, the Milky Way or the pole star, in Kumaoni or in any other Pahārī dialect in the volume; and the Devanagari in that scan is OCR noise, so nothing could be transcribed in script even where it exists. TIBETAN AND LADAKHI WERE NOT REACHED AT ALL: DSAL lists Jäschke (1881) and Das (1902) but hosts neither — its note is that a searchable database is still being built — and both, together with Atkinson's Himalayan Gazetteer, returned HTTP 503 from archive.org across repeated attempts. So there is no Ladakhi, Spiti, Bhutia, Monpa, Sherpa or Garhwali material here, and the Buddhist Himalaya, which has a fully developed astronomical tradition of its own, is absent from this database entirely.

### The maritime calendar and the peninsular forest

TWO RESULTS, AND THE SECOND IS A NEGATIVE THAT EXPLAINS SEVERAL OTHERS. FIRST: THE MALDIVE AND MINICOY SKY IS THE SAME TWENTY-SEVEN ASTERISMS, RE-INDEXED AGAINST THE MONSOON. Maniku's Dhivehi vocabulary gives every one of the twenty-seven a headword with its stars in Bayer designations — and defines each not by its place in the moon's circuit but by its number within a monsoon: eighteen nakaiy of the hulhangu or south-west monsoon, from Assidha (Aśvinī) to Dhosha (Jyeṣṭhā), then nine of the iruvai or north-east, from Mula (Mūla) to Reyva (Revatī), 'the ninth and the last'. Every other language in this database that has the twenty-seven has them as the moon's stations counted once round; Divehi keeps the names and re-hangs them on the SUN and the wind. That is a sailor's calendar — it answers when the season turns, not where the moon is — and it is why Mūla, an unremarkable nineteenth in the Sanskrit list, is here the hinge of the year. The system was administered: ނަކަތްޗާ nakaiychaa, 'the nakaiy man', was an office at the Sultan's palace. And it was kept true to the sun by a twenty-eighth, އަވިހި AVIHI, a variable intercalary nakaiy now disused — the only place in this database where a vernacular calendar's leap mechanism is recorded. Minicoy (Maliku), Indian territory in Lakshadweep, speaks this language and uses this calendar. SECOND: THE CHOLANAIKKANS HAVE NO CONSTELLATIONS, AND THE RECORDERS SAY WHY IN THEIR FIRST SENTENCE — 'absence of farming activities made sky-watching a never compelling affair'. They are forest foragers of fewer than two hundred people in the Nilambur reserves. They have two words for 'star', Koram and Udumbam, and identify no star and no pattern whatever: shown the night sky in the Kozhikode planetarium, the party smiled and walked out. They do not know that the sun rises at different points through the year and so do not connect it with the seasons. THIS IS THE CONTROL CASE FOR THE WHOLE DATABASE. tribal.json already had Radcliffe-Brown's flat statement that constellations are not recognised in the North Andaman, recorded as a result rather than a gap; here the same result comes with a cause attached, and it is the cause the rest of this compilation would predict. Every figure in this database that carries a story belongs to a community that plants something — the cot and the three thieves, the plough with its two bullocks and its ploughman, the sowing-star, the threshing floor, the seed drill, the Pleiades that say when to sow. What the Cholanaikkans do have is a meteor, Katui, 'embers of the fire sent by the gods' — and a meteor needs no calendar. THE FISHERMEN'S MEASURES WERE NOT FOUND, AND THAT IS THE WAVE'S REAL FAILURE. The plan aimed at the fist-and-finger star-altitude systems reported for the Indian Ocean — kai kanakku in Lakshadweep and Malabar, viral kanakku in Tamil Nadu, dhru in Gujarat — and the lexicographic route does not reach them. The Tamil Lexicon has கைக்கணக்கு kai-k-kaṇakku only as a memorandum of accounts and has no விரற்கணக்கு at all; its navigational vocabulary is generic (மாலுமி mālumi 'pilot, navigator', from the Arabic muʿallim that also names the Kutchi mālam manuals; சுக்கானி cukkāni 'helmsman'; காந்தப்பெட்டி kānta-p-peṭṭi 'magnet box', the mariner's compass). The one real find is சங்கு caṅku, the gnomon that measures the sun's altitude by its shadow — the classical instrument, not a rule of thumb, and the second entry in this database's 'Measuring the sky' object after Mizo suk-chen. A proper pass at the fist-measures needs the maritime literature (Tibbetts on Arab navigation, the Kutchi mālam manuscripts), all of it in copyright and none of it reached here. PENINSULAR TRIBAL, LARGELY DRY AGAIN. Thurston's volume II was downloaded and searched for nine sky terms and returned one hit, on 'constellation', with no star name — confirming from a second volume what tamil.json found in the other six. No Sora, Savara, Kui, Irula, Kurumba, Chenchu or Koya source could be obtained: the dictionary and monograph identifiers tried on archive.org returned empty metadata, and none of those languages is on DSAL. The Vahia and Halkare Pardhi paper, listed in the plan since Wave 1, is still not obtained.

### The occupational and caste register

THE OCCUPATIONAL AND CASTE AXIS IS ALMOST UNRECORDED, AND THAT IS THIS WAVE'S RESULT. The plan aimed at sky-names keyed to what people do rather than to what they speak — pastoralists (Dhangar, Kuruba, Gujjar, Rabari, Bharvad, Golla), fishing castes, the Banjara outside Vidarbha. Three of the largest folklore compendia of colonial India were downloaded in full and cross-searched: Enthoven's Folklore of Bombay (1924) and both volumes of Crooke's Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), every line containing a sky word tested against twenty occupational and caste terms. THE CROSS-SEARCH RETURNED ONE HIT IN THREE VOLUMES, and it was a false positive. This is the same shape the database has met four times already: Russell and Hiralal yielded one community with named figures in four volumes (the Dhuri), Thurston almost nothing in seven, Rose's Glossary nothing in the volume obtained. The colonial compendia record sky-lore by LANGUAGE and by TRIBE, and essentially never by trade. WHAT THE COMPENDIA DO HAVE HAD MOSTLY BEEN TAKEN ALREADY. Enthoven's chapter on stars and planets was worked in an earlier pass and eight entries in marathi_gujarati.json come from it, including the two best occupational items in the whole database: GADLI, Rohiṇī and Kṛttikā together, 'supposed to indicate the rise and fall in the cotton-market' — the only commodity omen here — and the Konkan death-divination in which a man who cannot make out the pole star, or in the other version Arundhatī, has six months to live. Re-reading the chapter yielded three things it had missed, entered here. FIRST, THE FOUR MAṆḌALAS. A meteor is read by which quarter of the sky it falls from: Vāyu-maṇḍal portends an epidemic, Varuṇa-maṇḍal is favourable to human happiness, Indra-maṇḍal threatens kings, Agni-maṇḍal threatens war between nations. This is a partition of the sky the database did not have — the Sanskrit compilation carries the nine vīthīs, the planets' roads, and Rajasthani keeps one of them, but the maṇḍalas divide by presiding deity and exist only to answer where a meteor came from. And in the same passage is the sharpest occupational split recorded anywhere here: a meteor falling into the sea forebodes evil to the dwellers on earth generally, but IN THE KANARA DISTRICT the same fall is held to promise rain. A coast that wants rain reads the omen the other way up. SECOND, TĀRĀ-BĀRAS, the name of the rite of showing the pole star to a couple as soon as the marriage knot is tied — the only name for a sky-RITE in this database, everything else here naming a star, a figure, a wind or a season. THIRD, CROOKE ON MŪLA, which corroborates a Wave 4 finding from nine hundred kilometres away and thirty-five years earlier. Turner's Nepali dictionary has मुल्याहा mulyāhā, 'born under mul', meaning as a noun 'an unfortunate person, an orphan'. Crooke gives the social fact behind the word: the twenty-seven asterisms serve only to cast a marriage horoscope, and the one an ordinary cultivator must reckon with is the unlucky Mūla, because a son born under it needs an elaborate purification. An asterism that matters as a social category rather than as a season or a shape. THE SCHEMA CHANGED HERE, WHICH IS WHAT THIS WAVE WAS REALLY FOR. The expansion plan flagged from the start that this database is keyed on language while the question being asked is partly about communities, and that the mismatch had already bitten once — the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entries in tribal.json had to be argued into a caveat because the Dhuri are a caste and not a language. An optional `community` field is now part of the schema, carried by the three entries in this file and back-filled onto the five earlier entries that had a community buried in their `region` string: the Dhuri rice-parchers of Chhattisgarh, the Deshasth Brahmans of Dharwar, the Konda Dora of the Vizagapatam Agency, the Uppu Yerukala or Korava of the Telugu country, and the Lingāyat cultivators of Bellary whose kārte rain-calendar Thurston recorded. Eight entries out of 777 carry a community, and that ratio is the finding restated.

### Adivasi & tribal traditions

Four communities carry a star nomenclature deep enough to be called a system, and they are not the ones a Sanskrit database would predict. The Mundas are first by a distance: Hoffmann's Encyclopaedia Mundarica vol. VII (cols. 1919-1925, s.v. ipil) is a seven-page star map with about thirty named objects, a plate, and a stated method, and it opens by saying that the Munda 'neither knows, nor cares to know, what a horoscope is'. Santali is second, through Campbell (1899) and Bodding vol. V (1936); Kurukh has eight or nine names in Grignard (1924); Gondi has a large modern field survey (Vahia & Halkare 2013, in copyright, paraphrased here) and essentially nothing in the colonial record. Toda has Rivers (1906) — three pages, but unusually careful, and he drew the Great Bear on paper to have it named rather than trusting a verbal description. Ho, Khasi, Nicobarese and Andamanese yield a handful of terms each. The organising principles are agricultural and domestic rather than zodiacal: nothing here divides the ecliptic, nothing tracks the moon's monthly stations, and where the nakshatra system does surface it has been converted into something else — Santali ruhni is not Aldebaran but the seven-day sowing week in Jeṭ, and Bodding marks the planet names sukro and Sani '(only in books)', meaning they are printed but not spoken. Three figures recur across unrelated language families and are the real find. (1) Ursa Major is a cot: Santali buḍhi parkom ipil 'the old woman's cot', Kurukh khaṭī-pāwā bīnkō 'the cot-feet constellation' with the three handle stars called ḍhālbar 'thieves', Gondi Sedona Katul with Kalher 'thieves' and a story that the old woman must never fall asleep or the world ends, and — printed in 1916, before any of the fieldwork — the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri belief that the Great Bear is a cot with three thieves tied to it. Mundari alone turns the same cot into a bier, with Alioth and Mizar as mourners walking away from the grave. (2) Orion is a plough or a yoke, never a hunter: Santali and Mundari araṛ ipilko 'the yoke stars', Mundari siṭan ipil 'the ploughman' for Rigel, Kurukh ugtā-pagṛī bīnkō, Gondi Nangar. Only the Toda break this, reading the sword as a porcupine the belt stars are running away from. (3) The Milky Way is a road with livestock on it: Mundari gaiko hora 'the cattle road', walked by Lugu, Siṅgboṅga's cowherd, who is himself the morning star; Kurukh gāy-chour bīnkō, the cattle-track out of the village; Gondi Dhor Sari, the path of the animals; Santali hat dahar, the market road. Only the seafaring Nicobarese make it water — dāk-oal-kalahoiya, 'river in the sky'. A fourth, subtler thread is a bird on a nest with something thrown at it: Mundari putam ipil (the dove, Aldebaran) with jarom ipilkiŋ (her two eggs) and muṅgaru ipilko (the mallet flung at her, the Pleiades); Santali potam bele (the pigeon's eggs, ε Lyrae) with bele kombro (the egg thief, Vega); Gondi Purad and Mes (a bird and its eggs) with the Pleiades thrown at them. Three recorders working a century apart, three different parts of the sky, one story. Meteors are the excrement of the stars in Santali (ipil ic'), Mundari (ipilko ic') and Gondi (sukum pelkta) alike, which follows from stars being living beings — in Ho they are grammatically animate, as Burrows' paradigm ipil / ipilkiŋ / ipilko shows, while trees are not. Comets are a broom in Mundari, Kurukh and Gondi, and in Khasi a star smoking a pipe ('lur-dih-duma). DRY SOURCES, recorded as findings rather than omitted. Bhili: nothing. Neither Russell & Hiralal's Bhil article nor any public-domain dictionary gives a Bhil star name; the only substantial treatment is Shetye, Halkare & Sule, JAHH 26(2), 441-468 (2023), which is in copyright and which could not be obtained in full, so no Bhili entry is offered rather than a guessed one. Naga: Hodson's The Naga Tribes of Manipur (1911) has sun- and moon-worship at Mao, an eclipse rite and a dog-and-moon tale, and not one star name; searched for Pleiades, Orion, Great Bear, Milky Way, pole star and constellation with zero hits. Khasi: Gurdon's The Khasis (1907) likewise yields only Ka Sngi (the sun, feminine) and U Bynai (the moon, masculine) and the story of the moon's spots — every Khasi entry here comes from Nissor Singh's dictionary instead, and the English-Khasi dictionary of 1920 was rejected because its 'Milky Way' is a translator's descriptive coinage, not a Khasi name. Andamanese: Man found exactly one named constellation in the whole archipelago (bela-, Orion's Belt), and Radcliffe-Brown forty years later in the North Andaman states flatly that individual stars and constellations are not recognised there at all — the stars are simply Catlo, the big ones, named for a beetle, and Katan, the small ones, named for the firefly. Russell & Hiralal's four volumes, grepped end to end, produced sky cosmology (Bhuiya, Turi, Dumal) but only one community with named figures, the Dhuri. DSAL hosts no Munda, Kurukh, Gondi, Bhili, Khasi or Andamanese dictionary at all. Bodding's Santal Dictionary is on the Internet Archive only as vol. V, so his entries for arar ipil, buḍhi parkom and ipil itself could not be read; likewise Encyclopaedia Mundarica vols. IX, XI and XIV-XVI are missing, which is why several Mundari names rest on the ipil article alone. ELEVEN GOND ENTRIES ADDED ON A LATER PASS, from a re-read of Vahia & Halkare's Table 5 and their fifteen village accounts. The Sun and the Moon are Lingo and Jango, the two Gond culture heroes — no other language in this database names the Sun after a person of its own mythology. The rainbow is Kamarpatta or Gulel, a belt or a catapult, and it joins the Kolam and Banjara rainbows to make the bow the shared figure across all three communities surveyed. The four quarters of the horizon are named and are used for burial rather than for travel, and the southern one at Lodha is Rakshas Disha, which is the Pardhi rakshasbaku in another family. The broom, Kayshar, turns out to sit on the Pleiades in three villages and on comets in the rest, one word covering both. And the three thieves at the cot are, in one village, not thieves at all but a nobleman, his wife and his officer walking towards salvation.

### Modern field surveys of Adivasi astronomy

Five modern field surveys, covering eleven communities that the printed record of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries does not reach at all. tribal.json was built from colonial lexicography and ethnography and could name only five communities with a sky nomenclature deep enough to call a system; this file adds the Banjara, the Kolam, the Korku, three Nicobar island communities and the Bhil, Mavchi Bhil, Vasave Bhil, Pawra and Kokna, all recorded between 2013 and 2023 by teams working village by village with a questionnaire. Every one of these papers is in copyright, so every entry here is paraphrased and every `quote` is null, on the footing tribal.json already established for its twenty Gondi entries. THE FOUR THREADS tribal.json IDENTIFIED ALL HOLD, AND ONE OF THEM GETS SHARPER. (1) THE COT: the Big Dipper is a cot in Kolami (Mandater), a cot of the DEAD in Lambadi (Jamakhat, from Yama), a hen-basket on Chowra (Lonob) and a COFFIN on Teressa (Rohiung), and the Bhil, Pawra and Kokna all have the cot with its leg pulled crooked by a thief. Lambadi is Indo-Aryan, Kolami and Bhili are Dravidian and Indo-Aryan respectively, Korku is Munda, Nicobarese is island Austroasiatic — and the death sense, which tribal.json found only in Mundari's bier, now appears three times in unrelated languages. (2) THE THIEVES: three of them, everywhere, but WHO they are is local. Korku numbers them (Pahila, Dusara, Tisara chor); the Kolams make them a Kolam, a Gond and a Pardhan; the Bhils make them the village elder, the chief, the sheriff and the revenue collector. The figure is shared, the cast is politics. (3) ORION IS AN IMPLEMENT, NOT A HUNTER: a seed drill for the Kolams (Tipan) and the Bhils (Pambar), a full plough with two bullocks and a ploughman for the Korku (Harnangar, Doba 1, Doba 2, Nangarnara manus). The single exception is the Banjaras, a trading people, who keep the mainstream deer (Halni) and, the paper notes, barely look at Orion otherwise. (4) THE MILKY WAY IS A ROAD WITH ANIMALS ON IT: Kolam Margam 'an animal path', Banjara Mardaar wat 'the path of the dead or of animals', Bhil and Mavchi 'the path of cows'. The Nicobarese are the exception the earlier file already predicted: on Camorta and Teressa it is a spring of water. THE BIRD AND ITS EGGS, which tribal.json called a subtler fourth thread, turns out to be the most productive figure of all. Kolam Kovela Kor is the Pleiades as one large bird and several small ones, Kolam Bhori is Aldebaran the bird with two eggs, Korku Pankheru is Sirius the bird with Bhori Aakom its eggs — the same word Bhori in a Dravidian and a Munda language — and among the Bhil, Pawra and Kokna a single bird named hulgi carries Orion's Belt, the Pleiades and a triangle of Auriga as its eggs in different villages. The figure is stable; the stars it lands on are not. TWO OTHER RESULTS. Kolam Irukmara, the Mahua tree at Crux with an old woman and a young woman gathering its flowers beneath it, is almost certainly the same word as Gondi Irukna Mara, which tribal.json had to record as unidentified for want of a modern equivalent; this file does not alter that entry but the two should be read together. And the Bhil Milky Way at Varpada is a kinship rule drawn on the sky: the band forks because a woman meeting her husband's elder brother on the road must turn aside, and the avoidance is a real rule of conduct in these communities. NEGATIVE AND UNOBTAINED. The Banjara pole star, which this summary previously recorded as identified but unnamed, is named twice in the paper's appendix as Dhruv Tara and is now entered — the negative finding was true of Table 1 and false of the paper, and it is corrected here rather than quietly dropped; no name is claimed for none for the Korku words for comet and meteor, which the paper describes ('a broom star', 'stellar excreta') without printing; and none for the Korku Lupus figure, for which only the English gloss 'Tree of Mahua' is given. The second-hand Nicobarese lists quoted inside the 2018 paper from Rajamanickam (1997) and Justine (2013) — Onchiana for Centaurus, Thyan for Orion, Mahayuvan for Crux, Musaha for Ursa Major, Gna-gna-hyaam for the Pleiades, and Justine's Chowra and Kondule constellation lists — are NOT entered: they are transcriptions at second hand, and this database does not rest an entry on those. They are the obvious next thing to chase. Three further papers of the same programme were not obtained and no entry is offered from them: the Pardhi study, the Cholanaikkan study, and the Warli, Dhodia, Katkari and Kokna study. THIRTY-SIX BANJARA AND KOLAM ENTRIES ADDED ON A LATER PASS from the village appendices of the 2014 paper, pp. 77-84. The largest single gain is the compass: six Banjara quarters and four Kolam ones, where the Banjara north is Dongari, 'the hills' — the same word the Pardhi use, in this same file — and the two Kolam villages that gave the quarters swap north and south between them, which is recorded as disputed rather than resolved. The Kolam rainbow Ayak is the grandparents, the grandfather standing at the violet end and the grandmother at the red, the only name in this database that divides a sky object by colour and puts a person at each end. The five animals around Samdur that gauge the coming monsoon are named at last — Namli the peacock, Barre the buffalo, Pande the frog, Mekam the deer, Gurram the horse, and a sixth, the pig Ture — with the recorders' suggested constellations carried as disputed because the suggestions are theirs and not the informants'. Kavadi Kunde, the tower of three pots, is Cygnus in most villages and Orion's Belt in two, and the paper says so itself. And the Banjaras see an old woman, yadi, spinning cotton under a banyan tree in the face of the Moon — the only reading of the lunar maria anywhere in these fifty-seven languages.

## Caveats, per research file

Read these before treating any entry as settled.

### Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi & Rajasthani

- The Rajasthani entries were added in a later correction pass and the claim they replace was wrong. This file previously stated that no Rajasthani star name could be verified and that Lalas 'is in copyright and was not consulted' — treating copyright as a reason not to read a source, where the rest of this database treats it only as a reason not to quote one. Both Rajasthani dictionaries are on DSAL. Macalister (1898) is public domain and is quoted verbatim; Lalas (2nd ed. 2013) is in copyright and is paraphrased with `quote` null, exactly as the Gondi material in tribal.json is. The seven entries are still a first pass over two dictionaries, not a survey of Rajasthani: the Panjab and North Indian Notes and Queries remain silent on Rajputana, Fallon's Māṛ. tags still never fall on a sky word, and no Rajasthani ethnography has been searched.
- The `register` field is an analytic judgement by the compiler, not a label found in the sources. `borrowed` is used for both tatsama forms (dhruv-tārā, ākāś-gaṅgā) and tadbhava reflexes in vernacular phonology (sūk < Śukra, kirhkaṭī < Kṛttikā, rohṇī, magghā); `vernacular` is used mainly for the Perso-Arabic astronomical vocabulary naturalised through Urdu; `folk` for names a dictionary or ethnographer flags as colloquial, rural, proverbial or metaphorical. Boundary cases (agast, ket, hathiyā, nakhat) are Sanskrit words that have become folk-calendrical property, and are tagged `folk` because that is how the sources use them.
- No entry in this file is tagged `tribal`. Fallon systematically supplies Santali equivalents (Ursa Major buṛhī parkom, Milky Way panjar / ḍahar, comet chanḍbol ipil) and they are quoted in the notes where they occur, but Santali is Munda, outside the four languages of this source group, and no entry is claimed on that basis.
- Script discipline: Platts prints Devanagari beside the Urdu script only for words he classes H (Hindi) or S (Sanskrit); for A (Arabic) and P (Persian) headwords he prints the Urdu script alone. Nearly all the interesting folk names are sub-entries printed in transliteration only - in those cases `name_native` is null rather than back-transliterated. Where Devanagari and the Urdu script are both given the Devanagari is placed first, separated by a slash. The printed originals of Platts, Fallon and Shakespear use Nastaʿlīq; the DSAL digital text renders it in naskh, and that is what is reproduced here.
- Notes and Queries citations give the volume and the numbered note, which is the standard and unambiguous locator for these journals; a printed page is added where the running head was legible in the scan. The scanned OCR of these volumes garbles diacritics badly, and quotations from them have been normalised in the diacritics only - wording and word order are as printed. Where a reading is uncertain the entry says so in `confidence`.
- Fallon (1879) glosses Arabic suhail as 'the dog star', i.e. Sirius. This is an error - Shakespear (1834), Platts (1884) and Fallon's own agas'ti entry all give Canopus. No independent Hindi, Urdu or Punjabi name for SIRIUS was found anywhere in these sources, and none is claimed. Likewise no vernacular name was found for Antares, the Hyades as a separate group, or Cassiopeia.
- Fallon (p. 115) offers 'H. nāo' (boat) as the Hindi for Argo Navis. That looks like a lexicographer's translation of the Latin constellation name rather than an attested folk usage, so it is deliberately excluded from the entries.
- McGregor's Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary (1993), Bahri (1989) and Caturvedi (1970) are in copyright. They were consulted to check which of these names survive into modern standard Hindi - kacpaciyā/kacpacī, hathiyā kī rāh, quṭub, suhel, pucchal tārā all do - but they are cited in `notes` only and never quoted.
- Several names are attested for one sky object by more than one source with divergent regional marking: palang tīn cor, dum kā tārā and gagan ke bacce-wālī murġī are marked dakh. (Deccani) by Shakespear in 1834 but appear unmarked in Platts and Fallon fifty years later, which may mean northern spread, or may mean only that Platts and Fallon did not mark their sources. Both readings are left open.
- The Panjabi Great Bear divides differently from the Hindustani one: Dames records the four bowl stars and the three handle stars under separate names (palang-pāwe, traṅgaṛ) in Jhang, while O'Brien's Multani Glossary makes traṅgar the whole constellation. Both are entered, with the disagreement stated.
- DSAL's search-results view of Lalas drops words silently. Its ध्रुव entry (p. 1968) returns 'दिशा की ओर स्थित एक प्रसिद्ध तारा' where the page view has 'उत्तर दिशा की ओर स्थित एक प्रसिद्ध तारा'; the same entry's sense 13 loses उत्तर again. Every Rajasthani gloss used here was therefore re-read on DSAL's page view (…_query.py?page=N), which reproduces the printed punctuation, the sense numbering and the abbreviations, and the source_url fields point at the page rather than at a query. The same caution applies to Macalister, whose search view strips both diacritics and full stops: its search view prints 'सातरसा satarasa m The Pleiades', its page view 'सातरसा sātarasā , m. The Pleiades.', and the quote here is the latter.
- Rose's volume I was obtained on a later pass, archive.org having refused it earlier. Its star-worship section (pp. 128-129) yields one Punjabi name, entered above, and confirms rather than extends what Fallon and Maya Singh already gave for comets and meteors: a comet is a dumdār sitāra bringing epidemic or famine, and meteors are hot coals thrown from heaven at the devil, which Rose marks as a Muhammadan belief. The section also carries the nakshatra weather couplets attributed to Sahdeo, which are the Punjab's counterpart of the Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍaḷī material already quoted in this file for Bihar and Rajasthan; they name asterisms without naming stars and no entry is made from them.

### Sindhi & Kashmiri — the north-west

- MEWARAM PRINTS NO ROMANIZATION AT ALL. His dictionary runs from the Sindhi script to English, and the roman in this file is therefore the compiler's reading, not the source's — the one place in this database where that is true of a public-domain source. It is a reading of a POINTED text: Mewaram marks the short vowels (ڪَتِيۇن, سُها, ڊۇهُ), so the vowels are his and not guessed, but the Latin letters chosen for the Sindhi implosives and retroflexes are conventional. `name_native` is the script exactly as the page image shows it, and every quote was taken from the DSAL page view rather than the search view, which strips pointing.
- Grierson is the opposite case and needs no such warning: he prints the roman, a Devanagari adaptation of the Śāradā spelling and a Sanskrit gloss for every headword, so both the roman and the script here are the source's own. His diacritics are dense (kraʦi-kūr ü, ह॑स्तु॒) and are reproduced as DSAL renders them.
- The `register` tags follow the convention set in hindi_urdu_punjabi.json, which reads oddly at first sight and is applied here for consistency rather than because it is ideal: `vernacular` covers the naturalised Perso-Arabic astronomical vocabulary as well as words formed in the language itself, because the field's own definition is 'not a Sanskrit loan'. So suhā, quṭubu, jadī, kahkashānu, sitāro, zuhrah, sawābita and suraiya are all `vernacular` while being Arabic or Persian. The names that are actually Sindhi or Kashmiri inventions — ṭīṛū, ḍūhu, choṭīa tāro, sānjhī tāro, vihāū, kraʦi-kūrü — are called out individually in their notes, because the register tag alone will not separate them.
- One Sindhi page reference is in roman numerals. سَپْتَ رِشيِ and سَواتِ come from the appendix of astronomical terms at the end of Mewaram's volume, which is paginated separately; they are cited as p. xxii, which is how DSAL indexes them.
- Two entries stand at one headword with a non-astronomical sense that is probably a different word: Sindhi وِهائۇ vihāū is 'the morning star; Aurora; a purchaser', and ڊۇهُ ḍūhu is 'the north star' and also an adjective 'motionless, stable' — but ڊوهُ ḍohu at the next headword is 'deceit', a separate word with a different vowel. A bare attestation of either spelling in a Sindhi text is not evidence for the star.
- Rose's Glossary was searched and is recorded as a near-total negative rather than omitted, but the search was incomplete: only the third volume could be downloaded from archive.org, the first two returning HTTP 503. What the third volume yields is one mention of the pañcaka in a Lahauli funerary context and no star name whatever. That is consistent with the pattern already seen in this database — caste-and-tribe compendia are dry, and when they yield they yield one community in four volumes — but it is not a finished search.
- Kashmiri is thin here and that is the finding, not a failure of searching. The dictionary was queried in full text for star, stars, Pleiades, Orion, Great Bear, Ursa, Milky Way, comet, meteor, Venus, morning star, evening star, Sirius, Canopus, pole star, polar star, Alcor, constellation and asterism, and the Orion, Sirius, Canopus and evening-star searches returned nothing astronomical at all.
- THE NORTH-WEST WAS FINISHED ON A LATER PASS and the result is one large positive and one large negative. Positive: Baloch's Jāmiʻ Sindhī lughāt, which this file had recorded as unsearched because it is monolingual, yields eleven entries once it is queried in Sindhi instead of in English — including the northern cot for Ursa Major, a named Sirius, and the Katī-and-Scorpion proverb. Negative: Hassan's A Pronouncing Dictionary of Kashmiri Language, listed and LINKED on DSAL, returns nothing at all. Every query in Devanagari, in Perso-Arabic and in roman comes back 'No results', and the page view /cgi-bin/app/hassan_query.py?page=N returns an empty frame for pages 1, 5, 50, 200 and 500. This is a THIRD kind of DSAL gap, distinct from the two this database already documents: not a dictionary listed without a link, and not a search view that silently drops words, but a live search form served over an empty database. Kashmiri therefore still rests on Grierson 1932 alone.
- Rose's Glossary of the Tribes and Castes of the Punjab, volumes I and II, were obtained on the later pass — archive.org had refused them — and are all but dry, which confirms for the whole work what volume III had already suggested. Volume II has one line, on orienting a corpse's head towards the pole star. Volume I has a section of Sahdeo's nakshatra weather-couplets, the Sialkot story of Shukar, and one Punjabi Venus name, which is entered in hindi_urdu_punjabi.json. Its comet name is NOT entered: two independent scans of the same printing give two different readings of it and neither is legible, so the word is recorded as unread rather than guessed.

### Marathi, Konkani & Gujarati

- Marathi is over-represented here, and that is a finding rather than a sampling error: Molesworth's 1857 dictionary is by a wide margin the richest source in the set, and DSAL's combined Marathi search puts three further dictionaries (Date's Maharashtra Sabdakosa, Vaze, Tulpule & Feldhaus) behind the same query. Konkani and Gujarati have nothing comparable, so the imbalance in the file partly reflects the imbalance in the lexicography.
- SCRIPT DISCIPLINE. name_native is filled only where the source actually prints an Indic script. That is true of every Marathi entry (Molesworth, Vaze, Tulpule and Date all print Devanagari) and of none of the others. Enthoven's Folklore of Bombay prints roman only, in italic and without any diacritics; the Bombay Gazetteer prints roman with acute accents; Maffei's English-Konkani half prints roman only (his Konkani-English half uses Kannada script). Khatale and Bagale are certainly Molesworth's खाटलें and बाजलें, but the Enthoven entries leave name_native null rather than back-supply a script Enthoven never used.
- OCR. All the non-DSAL sources were read from archive.org djvu.txt derived from 19th- and early-20th-century scans, and the OCR is damaged. Quotes were taken only from passages that render cleanly, and where a word is known to be mis-scanned this is stated in the entry's notes (Enthoven's Agastya prints as 'Agasiya' and Saptarishi as 'Saftarishi'; Maffei's (H. K.) mark prints variously as '{U, K.}' and '{B. K.}'; the Nasik gazetteer's Hasta prints as 'Rasta'). Where a whole passage was too corrupt to quote, it was left out.
- GUJARATI IS THE WEAK POINT, AND THE REASON IS MECHANICAL, NOT SUBSTANTIVE. DSAL has no Gujarati dictionary. Four Gujarati dictionaries on archive.org were downloaded and searched — Belsare's Etymological Gujarati-English Dictionary, both volumes of Mehta & Mehta's Modern Gujarati-English Dictionary, and Montgomery's A Dictionary English and Gujarati (1877) — and their ENGLISH sides confirm that the entries exist and that the expected Sanskritic set is there (Kṛttikā = the Pleiades, Svātī = Arcturus, Saptarṣi = Ursa Major, Dhruva = the polar star, Ākāśagaṅgā = the Milky Way; Montgomery has headwords for both PLEIADES and MILKY-WAY). But in every one of them the Gujarati script and the roman transliterations alike come out of the scan as noise — Montgomery's Gujarati for PLEIADES reads 's(uiSt (t4A)n.' — so no name could be transcribed to the standard this file uses, and none was guessed. The two Gujarati entries here therefore rest on the gazetteers, which romanize. A Gujarati pass with usable page images, or with Shapurji Edalji's 1868 dictionary, is the obvious next step, and it should be aimed squarely at whether Gujarati has anything answering to Marathi's विंचू, खाटलें, मेढ and हत्ती.
- THE COT FIGURE IS NOT DIAGNOSTIC. Enthoven applies it, on one page, to both Orion and the Great Bear. A folk report that 'the cot' is a constellation therefore does not by itself identify a star group, and cot-names collected in other Indian languages should not be assumed to mean Ursa Major.
- HOMONYM TRAPS. विंचू is the ordinary Marathi word for a scorpion and for Scorpius, so an isolated occurrence is not evidence for the Pleiades. हत्ती is the ordinary word for an elephant. मेढ is the ordinary word for a forked post. काथ्या is also coir rope. खाटलें is also, in Date, a bullock-cart. Every one of these needs its astronomical sense certified by the dictionary, not inferred from context.
- COMPETING NAMES, recorded rather than resolved: Citrā (Spica) has two Marathi rain-names, अंधळ्या and कडप्या, keyed to different effects of the same rain; the Milky Way has three names in Enthoven and eight in Molesworth; Punarvasu and Puṣya each have two agriculturists' names; and Enthoven's own index disagrees with his body text on whether the Milky Way name is Kavadgantak or Kavadghantak.
- REGIONAL MARKS. Molesworth's R (used on कात्या, काथ्या) means, by his own Preface (p. xvi), the Rajapur district and the country south of it — the southern Konkan, bordering Konkani territory; C means the Konkan generally. Date's mark (कुण.) on खाटलें could not be expanded: DSAL's front matter for the Maharashtra Sabdakosa is an un-OCRed image PDF. It is most plausibly कुणबी, the cultivator dialect, but that is not verified.
- DSAL ENDPOINT NOTE for anyone rebuilding this: molesworth_query.py, vaze_query.py and tulpule_query.py support full-text search (matchtype=containing without searchhws), which is how the English-side hunt was done. date_query.py returns empty pages for every query; Date's entries are reachable only through the combined marathi_query.py endpoint, and only by exact headword. Full-text search on marathi_query.py also fails.
- OUT OF SCOPE but noted in passing: the Dharwar gazetteer (1884, p. 271) records a distinct Kannada set of 'star-chambers' — Mrigshirshe, A'rdi, Maghe, Hubbe, Hastu, Chette, Dhanishte — grouped into mungári and hingári seasons. The Gujarat Parsi section of the gazetteer (Vol. IX Pt II) gives Avestan star names (Teshtar = Sirius, Haptoiringa = the Great Bear); those belong to Zoroastrian tradition, not to the Gujarati language, and are excluded.
- SANSKRIT LINKAGE. sanskrit_db_id points into docs/star-names/star-names.json. It is null where the vernacular term names something the Sanskrit database has no entry for (a comet, a meteor, a planet, a block of asterisms, a sowing season). No file under docs/star-names/ was modified.

### Bengali, Assamese & Odia

- SCOPE. This file holds Bengali, Assamese and Odia only. The Munda and Dravidian parallels that make the western-Odia folk layer intelligible — Santali arar 'the Yoke' for Orion's Belt, Mundari moṅgaru ipilko 'the wooden mallet' for the Pleiades and topaḍ parkom ipilko 'the bier stars' for the Big Dipper, Kurukh khaṭī pāwā bīnkō and ugtā pagsi bīnkō, the Mundari and Kurukh cattle-track names for the Milky Way — are documented in the notes of the Odia entries with author, page and edition, but are NOT entered here as records: they belong to the sibling file sources/tribal.json, which covers them in far more detail. One body of tribal material found in this pass appears NOT to be covered there and should be added to it rather than to this file: Sarat Chandra Roy, The Birhors (Ranchi, 1925), pp. 386 and 496, giving Birhor [biy] Bhurka for Venus as morning star, Kidu Ipil for the evening star, Kumbūru lagu Ipil 'thief-driving star' for a bright object rising before Bhurka, the famine forecast read from which of the two apparitions is the more prominent in a given year, and chāndi for a meteor, at which all Birhors spit.
- COPYRIGHT. Praharaj (1931-40), Dāsa (1937), Haughton (1833), Ram Comul Sen (1834), Bronson (1867), Campbell (1899), Hahn (1903), Risley (1891) and Roy (1925) are out of copyright. Two are not: DSAL prints copyright notices for the Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, 3rd ed. (2000, Shishu Sahitya Samsad) and the Candrakanta Abhidhana, 2nd ed. (1962, Assam Sahitya Sabha), and the Encyclopaedia Mundarica's status was not established. What is quoted from those is in every case a single short lemma, quoted because a name without its printed definition is not citable evidence. Anyone republishing this database should re-examine that judgement.
- OCR AND SCRIPT. Three separate transcription problems are flagged per entry rather than silently fixed. (1) The DSAL transcription of the Candrakanta Abhidhana renders the Assamese vowel sign ৃ as ৱ throughout — মৱত্যু for মৃত্যু, কৱত্তিকা for কৃত্তিকা, বৱষ for বৃষ. (2) The archive.org OCR of Hoffmann, Campbell and Roy mangles the roman diacritics (moT^garuipilko for moṅgaru ipilko, Bhtirka for Bhurka); these are quoted as scanned with the normalised reading marked editorial in the notes. (3) The archive.org OCR of Bengali, Assamese and Odia SCRIPT is unusable in every scanned book tried — Bronson, Carey, Morton, Sykes, Sutton, Ram Comul Sen. Where the script was needed it was read off the page image; where it could not be read, the entry was dropped rather than back-transliterated.
- WHAT I READ MYSELF. Every DSAL quotation was fetched and its presence at its own source_url verified programmatically. Of the page-image sources I read three images directly — Haughton p. 419, Ram Comul Sen vol. 2 p. 168, Bronson p. 439. The remaining image-sourced material (Bronson p. 327, Hahn's Kurukh set, the Hoffmann passages taken from the scans rather than the OCR stream) was transcribed by a second reader working to the same rules; those entries are graded 'likely' rather than 'certain' and say so in their notes.
- Praharaj duplicates many headwords under variant spellings (ଶୁକ୍ ତରା / ଶୁକ୍ ତାରା, ପହରିକିଆ ତରା / ପହରିକିଆ ତାରା, ହରିତାଳିକା / ହରିତାଲିକା / ହରିତାଳୀ) and the duplicates sometimes disagree — the three Haritāḻī entries cannot agree whether the Milky Way runs north to south or south to north. Where duplicates exist one has been made the entry and the others named in its notes. He also prints Bengali and Hindi equivalents in a synonym column; those are second-hand and their DSAL transcription is unreliable (the same Bengali word appears as লেজেতারা at one duplicate headword and নেজান তারা at the other), so no entry rests on them.
