- DSAL's headword index and the query URL are byte-sensitive: পপীয়া is indexed with the precomposed U+09DF and ଯାମ୍ୟ with U+0D5F, and a query typed with the nukta sequence returns nothing. DSAL's `page=N` browse also silently jumps to the start of an indexing block, so it is not a reliable citation target. Every source_url here is a headword or full-text query that was fetched and checked, except where a `page=` URL was verified to contain the quoted text.
- REGISTER tags describe how the NAME is formed and where it is used, not the etymology of every morpheme. কালপুরুষ is 'vernacular' although both its parts are Sanskrit, because the application to Orion is an eastern New Indo-Aryan development. ନଙ୍ଗଲ ଜୁଡ଼ା is 'folk' rather than 'tribal' because Praharaj marks the WORD provincial Sambalpuri and attributes only the OBSERVANCE to the Khaṛiās. 'tribal' is reserved for names recorded in a tribal language.
- LITERAL MEANINGS marked as the compiler's in the notes (kukurabāhī, keuñṭi, bāj-khaṭ as 'bier', khacuā) are readings of the compound, not the dictionaries'. Where a dictionary supplies the gloss itself — kaṭhalā = the carpenter's mallet, jhām̐ṭā = because it is shaped like a broom — that is stated.
- sanskrit_db_id points at the entry in docs/star-names/star-names.json for the same SKY OBJECT, so the two databases can be joined on the object. It does not assert that the vernacular name descends from the Sanskrit one; the register field says that. It is null where no counterpart entry exists (Venus, comets, meteors) or where linking would assert a false identity — ଲୋପାମୁଦ୍ରା, a small star south-east of Canopus, is deliberately NOT linked to lopamudravallabha, which is Canopus itself.
- NOT SEARCHED, and worth a later pass: the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, which is large and was not reached; Bodding's Santal Dictionary vols 1-4, which are not readily findable online and would almost certainly deepen the Santali set; Encyclopaedia Mundarica vols 1, 4 and 8, which carry cross-references to the Orion and Pleiades material that were not chased to printed pages; and Bengali-language popular astronomy and almanacs, which are effectively unsearchable because Bengali-script OCR yields no greppable text — they would have to be read page by page.
- The register value 'tribal' is unused in this file by design - see the scope caveat. The registers present are borrowed, vernacular and folk. 'folk' is applied only where the dictionary itself marks the word rustic or provincial: Praharaj's ଗ୍ରା. (gramya) and ପ୍ରାଦେ. (pradesika, with the district named - Sambalpur, Garjat), and Dāsa's গ্রা◦.

### Tamil

- LINKING RULE for sanskrit_db_id: the id links on REFERENT identity, i.e. it points to the entry in docs/star-names/star-names.json that denotes the same sky object, choosing the closest-matching Sanskrit name where several exist. It does NOT assert that the Tamil name is a borrowing or a translation of that Sanskrit name — for the vernacular entries (aṟumīṉ, eḻumīṉ, naṭunāḷ, kāṟṟumuntunāḷ, mācu and the rest) it is precisely the point that no Sanskrit counterpart name exists. Where the Tamil name IS the Sanskrit name in Tamil phonology, the notes say so. Planets have no ids because the Sanskrit database does not carry them individually.
- The Tamil Lexicon prints its sources as Tamil sigla whose expansions are in front matter that survives on DSAL only as scanned images without a text layer. The sigla used in this file are expanded as: பிங். = Piṅkala Nikaṇṭu, திவா. = Tivākaram, சூடா. = Cūṭāmaṇi Nikaṇṭu, யாழ். அக. = Yāḻppāṇa Akarāti, (W.) = Winslow's dictionary. These four nikaṇṭu identifications are corroborated from the Lexicon's own headwords பிங்கலம், திவாகரம், சூடாமணிநிகண்டு and நிகண்டு, which describe each work. The regional labels Pond., Nāñ., Loc., Colloq. and (J.) are quoted as printed and their expansions are not asserted beyond what the entries themselves show.
- Every Caṅkam quotation was read in a Project Madurai UTF-8 e-text that was actually fetched, and every Tamil Lexicon and Winslow quotation was read at the DSAL query URL given. Nothing has been transcribed from memory, back-transliterated, or normalised. Where a text prints editorial asterisks, brackets or restorations (Patiṟṟuppattu 59, Akanāṉūṟu 17), the entry says so.
- Project Madurai e-texts are volunteer transcriptions of printed editions and carry occasional typographic damage; a few characters in the Paripāṭal file are corrupted. All lines quoted here were checked for legibility, but they are not a critical edition and line-numbering follows the file's own markers where these exist.
- One line-number discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved: the Tamil Lexicon cites veṇmīṉ at Paṭṭiṉappālai 14, while both the Project Madurai plain text and Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar's own numbering in U. Vē. Cāminātaiyar's edition put it at lines 1-2, the poem's opening couplet.
- Caṅkam dating is contested. The 'c. 1st-3rd c. CE' and similar ranges in source_date are conventional and approximate; nothing in this file depends on them.
- The identifications of Caṅkam star-words with particular modern objects are the Tamil Lexicon's and the mediaeval commentators', not the poems'. The verses generally say 'the white star', 'the red star', 'the northern star'; it is Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar and the nineteenth- and twentieth-century lexicographers who say Venus, Mars, Arundhatī. Entries where this matters are marked 'likely' or 'disputed' and the reasoning is in the notes.
- The mīṉ / mīṉ 'star' / 'fish' homonymy is systematic and dangerous: a large majority of Tamil Lexicon headwords ending in -mīṉ are fish. Every -mīṉ entry in this file was taken from a headword whose printed definition is astronomical, and the notes flag the fish-homonym wherever the same spelling carries one (ciṟumīṉ, viḻumīṉ, cemmīṉ, vāṉmīṉ). The parallel veḷḷi 'silver / whiteness / Friday / Venus' trap is flagged on every veḷḷi entry.
- Edgar Thurston's Castes and Tribes of Southern India (1909), all seven volumes searched in full text on archive.org, yielded almost nothing for Tamil vernacular star-names: what star material it has is Brahmanical marriage ritual (the showing of Dhruva and Arundhatī), nakshatra-matching for marriages, and festival dates. The one substantive Tamil item — the Nāṭṭukkōṭṭai Chetti Ārudrā rite — reaches this file through the Tamil Lexicon's own citation of Thurston vol. V p. 264, not through a passage located directly. No community-specific Tamil sky-lore of the kind the sources were searched for was found there.
- Fabricius's Tamil and English Dictionary (4th ed., 1972) IS on DSAL — this file previously said it was not — and was searched on a later correction pass. It adds no name to this file and confirms its negatives: 'Sirius', 'Antares', 'Arcturus' and 'Canopus' return nothing at all in full-text search, so the absence of Tamil names for those four stars now rests on three independent dictionaries rather than two. Its one novelty is rejected: at s.v. நட்சத்திரம் (p. 584) Fabricius glosses நட்சத்திரமாலை naṭcattira-mālai as 'the galaxy or milky way', where the Madras Tamil Lexicon (p. 2135) gives the word only as a cluster of stars, as the lunar zodiac of twenty-seven asterisms, as a synonym of நட்சத்திரவீதி the moon's path, and as the title of a treatise — no Milky Way sense anywhere. Fabricius is a Tamil-English dictionary made for missionaries and the gloss looks like his own; no entry is claimed on it. Winslow (1862) was consulted throughout and is quoted or cited where it adds colloquial evidence the Tamil Lexicon lacks.
- Modern scholarship on Tamil astronomy and on Caṅkam chronology is in copyright and has not been quoted anywhere in this file; no in-copyright translation of any Caṅkam poem has been used, and the English renderings that appear in usage_note fields are the compiler's own working paraphrases, offered as orientation and not as translations of record.
- This is a lexicographical and literary compilation, not a field survey. Living folk and fishermen's star-names in coastal Tamil Nadu, and any tribal astronomies of the Nilgiris or the Western Ghats, are almost certainly richer than what two nineteenth- and twentieth-century dictionaries preserve; no entry in this file is tagged 'tribal' because no citable tribal Tamil star-name was found in the sources searched.

### Telugu & Kannada

- KITTEL EDITION. The Kannada material is quoted from the text DSAL keys, which is the revised and enlarged edition of Kittel published by the University of Madras in 1968-71, not the Basel Mission first edition of 1894. The definitions are Kittel's own and the page numbers are those of the DSAL text; source_date is given as 1894 for the work, but anyone citing a page should use the citation string, which names the edition. The 1894 pagination has not been separately verified here, and the archive.org scans of the first edition OCR the Kannada script too badly to check it against.
- BROWN EDITION. The Telugu material is the 1903 revision of Brown's dictionary (Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, Madras), which is the DSAL text, not the 1852 first edition. Where the 1903 revisers added or altered an entry this cannot be detected from the DSAL text alone.
- DSAL TYPOGRAPHY. The keyed DSAL text carries visible faults which are reproduced verbatim in the quotes rather than silently mended: 'kummara-sārc-ṭsukka' and 'The The name on the constellation' at Brown p. 296; 'tēlu-vāsi' for tēlu-rāsi at p. 554; 'the cource of Canopus' at p. 24; 'శక్రుడు' for శుక్రుడు at p. 1226; 'twenty lunar mansions' for twenty-seven at p. 628; the garbled 'ఛ?ుక్క' at p. 449; the headword for Brown p. 626 filed under ధ్యానము when the entry is ధ్రువుడు; 'constellaiion' at Kittel p. 646.
- ROMANISATION. name_roman follows the source's own transliteration where the source gives one (Brown's ṭsukka is normalised to cukka, and Kittel's ar̤il to aṟil, for consistency within this file); where the source romanises only and prints no native script — the Thurston material — name_native is null and has NOT been back-transliterated.
- GWYNN. Gwynn's Telugu-English Dictionary (1991) is in copyright. It is used for one entry only, the Telugu Milky Way, and the quote there is confined to the bare lexical gloss; nothing of his discussion is reproduced.
- THE TELUGU DEŚYA SET IS BROWN'S, NOT A FIELD RECORD. Brown gives no source for these names and no indication of where or by whom they were used; they are likely to come from a Telugu nighaṇṭu tradition rather than from his own enquiry. Their currency in speech in 1852 or 1903 is not established by this evidence, only their currency in the lexicon.
- GAZETTEERS NOT PRODUCTIVE. Mysore Gazetteer vol. I (Hayavadana Rao, 1927) was downloaded and searched: it contains no nakṣatra or kārti material. The Bellary agricultural star-calendar is therefore carried here on Thurston alone. District gazetteers for Hyderabad and the Telugu districts were not obtained.
- REEVE/SANDERSON NOT USABLE. The Reeve-Sanderson Canarese-English Dictionary (1858) was downloaded from archive.org, but the OCR of the Kannada script is too corrupt to quote verbatim, so it contributes nothing and no entry rests on it. Sankaranarayana's Telugu-English Dictionary was not located in a usable full-text form.
- IDENTIFICATIONS. modern_star for the lunar mansions is taken from the Sanskrit database's yogatārā identifications, not from Brown or Kittel, who almost never give one (the exceptions — Arcturus for Svāti, Spica for Citrā, Canopus for Agastya, Sirius for Lubdhaka, the Pleiades for Kṛttikā — are quoted where they occur). A vernacular name and its Sanskrit counterpart are assumed to denote the same star; where a source's own identification conflicts with that, as with Arundhatī, confidence is set to disputed and the conflict is stated.
- REGISTER IS A JUDGEMENT. Only one name in the whole file is graded for register by its source: Brown calls asilēru 'a vulgar name'. Every other register tag is the compiler's, assigned on the word's material (Dravidian vs Sanskrit), its formation (native compound vs borrowing), and the source's own labelling ([Tel.], Tbh., My., Prv.). Names whose material is Sanskrit but whose compounding is not — sañje-tāraki, sappapu-cukka, jannapu-cukka, maddela-rūpu-rikka — are tagged vernacular, and the reasoning is stated in each entry's notes.
- Jyotirvinodini (1931) additions verified against the book's archive.org OCR, 2026-08-18. Held back pending page-image verification: ಜಮದಗ್ನಿ (Jamadagni = β Cas, reported by a research agent from Appendix III but absent from the OCR), ಶರ್ಮಿಷ್ಠಾ for Cassiopeia (a loan of Dikshit's 1892 Marathi coinage — no register fits a modern inter-vernacular loan yet), ಕುರ್ಚಿ (a shape description in context, not clearly a name), bare ಸ್ವಸ್ತಿಕ for Cygnus (the OCR's svastika passages concern Crux and the zenith). The book's Appendix II identifies Ārdrā with γ Geminorum — anticipating Shylaja & Pai (2024) by ninety years; recorded here as a note since the object index carries no Gemini star beyond Punarvasu.

### Malayalam, Tulu, Kodava & Sinhala

- Gundert 1872 is quoted through the DSAL digitisation; his old orthography (ററ for ṟṟ, ളള for ḷḷ) and DSAL's automatic romanization are reproduced as printed, including obvious OCR damage marked /?/. Page numbers are Gundert's own.
- Register tagging is the compiler's, applied by a stated rule: 'borrowed' where the source marks the word S. or Tdbh./tadbhava or Eḷu ('E. of'), i.e. a Sanskrit or Pali word in the local phonology; 'vernacular' where the word is formed from inherited material in the language itself, including calques whose morphemes are all native; 'folk' where the source marks it dialectal, rural, or as an omen/festival term; 'tribal' is used nowhere in this file, since none of these four languages is tribal and no tribal source was reached.
- The identification of ഞേങ്ങോല്‍ / മുഴക്കോല്‍ with Orion's Belt is the compiler's inference from Gundert's rising datum, not the source's. Gundert names no stars. It is filed as disputed and should not be cited as an attested identification.
- Gundert's own star identifications are occasionally wrong or eccentric and have not been silently corrected: ഋക്ഷം glossed 'Ursa minor' where Sanskrit ṛkṣāḥ is the Great Bear; അത്തം (Hasta) as 'Coma Berenices'; ചിത്ര given as both Spica and 'bright star in Bootes'; ആതിര (Ārdrā) placed in Gemini. Each is flagged in the entry's notes.
- For Tulu, the OCR of the Kannada script in Männer 1886/1888 is unusable; every Tulu form here was read from a page image, and one reading — the medial conjunct in ಹೊರಸಿನ್ಟ (Ursa Major) — remains uncertain even at 2400px. Männer's own romanizations are given where he prints them.
- Burrow & Emeneau's Dravidian Etymological Dictionary (2nd ed. 1984) is in copyright. It is quoted here only as raw lexical data at minimum length, for attestation of forms that appear nowhere else; the analysis built on it is paraphrase.
- Cole 1867 prints Kannada script for Kodava, but the archive.org OCR of it is heavily damaged; the Kodava script forms are reconstructions from the scan checked against Cole's own romanizations, and the romanizations should be preferred where they differ.
- Carter's entries tagged 'E. S.' are Carter citing his own English-Sinhalese volume — a signal that the Sinhala is his coinage rather than attested vernacular. Every such item (the Ursa Major bear-calques, sapta-mūnī-cāraya for Charles's Wain, visiṣṭha) is flagged in place and none is counted as vernacular.
- Carter p. 61 glosses Arundhatī as 'Pleiades'; this is an error, corrected by Jayatilaka p. 641 to Alcor. Jayatilaka p. 3166 prints Sinhala කුඩාවරහන against the romanization kuḍā-valahā, which do not correspond; that form has therefore been left out of the entries.
- Jayatilaka's dictionary is incomplete — the pages reached run only to about ග (p. 4095) — so a 'not in Jayatilaka' result for a headword later in the alphabet means outside coverage, not absent from the language.
- The nakshatra numbering differs between and within the sources (Carter counts anura 17th and svāti 15th; Clough counts visākhā 16th; Carter is internally inconsistent about the 20th and 21st; both oscillate between 27 and 28 mansions). No number has been normalised.
- Not reached: Indian Antiquary vols. XXIV–XXVI, where Burnell's 'Devil Worship of the Tuluvas' continues (vol. XXIII was searched and contains no star material in the paḍdanas); the Malabar District Gazetteer of Innes & Evans (1908), which could not be located on archive.org and which may carry a fuller ñāṟṟuveḷa table than Gundert's; and any printed source on Lakshadweep or Malabar navigational star-lore, which repeated searching failed to turn up in the public domain.
- The Kannada 'karte' system — asterism rain-periods governing sowing, cognate with the Malayalam ñāṟṟuveḷa — is documented for the Lingayats of Bellary in Thurston vol. IV, but Bellary is Kannada country and the passage is therefore comparanda, not an entry in this file.

### The north-east — Mizo, Mara, Meitei, Garo and four Naga tribes

- Lorrain (1940) is public domain — he died in 1944 — and is quoted verbatim throughout, from DSAL's page view rather than its search view. Shakespear (1912) is public domain and is quoted from the archive.org full text. Sharma (2006) is in copyright: the seven Meitei entries are paraphrased and their `quote` is null, on the footing this database uses for the field surveys.
- TEN OF THE TWENTY-NINE MIZO ENTRIES ARE GRADED `unidentified`, and that is the honest shape of the source. Lorrain names a figure and then, about a third of the time, says nothing further than 'the name of a Lushai constellation'. Those entries are kept rather than dropped — an unidentified indigenous figure is a result, and the number of them is itself the finding, since no other language in this database has anything like twenty-two named sky figures. Where Lorrain gives Western stars they are reproduced exactly; where he does not, `modern_star` says so in words and nothing is guessed.
- Si-mei-talh is graded `likely` rather than `certain` for a reason worth stating: 'three small stars in Orion' is almost certainly the Belt, but the Belt stars are second-magnitude and not small, so the identification may be wrong and the Bayer letters are deliberately left out of modern_star.
- Literal meanings are given only where Lorrain glosses the elements at their own headwords. arsi êk rests on his entry for êk (p. 122), which cross-refers to it; si-mei-khu is marked as the compiler's reading of elements Lorrain glosses separately, which is why it is in `literal_meaning` and not in the quote. Si-ruk, Zâng-khua, Si-archang, Si-kawi-kâp and the rest are left unglossed, because a transparent-looking Mizo compound is not evidence of anything without the dictionary saying so.
- One printed error is reproduced as printed: Si-archang's gloss reads 'arranged in an are resembling the curve of a cock's tail feathers', where 'are' is a compositor's error for 'arc'. The quote is as DSAL renders the page and the correction is stated in the entry's notes.
- The Lakher entry's page reference is soft. Shakespear's Part II on the Lakhers is separately paginated in some printings, and the page here is taken from the running head of the archive.org scan used; the entry is graded `likely` on that account, not because the reading is in doubt.
- Two entries carry no vernacular name at all. The general statement from Shakespear that 'many of the stars and constellations have received names' is entered as a source-level fact because it is the independent corroboration that Lorrain's list is a system and not a lexicographer's miscellany. The precedent is the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entry in tribal.json and the four name-less entries in tribal_fieldwork.json.
- Register is `tribal` throughout except Meitei dhrubatarā, which is `borrowed` — Sanskrit Dhruva-tārā in Meitei script. Calling the Mizo material `tribal` rather than `vernacular` follows this database's use of the tag for a distinct non-Sanskritic tradition, not a judgement about the Mizo as a community; the same tag covers Santali, Mundari and Nicobarese here.
- SUPERSEDED, AND KEPT SO THAT THE CORRECTION IS LEGIBLE — see the next caveat. The north-east is far from finished. Playfair on the Garos, Hutton on the Angami and Sema, Mills on the Ao, Lotha and Rengma, and Endle on the Kacharis were all requested from archive.org and all returned HTTP 503; the mission dictionaries for Garo, Bodo, Ao and Angami are not on DSAL and were not reached by other routes. Sylheti was not searched. Khasi still rests on the five words Nissor Singh's dictionary gave tribal.json.
- SOURCES OBTAINED ON THE SECOND PASS. The caveat immediately above this one, left standing as it was written, records that Playfair, Hutton, Mills and Endle were all requested from archive.org and all returned HTTP 503. They were obtained afterwards by a different route, which is worth writing down: fetch archive.org/metadata/<id> for the item's real server and directory, then request https://<server><dir>/<filename> directly. The /download/<id>/<id>_djvu.txt path that 503s is a redirect layer, not the file. Every north-eastern monograph named as unreachable in that caveat has now been read.
- All six monographs are public domain. QUOTES ARE TRANSCRIBED FROM THE PAGE IMAGES, RENDERED AT 300 dpi FROM THE SCAN'S OWN PDF, and the OCR was used only to find the passages. This matters: the OCR of these books destroys ü, which every one of the four Naga monographs uses heavily, and a first pass taken from the OCR got five names wrong. Checking them against the page images corrected Angami Pfiüdzücha (not Pfüdzücha), Angami Rhupeko (not Bhupeko), Sema Azüghongu or Aïzüghongu, Rengma Aniza 'Wikhu (not 'Wükhu), Rengma Wachi asükuwa, and Rengma Amui asăm kepuwa, whose breve no scan reproduces. Where the OCR has damaged an ENGLISH word inside a quote and the printed reading is not in doubt, the restoration is marked with square brackets — 'the Pl[e]iades'; 'the carrying of the bedy' is left as it stands, because the same sentence prints 'body' correctly two words later, and because Hutton's own text prints 'Amgamis' for 'Angamis' on the Pleiades page. NO VERNACULAR NAME IS RESTORED FROM CONTEXT. Where two scans of one printing disagree on a name and no page image settles it, both readings are recorded and neither is preferred: this happens once, at Garo Noringro-Nojingjo / Noringro-Rojingjo.
- Playfair prints a raised dot for the Garo glottal stop. The two scans render it as ° and as ", and it is written · in the entries. The scan cited for the Garo entries is in.ernet.dli.2015.500276 rather than dli.csl.5842 because its printed page numbers are legible.
- Mills letters his three Rengma languages A, B and C and his two Ao dialects C and M. The letters are reproduced in the name_roman fields exactly as he prints them, and every Rengma entry repeats his key so that no entry has to be read beside another to be understood. A is the southern section of the Western Rengmas, B the northern section, C the Eastern Rengmas; for Ao, C is Chungli and M is Mongsen.
- Two Rengma entries carry no vernacular name — the eclipse beliefs and, in part, the solar halo — on the same footing as the two nameless entries already in this file. Mills gives the belief without the word, and the belief is worth the record. They are marked by a null name_roman, and a reader counting names rather than entries should exclude them.
- Confidence grading follows the sources' own hedges and nothing else. Parry's four 'I have not been able to identify' figures are `unidentified`; his two 'possibly' identifications are `disputed`; Savidge's identifications, reported by Parry rather than made by him, are `likely`. Hutton's 'probably the Gemini' is `disputed` and his 'probably Mercury' likewise.
- Parry's Lakher chapter quotes Lushei names throughout as comparanda. Where Lorrain already supplies the name it is not entered twice: Parry's material is carried inside the Lakher entries' notes instead, which is where it belongs, since his purpose in printing it was comparison. Only two Lushei names appear as new entries — Pukula Thang and Hmar Arsi Sen — because Lorrain's 1940 Dictionary has neither. This closes the loose end recorded in the expansion plan as 'the stories Shakespear says attach to most Lushai constellations': Parry gives the stories for Chhohreivung, Zangkhua, Siruk, Dingdi-puanta, Khiangte zong zim, Nufa thembu in chuh and Sikawikap.

### Nepali, Newar, Kumaoni & Tibetan — the Himalaya

- ALL BUT TWO ENTRIES IN THIS FILE ARE PARAPHRASED, AND THE SOURCES ARE OLD. Turner 1931, Jørgensen 1936, Manandhar 1986, Malla 2000 and Schmidt 1993 are every one of them still in copyright — Turner died in 1983 and Jørgensen in 1974, so their dictionaries of 1931 and 1936 run to 2053 and 2044 respectively. Copyright here is a reason not to quote, never a reason not to read; the findings are paraphrased, the pages cited and `quote` is null throughout. The two exceptions are the Kumaoni entries from Grierson's Linguistic Survey (1916), which is public domain and is quoted.
- The Kumaoni quotes reproduce bad OCR verbatim and the romanizations are editorial. archive.org's scan of the Pahārī volume renders 'Lampuchhā tāro' as 'Lampuchhs taro' and splits the two-column vocabulary so that headwords and glosses fall out of alignment — several English glosses in that stretch ('evening star', 'moon') have no recoverable headword beside them and are therefore NOT entered. Both Kumaoni entries are graded `likely` on that account. The volume prints its vocabularies in roman only, so `name_native` is null and nothing was back-transliterated.
- Turner's own uncertainties are reproduced, not resolved. He prints a question mark before the gloss of hã̄sule pã̄ṛule 'a partic. constellation', and that entry is graded `unidentified`; his etymology of kirkiṭi ends in the words 'after what?', and the entry says so rather than supplying an answer.
- One identification is the compiler's and is argued rather than sourced. Turner defines तिन्-तारे tin-tāre as 'three particular stars that always appear in a straight line' and does not say which; the entry gives Orion's Belt on the ground that no other three stars answer that description at this latitude. If that inference is rejected, the entry should fall back to `unidentified` — it is stated in the entry's notes so a reader can.
- Bhadrā is glossed by Turner as a constellation and is entered as he gives it, but it is strictly a karaṇa — half a lunar day — rather than an asterism. The entry says so. Where a lexicographer and the technical literature disagree, this database records the lexicographer and flags the disagreement.
- Malla's Nepal Saṃvat dates are converted to Common Era years by adding 879, which is the standard equivalence and is accurate to within the months of the Newar year. The dates belong to the manuscripts Malla cites, not to the words: tāhāva nagatiṃ is certainly older than the 1691 manuscript that happens to preserve it.
- Schmidt's Practical Dictionary of Modern Nepali (1993) was searched and yields nothing this file does not already have from Turner — तारा tārā 'star' and ग्रह graha 'planet, star in astrology' — so no entry rests on it. That a modern learners' dictionary has two sky words where Turner has twenty is a fact about dictionaries, not about Nepali.
- The Indian Himalaya is a stated gap and not a searched-and-empty one. Jäschke's and Das's Tibetan dictionaries, which would give Ladakhi, Spiti and Bhutia, are listed by DSAL but not hosted — 'we are currently building a searchable database out of this data' — and both, with Atkinson's Himalayan Gazetteer, returned HTTP 503 from archive.org on every attempt made here. Garhwali was not reached at all. The Buddhist Himalayan tradition, which has an elaborate astronomy of its own, is absent from this database and its absence should not be read as a finding about the region.
- WAVE 4b — THE BUDDHIST HIMALAYA — WAS ATTEMPTED AND IS ALL BUT UNREACHABLE, and the reason is worth recording precisely because it is not the reason expected. Jäschke (1881), Das (1902) and Atkinson's Himalayan Gazetteer were all obtained on the later pass, by way of archive.org's metadata endpoint. The obstacle is not access but OCR: Jäschke's and Das's transliterated Tibetan is set with diacritics that both scans destroy, so that the twenty-eight lunar mansions Jäschke lists at rgyu-skar come out as an unreadable string, and Das's Tibetan-script column is recognised into the wrong letters — smin is rendered as yin at the very entry that defines it. Two names survive because they recur identically across both dictionaries and are entered; everything else is left unread rather than reconstructed, which is the same decision this database made about the Korku paper's Greek letters and the Bhil paper's cipher.
- Atkinson's Himalayan Gazetteer, all three volumes, was read for Kumaoni and Garhwali star-names and has none. The only sky word in the whole work is a footnote glossing dhruva as Ursa Major or the pole star, taken from Wilson. Kumaoni therefore still rests on the two entries in this file, and GARHWALI, LADAKHI, SPITI, BHUTIA, MONPA, SHERPA AND LAHULI REMAIN ENTIRELY UNATTESTED — none of them has a dictionary on DSAL, and the Linguistic Survey's Tibeto-Burman volumes give the bare word for 'star' in each and nothing more, which this database does not enter because a table of forty words meaning 'star' answers no question it asks.

### The maritime calendar and the peninsular forest

- Maniku (2000) and the Cholanaikkan paper (2017) are both in copyright: their findings are paraphrased and `quote` is null. The one quoted entry in this file is the Tamil gnomon from the Madras Tamil Lexicon, quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view as the rest of tamil.json is.
- ONLY SEVEN OF THE TWENTY-SEVEN NAKAIY ARE ENTERED, AND THAT IS AN EDITORIAL DECISION, NOT AN OMISSION. Maniku gives all twenty-seven and this file could have listed them; FORMAT.md's opening argument is that a table of the inherited asterism names in one more language would be 'large, easy to compile, and nearly uninformative'. What is informative here is the SYSTEM — the re-indexing against the monsoons, the intercalary avihi, the court office — and the members whose position in it is structurally interesting: the first and last of the north-east monsoon, and three whose star-lists or glosses add something. The other twenty are named in the nakaiy entry's usage note and can be read in Maniku at the pages cited from it.
- Divehi is included on the same footing as Sinhala, which this database has carried from the start: the language of Minicoy (Maliku) in Lakshadweep is Mahl, which is Divehi, and the nakaiy calendar is used there. The `region` field says so on every entry. A reader who wants the database confined to the Republic of India should filter on region, not on language.
- One error of Maniku's is reproduced rather than corrected: at މިއަހެލިއަ miahelia he lists 'Lambda, Phi one, Aldebaran and Phi two in Orionis', putting Aldebaran in Orion where it is α Tauri. The group he means is not in doubt and the slip is his; the entry says so.
- The Cholanaikkan entries carry NO iso639_3 code. Cholanaikkan is a Dravidian speech of the Nilambur forests with fewer than two hundred speakers and no code the compiler could assign with confidence; a wrong code is worse than none, so the field is null and the region field carries the identification. This is the only language in the database without a code.
- `ChootuPaayuka` is graded `likely` because the recorders derive it from Malayalam — cūṭṭu, a torch of dried coconut leaves, and pāyuka, 'to run fast' — and it may therefore be a Malayalam description offered to them rather than a Cholanaikkan name. The distinction matters in a community this small and this closely surrounded by Malayalam, and it is recorded rather than resolved.
- The Cholanaikkan negative is entered as a usage note on the word for 'star' rather than as a free-standing claim, because that is where a reader will meet it. The full statement — no identified stars, no patterns, the planetarium visit, the sun not connected with the seasons — is in the summary findings, which is where this database keeps its negatives.
- The fist-and-finger measures are recorded as NOT FOUND rather than as absent. The Tamil Lexicon was searched for கைக்கணக்கு and விரற்கணக்கு and for navigation, mariner, sailor, helmsman, compass, fathom and altitude; the first exists only as a book-keeping term and the second not at all. That is a fact about the lexicon, which is a literary and not a maritime record. The practice is well attested in the secondary literature and this database has simply not reached a citable primary source for it.

### The occupational and caste register

- Both sources are public domain and are quoted verbatim from the archive.org full text: Enthoven died in 1952 and Crooke in 1923. The scans are clean enough to quote except at one point, noted in the Tārā-bāras entry, where a sentence breaks mid-clause across a footnote marker and the quote carries an ellipsis.
- THE NEGATIVE IS THE MAIN RESULT AND ITS METHOD SHOULD BE STATED. Every line of the three volumes containing any of star, stars, constellation, Pleiades, Orion, Great Bear, Milky Way, galaxy, comet, Saptarshi, Arundhati, Krittika or Rohini was extracted with four lines of context either side and tested against Dhangar, Koli, Kunbi, Rabari, Gujjar, Bharvad, Ahir, Gowli, Golla, Kuruba, Idaiyar, fisher, shepherd, herdsman, cowherd, Bhandari, Agri, Mahar, Ramoshi and Vanjari. One line matched, and it matched on the word 'shepherd' inside an unrelated phrase. That is a fact about what colonial folklorists collected, not a claim that pastoralists and fishermen have no sky.
- The four maṇḍalas are graded `likely` and their `modern_star` says in words that the source does not locate them. Enthoven names the divisions and their omens and never says which stars belong to which; the obvious guess — that they are the directional quarters of the classical dikpāla scheme — is a guess, and this database does not force identifications.
- Tārā-bāras is graded `likely` for a textual reason and not a substantive one: Enthoven gives the name only in a footnote, and the sentence it is attached to is broken in the scan. The rite itself is not in doubt and is corroborated by the Telugu and Assamese Arundhatī entries already in the database, which record the companion showing of Arundhatī to the bride.
- The new `community` field is OPTIONAL and most entries will never carry one. It records the caste, occupational group or ethnonym a source names, in the source's own words, and it is not a claim that the name belongs only to that group — Enthoven's 'Konkan and Deccan Hindu families of the higher castes' is his phrase and his social framing, reproduced rather than endorsed. Where a source names no community the field is absent, which is the honest default and is true of 769 of the 777 entries.
- Back-filling the field changed five entries in three earlier files and changed nothing else about them: the community was already stated inside their `region` string and has been lifted out, not invented. The region strings were left as they stand so that nothing is lost if the new field is ever dropped.

### Adivasi & tribal traditions

- Every name here was read from OCR of a scanned page, not from a keyed text. Colonial-era romanisations of Munda, Kurukh and Andamanese are dense with diacritics and the DjVu OCR loses them systematically: Hoffmann's retroflex ṛ comes out as 'rd', Bodding's hooked vowels as 'g' and 'q'. Where a form could be checked against a second scan of the same book, or against its own alphabetical entry elsewhere in the same work, that was done and the reading is given plainly. Where it could not, the notes say so and print what the scan actually shows. Four names are flagged in their notes as unresolved: Mundari topagara/topoḍ-akan, Mundari barai ipil, Santali bele kombro (final syllable) and Andamanese ig-yádowa-.
- Nothing was quoted from a source in copyright. The twenty Gondi entries are paraphrased throughout from Vahia & Halkare (2013) and their quote fields are null; the same applies to the Bhil paper of 2023, which is cited in the summary as a lead and used for nothing else. Elwin's Baiga and Muria monographs were not used, for the same reason.
- Modern identifications are the source's own except where the source gives none, in which case the fields are left empty and confidence is 'unidentified'. Nine entries carry that grade — Santali Kaemaiya and sin ipil, Kurukh mugrā, Khasi 'lur-mangkara, Toda Keirt, and Gondi Purad/Mes, Khala, Irukna Mara and Khayan — and they are kept rather than dropped, because an unidentified indigenous figure is a result. Seven more are graded 'disputed' where the sources disagree with each other or with themselves.
- Page numbers were derived from the running heads of the specific Internet Archive scans cited, not from a physical copy, and for two-column dictionaries they may be out by one. Encyclopaedia Mundarica is cited by column number, which is how it is paginated. Burrows' Ho grammar has no recoverable page numbers in its OCR and is cited by headword only; Whitehead's Car-Nicobarese dictionary likewise.
- Register is assigned as the source presents the material. 'borrowed' marks the four cases where a community is recorded using a Sanskrit-derived term — Santali ruhni and sukro/Sani, Mundari Sukura/Sukurani, Gondi Dhruva Tara — and in every one of them the recording ethnographer says himself that the term is a loan, a book-word or a late addition. Those judgements are theirs, not mine.
- Several of these sources are condescending about the people they describe, and that bears on reliability. Rivers concludes that most or all Toda star ideas are borrowed, a judgement he reaches partly on the assumption that Toda folklore is thin. Man explains the single Andamanese constellation name by saying the islanders 'never venture upon any distant voyages'. Hoffmann calls the Munda bed 'a miserable bed' and Munda star-folklore 'rather scanty' — immediately before filling seven columns with it. Russell's framing throughout is evolutionary. None of that editorialising is reproduced in the entries; where it affects what was collected, the notes say so.
- The languages field carries one addition to the brief's list, Chhattisgarhi, for the three Dhuri entries from Russell & Hiralal. They are marked register 'folk', not 'tribal': the Dhuri are a caste, not an Adivasi community. They are here because they are the earliest printed witness to the cot-and-three-thieves figure that four tribal traditions independently share.
- No Ho, Khasi, Andamanese or Nicobarese source consulted attached a story to a star name. For those communities this file records vocabulary, which is what survives; the narrative material is Munda, Santal, Kurukh, Gond and Toda.
- Two leads were identified and not followed to the end: M.B. Bhaduri, 'Astronomy of the Mundas and their star names', Man in India, read at the second Oriental Conference and attacked at length by Hoffmann for its errors; and the JAHH series by Vahia, Halkare and colleagues on the Korku, Kolam, Banjara and Pardhi, which extends the same fieldwork to communities outside this file's language list.
- THREE SOURCES ADDED ON A LATER PASS, all obtained from archive.org by way of the metadata endpoint after the ordinary download path had refused them. Their quotes are transcribed from the archive.org OCR, not from page images, because none of the three uses a diacritic the OCR could destroy; where the OCR has damaged an English word inside a quote the restoration is bracketed — 't[h]e', 'p[l].', '[li]ke' — and nothing is mended silently: Elwin's The Baiga (1939), Ramamurti's Sora-English Dictionary (1938) and Winfield's A Vocabulary of the Kui Language (1929). Elwin died in February 1964, so the Indian term expired on 1 January 2025 and he is quoted verbatim rather than paraphrased; the expansion plan had listed him among the in-copyright sources and that is corrected here.
- The Baiga entries carry `language: Chhattisgarhi` with `community: Baiga`, not a language called Baigani. Elwin's own account is that the Baiga speak a form of the local Chhattisgarhi, and every name he records — Nangar, Kutela, Tengra, Chirai, Barhai, Dhimar, Jhal, Machhri, Dhanu, Ban, Sap, Chowkidar — is a transparent Chhattisgarhi or Hindi word. Filing them under an invented language would have made the database claim something Elwin does not. This is what the `community` field was added for.
- THE BAIGA SKY IS FIFTEEN FIGURES AND ELWIN LOCATES ALMOST NONE OF THEM. He names the Great Bear, queries Orion once, and for the other thirteen gives the figure and no position at all. Eleven entries are therefore `unidentified`, which is the largest block of them in this database. That is the honest reading of an ethnographer who was recording what people said rather than surveying the sky, and the alternative — matching a carpenter, a fisherman and a hoe to constellations by guesswork — would be worthless.
- Sora's sixteen-name list at the headword tuj-ən is entered only where Ramamurti glosses a name somewhere else in the dictionary; nine of the sixteen he does not, and they are recorded in the note to the generic entry rather than as nine unidentified rows. The two lunar-mansion entries are graded `likely` and their sanskrit_db_id is filled from the mansion number Ramamurti gives, which is a chain of two inferences and is flagged as such in both entries.
- THE SOURCE THAT PROMPTED THIS PASS, AND WHY IT IS NOT CITED ON A SINGLE ENTRY. M.N. Vahia, Nisha Yadav and Srikumar M. Menon, 'Perspectives on Early Astronomy in Indian Context' — an unpublished book manuscript prepared for the National Council of Science Museums, version 2 revision 5, PDF dated 11 July 2017, 111 pages, supplied privately and in copyright. Its section 4.1, 'Astronomy of some Indian tribes' (pp. 54-58), sets the Banjara, Kolam and Gond skies side by side in two tables. Every name in those tables is drawn from the authors' own two field papers, Vahia & Halkare 2013 and Vahia, Halkare, Menon & Calamur 2014, which this compilation already cited — so the book is a secondary condensation of sources already held, and citing it for a name it did not first print would put the wrong source on the record. What the book did do is show that this compilation had taken the two papers from their summary tables alone: the book's Gond column carries names for the Sun and the Moon that were not here, and its Kolam column a rainbow that was not here. Re-reading both papers end to end after that, including the village-by-village appendices the book condenses away, produced forty-seven further entries and four corrections. THE BOOK IS THEREFORE THE REASON FOR THE PASS AND THE SOURCE OF NONE OF IT, and is credited here rather than in the citation field. Nothing from it is quoted; it is in copyright and unpublished, and the material taken is in any case the papers'.

### Modern field surveys of Adivasi astronomy

- EVERY SOURCE IN THIS FILE IS IN COPYRIGHT AND NOTHING IS QUOTED. All five papers date from 2013-2023. The findings are paraphrased, the page is cited, `quote` and `quote_lang` are null throughout, and the wording of the glosses is the recorders' own only where a gloss is a single word or a fixed phrase for which no paraphrase is possible. This is the convention tribal.json set for its Gondi entries and it is followed here without exception.
- The Greek letters are unrecoverable from the Korku paper. The ADS scan of JAHH 19(2) renders every Greek glyph as a solid black box — in the page image, not merely in the extracted text — so 'Rigil Kent (α Cen)' reads as 'Rigil Kent ( Cen)'. Where the paper also prints the star's proper name the Bayer letter is unambiguous and has been restored (Alioth = ε UMa, Alnitak = ζ Ori, and so on). Where it prints only the lost letter and a constellation, nothing is restored: Bharada and Patni are graded 'unidentified', Pati 'unidentified' with its magnitude also garbled in the source, and Miryan 'likely' on a magnitude-and-position argument that is stated in its notes and not written into modern_star.
- The Bhil paper could not be read as text at all. Its embedded font subsets carry no ToUnicode map, so extraction yields a monoalphabetic substitution cipher — and a different cipher per font, so the running heads, the body and the table captions each scramble differently. Every Bhil, Pawra, Mavchi, Vasave and Kokna reading in this file was read off a rendered page image at 150 dpi. Nothing was decoded by solving the cipher, because a cipher solved against English prose is not evidence for the spelling of a Bhili word.
- THREE entries carry no vernacular name and are kept anyway: the Bhil cot; the Mavchi Bhil Pleiades as girls crushing grain; and the Bhil Milky Way as the road of Jeth and the daughter-in-law. In each the paper reports the figure in detail but prints no vernacular word for it. The precedent is the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entry in tribal.json. An identification without a name is a weaker record than a name with an identification, and the `name_roman` field says so in plain words rather than carrying an invented form. THIS CAVEAT USED TO SAY FOUR. The fourth was the Kolam identification of the three trailing stars as a Kolam, a Gond and a Pardhan, which the summary tables give without a word — but the appendix names them Dongal, and that entry now carries the name.
- Village counts are reported where the papers give them, because they are the best measure of how firmly held a figure is: the Korku cot and thieves are in all twelve villages surveyed, Kolam Kovela Kor in all ten, Banjara Jamakhat in all six, while Banjara Kamedi, Kolam Sappa and Kolam Danedare Pila rest on one or two villages each and are graded accordingly. A name from one village is not the same kind of fact as a name from twelve.
- The `region` field gives the district or island where the fieldwork was done, not a claim about the whole speech community. These surveys sampled particular villages, and the papers themselves show the same community differing village by village — the Kokna call the Pleiades a heap of hay in one village and a long-tailed bird in another.
- iso639_3 codes are assigned by the compiler from the community name the papers use, and the papers do not give codes. Lambadi (lmn), Kolami (kfb), Korku (kfq), Bhili (bhb), Mavchi (mvf), Vasavi (vas) and Kukna (kex) are straightforward. Two are less so: 'Pawra' is taken as Pauri Bareli (bfb), and the three Nicobar localities are assigned Central Nicobarese (ncb) for Camorta, Chaura (crv) for Chowra and Teressa (tef) for Teressa on the basis of the island named. Where a reader disagrees, the region field carries the fact and the code does not.
- Cross-references in the notes to tribal.json name the parallel and do not merge the entries. Kolam Irukmara and Gondi Irukna Mara are almost certainly the same word, and this file identifies it as Crux; the Gondi entry keeps its 'unidentified' grade, because one community's identification of a cognate is evidence about the other and not proof. The same restraint applies to Banjara Medi, Kolam Met and Korku Miryan, three threshing-pole names on three different stars.
- The register is `tribal` for every entry except two: Banjara Chanda for the Moon and Korku Dhur tara for the pole star, both tagged `borrowed` because the recorders themselves flag them as close to the Sanskrit. That is their judgement, not the compiler's, exactly as with the four borrowed tags in tribal.json.
- THE PARDHI PAPER WAS OBTAINED ON A LATER PASS and closes one of the three gaps this file recorded. ADS serves the full-text scan free at articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/2019JAHH...22..179H. Its text layer is partly a substitution cipher, as the Bhil paper's is — every italic and bold word extracts as a uniform shift of the alphabet — so the tables were read off page images rendered at 165 dpi, and the cipher was not solved. The remaining gap in the programme is the Warli / Dhodia / Katkari / Kokna study, which appears not to have been published: a public talk abstract summarises its findings in English (the Katkari Big Dipper as a cot with Koli, Warli and Konkana trailing it; Orion's Belt a bow and the sword an arrow; the Pleiades a big drum; Taurus a wedding procession), but a web summary of a talk is not a citable transcription and no entry rests on it.
- The Pardhi survey is the only one in this file whose informants are not cultivators, and the authors' own argument turns on it: eleven of the fourteen villages live by hunting and scavenging, the three Gav Pardhi villages took to farming under British rule less than a century ago, and the two vocabulary tables contain no farming word at all. Their conclusion is that the terminology was fixed while all Pardhi were hunter-gatherers. This database's own cross-family pattern — that Orion is an implement and never a hunt — is the mirror of that argument, and the Pardhi are its one exception.
- Village counts quoted in the usage notes are from the paper's Table 3, which tables each belief against the fourteen villages it was collected in. No other source in this file, and none elsewhere in this database, reports how many informants held a belief; where the count is given it is quoted, because 'thirteen of fourteen villages' and 'one village' are very different claims and a name-list flattens them.
- The Pardhi were gazetted a Criminal Tribe in 1871 and the stigma outlasted denotification; the authors say so at length and connect it to the community's isolation. Two entries name living surnames and their family goddesses. They are reproduced because the paper prints them as the content of the star-names, and for no other reason.
- THE SOURCE THAT PROMPTED THIS PASS, AND WHY IT IS NOT CITED ON A SINGLE ENTRY. M.N. Vahia, Nisha Yadav and Srikumar M. Menon, 'Perspectives on Early Astronomy in Indian Context' — an unpublished book manuscript prepared for the National Council of Science Museums, version 2 revision 5, PDF dated 11 July 2017, 111 pages, supplied privately and in copyright. Its section 4.1, 'Astronomy of some Indian tribes' (pp. 54-58), sets the Banjara, Kolam and Gond skies side by side in two tables. What the book did do is show that this compilation had taken the two papers from their summary tables alone: the book's Gond column carries names for the Sun and the Moon that were not here, and its Kolam column a rainbow that was not here. Re-reading both papers end to end after that, including the village-by-village appendices the book condenses away, produced forty-seven further entries and four corrections. THE BOOK IS THEREFORE THE REASON FOR THE PASS AND THE SOURCE OF NONE OF IT, and is credited here rather than in the citation field. Nothing from it is quoted; it is in copyright and unpublished, and the material taken is in any case the papers'.
- TABLES ARE NOT THE PAPER. Both Vahia papers put their findings in a summary table and then print a village-by-village appendix, and the appendix carries names the tables never show: the Banjara pole star, the six quarters of the Banjara horizon, the Kolam rainbow's two grandparents, the names of the five rain-animals around Samdur, the word Dongal for the Kolam thieves. This compilation's first pass worked from the tables, and four of its statements were wrong as a result — three entries said no vernacular form was printed when one was, and the summary claimed a negative finding about the Banjara pole star that the appendix refutes. All four are corrected in place and each correction says so in its own notes rather than being silently overwritten. The lesson generalises to every field paper in this file.
